en: The Great Collection Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja,
Scroll One. By the Duke of Su, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Special Advancement, [Li Hua].

The Imperially Enfeoffed Lord of Three Thousand Households, invested with the purple robe and posthumously honored as Minister of Works, bearing the posthumous title Dajian (Great Mirror), the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of the Great Guangzhi Daxingshan Monastery, translated by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling in the Tathāgata-realm Jewel-Adorned Maṇḍala. This maṇḍala was entirely sustained by the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgatas; it was accomplished through the outflow of great practices and the accumulation of vast stores of merit and wisdom.
It is the palace wherein all Bodhisattvas reside, and the place where the boundless, most profound Dharma is proclaimed.

This is also the sphere of the Tathāgata’s playful supernatural powers and unimpeded wisdom, which can give rise to vast skillful mindfulness and insight, entering the domain traversed by the wisdom of non-existence;
it extols immeasurable, supreme merits throughout the entirety of future worlds.

The Bhagavān has directly realized all phenomena; he turns the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma with equanimity and mastery; he is skillful in disciplining the assembly of disciples; he thoroughly understands the inclinations of all sentient beings; he has reached the further shore of all faculties; he has completely severed all afflictions, fetters, and habitual tendencies; and he spontaneously performs all buddha-activities without cessation.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of six million bhikṣus; all these bhikṣus were sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated. They had severed all fetters and bonds of affliction and were skilled in expounding all the most profound Buddha-dharmas.

Furthermore, they were able to penetrate the signless dharma (*animitta-dharma*), were upright, majestic, and uniquely endowed with dignified deportment, serving as a great field of merit and a place for growth, and dwelling well within the instructions and commands of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered from various buddha-fields; their number was immeasurable, inconceivable, beyond analogy, and ineffable.

In a single moment, these bodhisattvas sport within boundless Buddha-worlds, making offerings and serving all Tathāgatas; they exhort them to teach the Dharma and listen to it without weariness, constantly bringing all sentient beings to maturity.

Through skillful means, they are able to reach the supreme shore of purity, dwelling in unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) that transcends various conceptualizations and discursive proliferation (*prapañca*), their stages now adjacent to the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Their names were:

the Bodhisattva Vidyuddeva, the Bodhisattva Vijayin, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, the Bodhisattva Śūravīra, the Bodhisattva Vimatisamudghātin, the Bodhisattva Pradāśavikrāmin, the Bodhisattva Avalokitanetra, and the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta; he was accompanied by such leading Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas as these.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was expounding the profound Dharma of the Great Assembly for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the entire great assembly was situated in space, dwelling within precious pavilions. These pavilions were adorned with such supreme excellence that they were no different from the pavilions inhabited by the hosts of bodhisattvas in the Single-Jewel-Adorned Buddha-field within the Great Adornment World; each member of the assembly saw one another as they sat therein.

At that time, all forms and images within this trichiliocosm—including Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Jambudvīpa and the like, as well as villages, towns, cities, rivers, streams, springs, ponds, great oceans, groves, forests, grasses, trees, and all palaces situated upon the earth—were entirely obscured and no longer appeared.

The celestial palaces and all sentient beings of the desire realm, the form realm, the formless abodes, up to the Peak of Existence—including all categories of forms and colors—were likewise entirely non-apparent;
it was just as after the conflagration at the end of an eon, when the great earth has been consumed by fire and only empty space remains, with not a single form visible to the eye.

It was likewise so: within this trichiliocosm, there was not a single form or appearance that could be seen by the eyes of sentient beings, except for the forms and images of all those present in the assembly—the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others—who were clearly manifested within this jewel-adorned site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, within this place of enlightenment, a lion throne spontaneously emerged, measuring ten thousand *yojana* in height and breadth.

From this lion throne, pure radiance issued forth, universally illuminating the trichiliocosm and eclipsing the light of the sun, moon, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, such that all other lights no longer appeared.
The Buddha sat upon it.
At that time, the great assembly, having seen these extraordinary and most wondrous signs, leaped for joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, saying to one another:
"Such exquisite and skillful distinctions in the adornments of this sublime pavilion could not be fully described even if we were to live for an entire eon."

At that time, Śāriputra, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from the jeweled pavilion and stood in mid-air. He adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what cause and condition has this omen appeared first?

All forms and images within this trichiliocosm have been entirely obscured, becoming like the great void, while only these multi-storied pavilions adorned with various jewels where we now dwell have spontaneously manifested.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Do you now see this jeweled pavilion? He replied:
“I have seen it,” he replied. The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
"Are you able to fully praise the merits of this precious pavilion?
Śāriputra replied, "Even throughout the full span of my life, I could not exhaustively praise its true merits."

“In this way, Śāriputra! There is a world named Mahāvyūha (Great Adornment), wherein all the pavilions of exquisite jewels and all the assemblies dwell in mid-air; this present pavilion is manifested just like that.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where is that Great Adornment World located now?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

To the east, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in eight buddha-worlds, there is a world named Great Adornment. There, a Buddha named Single Jewel Adornment Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”
Śāriputra! For what reason is it called "Great Adornment"?
All the magnificent and sublime adornments within that world could not be fully described by me, even if I were to remain for the duration of an eon; therefore, it is named "Great Adornment."
Furthermore, for what reason is it named "Adorned with a Single Jewel"?
That Buddha constantly taught that only the great bodhicitta constitutes his jewel; therefore, it is named "Adorned with a Single Jewel."

That Buddha, while preaching the Dharma, ascended with the bodhisattvas onto a lion throne and a jeweled pavilion; they leaped into the air to a height of eighty koṭis of tāla trees, where he preached for the bodhisattvas the Seal of the Dharma on the Purity of Space:
"O sons of good family!..."
What is called the "Dharma Seal of the Purity of Space"?

It refers to the fact that all phenomena are free from both intrinsic nature and the absence of intrinsic nature. What does it mean to be free from intrinsic nature and the absence of intrinsic nature?
This means that all phenomena are without representation.
Why are they without representation?
Because all phenomena lack luminous manifestation.
What is meant by "lacking luminous manifestation"?
It means that all phenomena are far removed from objective conceptualization.
What is meant by "lacking objective conceptualization"?
It means that all phenomena have the characteristic of tranquility.
What is the characteristic of tranquility?
It means that all phenomena have the characteristic of non-duality.
What is meant by the absence of dual characteristics?
It means that all phenomena are free from differentiation.
What is meant by the absence of differentiation?
This means that all dharmas enter the characteristic of the single path.
How do they enter the characteristic of the single path?
It means that the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all dharmas are pure.
What is the purity of the characteristic of intrinsic nature?
It is because all phenomena transcend the three periods of time.
How do they transcend the three periods of time?
It means that all phenomena have no basis.
Why do they have no basis?
It means that all phenomena have no reflected image.
What is meant by "without image"?
It means that all phenomena transcend the sphere of cognitive objects.
What is meant by "transcending all spheres of cognitive objects"?
This means that all phenomena are pure internally and externally.
Why are they pure internally and externally?
It is because the nature of all phenomena is free from defilement.
What is meant by "absence of defilement"?
It refers to the fact that the nature of all phenomena is quiescent.
What is meant by "quiescent nature"?
It means that all phenomena are remote from mind, mentation, and consciousness.
How are they remote from mind, mentation, and consciousness?
It means that all phenomena possess the characteristic of transcendence and are fundamentally unarisen.
What is the characteristic of renunciation as being fundamentally unarisen?
It is because all phenomena are not grasped by a self. What is meant by "not grasped by a self"?
It means that all phenomena are without a master.
Why are they without a master?
It means that the nature of all phenomena is selfless.
What is the selflessness of nature?
It means that all phenomena are primordially pure.
What does "primordially pure" mean?
This means that all dharmas are fundamentally without nirvāṇa. Why is there no nirvāṇa?
Because the nature of all dharmas is like an illusion.
What is meant by "nature is like an illusion"?
It means that all phenomena lack substantial reality.
What is meant by "lacking substantial reality"?
It means that all phenomena lack the characteristic of volitional construction.
Why do they lack the characteristic of volitional construction?
It means that all phenomena are far removed from the characteristics of body and mind.
How does one distance oneself from the characteristics of body and mind?
It means that all phenomena are devoid of characteristics because they are signless (*animitta*).
How are they devoid of characteristics and signless?
It means that all phenomena are immovable in their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Why are they immovable in their own-characteristic?
Because all phenomena have no basis of reliance.
What is meant by "having no basis"?
It means that all phenomena have no object of perception.
What is meant by "having no object of perception"?
"This means that all phenomena are far removed from the ālayavijñāna. "Śāriputra!
That Tathāgata One Jewel Adornment taught these thirty-two seals of the purity of space for the sake of the bodhisattvas."
At that time, immeasurable bodhisattvas realized that the nature of all phenomena is equal to space, and they attained the pure wisdom-patience of mastery over dharmas. "Śāriputra!
All the bodhisattvas in that world of Great Adornment are adorned with generosity, for throughout immeasurable eons they have practiced relinquishment in accordance with the Dharma;..."
They are adorned with pure ethical discipline, because their bodies and minds are purified and free from all defilements;
they are adorned with patience, because they harbor no intent to harm any sentient being;
they are adorned with diligence, because they accumulate the provisions for all dharmas.
They are adorned with meditative concentration, for they sport in all liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments;
they are adorned with wisdom, for they have distanced themselves from all afflictions and habitual tendencies;
they are adorned with great compassion, for they rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
They are adorned with great compassion, because they do not abandon any sentient beings;
they are adorned with great joy, because they are constantly delighted by all sentient beings;
they are adorned with great equanimity, because they harbor neither hatred nor attachment toward any sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In that world of the Tathāgata Single Jewel Adornment, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahākāśagupta, who is adorned with great merit and great majestic power, and has attained unimpeded wisdom."

They adorn their bodies with the primary and secondary marks; they adorn their speech with eloquence; they adorn their minds with supreme meditative concentration; they adorn their mindfulness with extensive learning and dhāraṇī; they adorn their reality with impartial equanimity; they adorn the inclinations of all realms of existence with wisdom; they adorn their superior resolve with the application of progressive advancement, because they have reached a state free from doubt regarding all phenomena;
they adorn themselves with the bases of miraculous power, because they sport with mastery in the various supernormal knowledges;
and they adorn themselves with merit, because they have attained the virtue of the "jewel-hand" and constantly practice giving.
They are adorned with wisdom, because they discern the various inclinations of sentient beings;
they are adorned with awakening, because they cause all sentient beings to realize the sublime Dharma;
they are adorned with eyes, because they are able to attain purity in the five eyes.
They are adorned with the ear, for they hear the meanings of all dharmas like an echo;
they are adorned with the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), for they speak inexhaustibly regarding dharma, meaning, phrasing, and eloquence;
they are adorned with power, for they attain the ten powers of a Buddha and destroy the enmity of Māra.
They are adorned with fearlessness, for they crush all external doctrines without being cowed;
they are adorned with merit, for they have attained the boundless merits of a Buddha;
they are adorned with the Dharma, for they manifest the Dharma from every pore like echoes.
They are adorned with clarity, because they are able to perceive the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas;
they are adorned with light, because they illuminate all Buddha-fields;
they are adorned with the knowledge of others' minds, because they are free from error.
They are adorned with instruction and admonition, so that one acts according to what has been taught;
they are adorned with supernormal power, manifesting all manner of diverse forms;
they are adorned with the praise of all Buddhas, abiding without attachment and attaining mastery.
"Adorned with all wholesome dharmas, he enters the realm of all Buddha-dharmas.
Śāriputra! That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja has accomplished such immeasurable merit."
Together with these bodhisattvas, they have resolved to come to this Sahā world in order to behold me, to pay homage, to prostrate, to serve, and to make offerings;

furthermore, it is for the sake of expounding this subtle dharma-gate of the Great Assembly, so that all the bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions may give rise to great joy and pure faith and delight;
and also so that the bodhisattvas may embrace and fully master the path of the Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāgaganagañja, surrounded by twelve koṭis of bodhisattvas before and behind him, gazed with single-minded devotion upon the Tathāgata Ekaratnavyūha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha; I pray that you will grant me your permission.
That Buddha replied, "Now is precisely the right time; go as you intend."
Immediately, having prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Single-Jewel Adornment, he stood facing him and thought:
"I rely upon the Buddha’s miraculous power of non-action.

Vanishing from that land, he suddenly disappeared; in the space of a single thought-moment, together with a multitude of bodhisattvas, he arrived here at the Jewel-Adorned Bodhimanda in this Sahā world.
Abiding in the void, they scattered various exquisite flowers and perfumes upon that world like falling rain,
namely: powdered incense, unguents, banners and streamers, silk canopies, moon-flowers,
great moon-flowers, most excellent flowers, sun-moon light-flowers, sun-lamp flowers, sun-essence flowers, and beloved flowers.
The great-love flower, the radiant flower, the *sattva* flower, the most excellent and wondrous *sattva* flower,
the universally stainless flower, the pure and stainless flower, the gold-light radiant flower, the space-radiant flower,
the great white fragrance-radiant-tactile flower, the hundred-petaled thousand-stamen flower, and the sorrow-removing flower.
Flowers that produce joy, flowers praised by the devas, dragon flowers, flowers that give rise to bliss and joy, flowers of dhyāna-branches,
flowers that bring happiness to the body, flowers that gladden the mind, flowers whose fragrance pervades the trichiliocosm,
flowers that pacify and eliminate all illnesses, flowers adorned with wondrous majesty, and flowers that flow forth boundless merit.
Virtue-flowers and Bodhisattva-flowers that illuminate and touch the ten directions rained down in such various wonderful forms,
piling up until they reached the height of the knees, pervading the entire trichiliocosm.
At that time, the great assembly, having seen these flowers, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
These various kinds of most excellent and wonderful flowers and the manifold exquisite music have never been seen nor heard before; from where have they come?"
"I pray that you will grant me an exposition.

The Buddha said, "It is that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha, who has come from the world-system of Great Adornment to this assembly. Remaining in mid-air, he first rained down such sublime and wondrous flowers as an offering to me and to this Dharma of the sutra."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāgaganagañja, together with the accompanying bodhisattvas, descended from the sky, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and stood to one side, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

That Tathāgata Ekaratnavyūha inquires after the World-Honored One’s health, asking whether he has little ailment and little affliction, whether his daily life is light and easy, and whether he dwells in peace and happiness.

Here are twelve koṭis of bodhisattvas who were formerly transformed and guided by the World-Honored One; they have come together with me to this Sahā world for the purpose of hearing the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.
That World-Honored One [sent them] because he wishes to cause these bodhisattvas to attain mastery over all dharmas.
"In order to accomplish the Great Dharma, we pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and accept us, and for our sake expound such profound essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja immediately manifested a great precious canopy in mid-air, adorned with various jewels, which covered the crown of the Tathāgata’s head; its radiance shone forth, pervading the ten directions. He then ascended the Tathāgata’s lion throne, a seat ten thousand *yojanas* high and wide.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha joined his palms in reverence and praised the Buddha with these verses:
"O Honored One of supreme Dharma, merit, and wondrous wisdom, Pure, stainless, and immeasurable;
Equal to space, tranquil and unmoving— I pay homage to you, the profound and peerless."
He can manifest the subtle and wondrous colors of physical forms, yet without departing from the Dharma-body he appears in these bodies;
his compassionate response to sentient beings is likewise such that he universally manifests forms adorned with a hundred merits.
Having already transcended sound, there is neither hearing nor seeing; having severed all speech, there is nothing to be taught or shown.
Though knowing the nature of words is like an echo in space, one expounds them through the heart of great compassion.
With a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, Knowing that the mind is like an illusion and lacks intrinsic nature;
Fully knowing that mental activities are devoid of discursive thought, One takes this ultimate, impartial mind as one's own mind.
Manifesting in various ways to deliver the world, the physical form of the Sugata is ultimately ungraspable;
yet by means of the essence of his wondrous support and merit, he manifests a body according to the inclinations of beings.
In the Dharma there is nothing to be attained, and the Buddha is likewise; He does not cling to phenomena and is free from conceptual discrimination.
Knowing that the Dharma can deliver sentient beings, He preaches it as appropriate to their needs, constantly and without interruption.
The great assembly collectively beholds the Buddha’s body; The manifested forms and characteristics are all distinct.
The World-Honored One has already transcended the marks of body and mind; Whatever he manifests brings joy to the multitude.
All phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are false conceptualizations and not real.
By knowing that all phenomena are thus, one attains perfect enlightenment and realizes nirvana.
Having severed conceptual discrimination and transcended the extremes of middle and end, one knows that all things are empty, quiescent, and devoid of intrinsic nature;
though knowing the nature of all phenomena to be pure, one skillfully explains the fruits of karma without any contradiction.
In the Dharma there are no sentient beings, no life-span, and no persons; it is tranquil like space, devoid of names and designations.
Having realized that these sentient beings do not truly exist, he causes them all to enter the gate of the Deathless.
Having already cultivated billions of inconceivable practices, you sought the unsurpassed path with diligence;
through these causes and conditions, you have now accomplished your task and reached the realm of non-action, awakening to nirvana.
The wondrous awakening to the nature of all phenomena is without distinction; it is equal across the superior, middling, and inferior.
Abiding in the wisdom of equality, one is free from discrimination; therefore, the Buddha is always without an unsettled mind.
Knowing that the aggregates, bases, and elements are all like illusions, And that the three realms are like the moon reflected in water;
That sentient beings are like dreams, their nature not real— For them, he preaches such dharmas that are not real.
In conventional truth, one speaks of attaining supreme enlightenment; yet it cannot be said that there is a mark of attainment or non-attainment.
Bodhi is without attainment, and the wheel is likewise: its turning is without the mark of turning, for there is nothing to be turned.
Having crossed over oneself, one leads others to the other shore; having liberated oneself, one liberates others from all fetters and delusions.
Having established oneself in peace, one establishes others in the Mahāyāna; both self and others together realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings are neither born nor do they perish; sentient beings are primordially and eternally pure.
The intrinsic nature of sentient beings is like an illusory form; once sentient beings awaken to this, they realize bodhi.
Form is like space, without arising; all worlds are likewise so.
This dharma is formless and free from the marks of form; by knowing this meaning, form is seen as quiescent.
Praising the Tathāgata’s virtues through metaphors, sentient beings who hear this praise all feel deep devotion;
the Buddha’s virtues are like space, immeasurable—this is the true, non-dual praise of the Buddha.
I pay homage to the one who awakens all sentient beings, Who is without observation, without mind, and reaches the state of non-attainment;
Only the Buddhas can praise the Buddha— I pay homage to the Honored One of Suchness and True Virtue.
Realizing that all sentient beings are devoid of self or person, and that the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas is of a single characteristic;
knowing that all phenomena are characterized by the departure from desire, I therefore make offerings to the Honored One of Equanimity.

At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāgaganagañja immediately caused the jeweled pavilion of the wondrous jewel-adorned bodhimaṇḍa to tremble in six ways. A voice issued from the sky, saying:

"World-Honored One Śākyamuni, all the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that you have accumulated over countless koṭis, nayutas, and hundreds of thousands of kalpas—this Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja is able to extol them all through these sublime verses."
"Good son! If one has not even heard of this in a dream, how much less could one see it?

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing these verses, can give rise to faith and understanding, and having understood them, practice accordingly, you should know that such persons will before long be able to roar the lion’s roar, just like the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Desiring to hear the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, I have come to this Sahā world to behold the World-Honored One, to pay homage, to make offerings, and to listen to this Dharma.”
Now, among those noble beings who have gathered here in this assembly, each harbors doubts regarding the Dharma.
We pray that the World-Honored One will cause them to attain the light of the Dharma regarding all phenomena and give rise to definitive wisdom.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
I now wish to inquire about the definitive meaning; I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me a small measure of skillful means.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This one of unimpeded wisdom thoroughly knows the prior and subsequent ripening of the faculties of all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One has attained illumination because he is free from all darkness and delusion.
The World-Honored One knows the meaning because he is skillfully able to discern the meanings of all phrases.
The World-Honored One knows the proper time because he bestows predictions without overstepping the opportune moment.
The World-Honored One is "one who knows the appropriate" because he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to what is suitable for them.
The World-Honored One is "one who sports" because he has attained mastery over all supernormal powers.
The World-Honored One is the Pure Observer, for he understands the mental activities of sentient beings as clearly as if they were in the palm of his hand.
The World-Honored One is the Lofty and Great, for none are able to see the crown of his head.
The World-Honored One is the Valiant and Courageous, for within the trichiliocosm, none are able to surpass or subdue him.
The World-Honored One is self-enlightened, for he has realized all dharmas without a teacher.
The World-Honored One is the guide, for he reveals the correct path among all paths.

The World-Honored One is the Great King of Physicians, for by means of the nectar-like medicine he is able to eternally eliminate and sever the diseases of sentient beings’ afflictions, hindrances, and obscurations.
The World-Honored One possesses great power, for he has attained the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, up to and including the three types of supernormal knowledge.
The World-Honored One, the Great Fearless One, utters the great lion’s roar without fear amidst all the world’s śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, and brahmās.

The World-Honored One, having accomplished the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), has attained the body of unimpeded wisdom regarding the three periods of time, as well as the purity of body, speech, and mind, the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), liberations, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; such are his unique qualities.
The World-Honored One abides in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), for with unimpeded wisdom he observes all sentient beings equally, just like space.
The World-Honored One abides in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), for with impartial wisdom he remains unmoved by the good or evil deeds, or the suffering and happiness, of all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One abides in great joy because he practices meditative concentration and liberation to reach the other shore.
The World-Honored One abides in great equanimity because his mind is free from hatred and love, like empty space.
The World-Honored One dwells in equanimity because he has entered the equanimous wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
The World-Honored One is without expectation because his wisdom is fully perfected and he remains far removed from fame and profit.
The World-Honored One, the All-Knowing One, possesses the purity of the five eyes and perceives all phenomena to their ultimate conclusion.

I know that the World-Honored One has accomplished such immeasurable and boundless merits; because we now delight in the Dharma, we wish to inquire briefly regarding this teaching, so that all sentient beings may, through skillful means, give rise to the wisdom of omniscience within the Dharma of equality.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, O Noble Being!”
"You have already received the prediction of enlightenment from as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
I now grant you permission to ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you in detail so that you may attain joy."
Thereupon, among the assembly, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Guṇarājaprabha, who asked the bodhisattva Gaganagañja:
"For what reason do you question the Tathāgata?"
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja replied with these verses:
"With a universal mind equal toward all sentient beings, With a wondrous mind dwelling equally on the further shore,
Awakening to the mindless mind and entering the subtle principle— For this reason, I question the World-Honored One."
Having attained light, free from darkness and pure, you are without doubt and able to sever all perplexity;
in order that others may attain certain liberation, I therefore ask the World-Honored One.
Knowing that both self and non-self are entirely pure, They constantly benefit sentient beings while abiding in non-self;
Liberating sentient beings from the bonds of the view of self— It is for their sake that I question the World-Honored One.
Your majestic deportment is well-established in pure discipline; your intention is as pure as space.
Firm and unshakable like Mount Meru, it is for this reason that I question you, the possessor of merit.
With boundless diligence and courageous non-retrogression, you are able to crush the host of Māra’s enemies—the pride within;
having purified yourself and cleansed others of the entanglements of affliction, I therefore inquire of you, O Exalted One.
Delighting in hearing of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence; Of meditative concentration, liberation, and the manifestation of the various supernormal powers;
And of the stainless, supreme wisdom that is pure and luminous— Therefore, I inquire about the meaning of purity.
Abiding in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, you manifest both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa;
being without arising, without abiding, and without coming or going, I therefore question you, O One of Pure Wisdom.
Your profound insight is boundless, reaching beyond śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all other multitudes;
none can challenge or fathom it, and thus I ask the World-Honored One such a question.
Delighting in the True Dharma and able to penetrate it, taking neither dharma nor non-dharma;
with a mind never distracted from wholesome dharmas—for this reason, I ask the Tathāgata about the Dharma.
O worthy sirs who perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas, who are able to protect the True Dharma and the Saṅgha;
whose fame is renowned throughout the three worlds and praised by all Buddhas— therefore, I question you, O ocean of merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, having answered the Bodhisattva Puṇyarājaprabhāsa with these verses, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of generosity so that it is like space?
How does one practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom so that they are like space?
How does one practice the two kinds of adornments—merit and wisdom—so that they are like space?

How does one not abandon the recollection of the Buddha, nor abandon the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of renunciation, the recollection of ethical discipline, and the recollection of the devas?
How does a bodhisattva practice all deeds such that they are equal to nirvāṇa?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the modes of conduct of all sentient beings?
How can one uphold the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma, knowing the nature and characteristics of those dharmas as they truly are, just as a Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to them?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully bring to maturity sentient beings who are originally pure?
How does a bodhisattva practice the Buddha-dharma in accordance with reality until reaching its ultimate consummation?
How does a bodhisattva possess indestructible supernormal powers and attain mastery over all phenomena?
How does a bodhisattva abide in the profound principle of the Buddha-dharma, which cannot be fathomed by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha?
How does a bodhisattva enter the skillful knowledge of dependent origination and remain far removed from all extreme views?
How does a bodhisattva, by means of the seal of the Tathāgata, seal true suchness with unceasing skillful knowledge?
How does a bodhisattva enter the profound principle of the dharmadhātu and perceive all phenomena as mutually pervasive, equal, and of a single nature?
How does a bodhisattva’s resolve become as firm as a vajra, such that they are unshakable regarding this Mahāyāna?
How does a bodhisattva become pure within their own sphere, just like the sphere of a Buddha?
How does a bodhisattva attain dhāraṇīs and never forget the practice of the Dharma?
How does a bodhisattva obtain the unhindered eloquence empowered by the Tathāgata?
How does a bodhisattva attain mastery within the cycle of birth and death?
How does a bodhisattva subdue adversaries and transcend the four māras?
How does a bodhisattva accumulate immeasurable provisions of merit to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva, appearing in a world where no Buddha exists, perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva attain the ocean-seal samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) and remain untainted by the mental activities of all sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva attain freedom from defiled attachment, with a mind like space or wind, free from all obstructions?

How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the proper conduct, practicing so as to leave darkness behind and obtain illumination, attaining spontaneous wisdom without depending on external conditions, and swiftly reaching the omniscience of the Great Vehicle?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, O Noble Being!”
He spoke again: "Excellent, excellent,
O noble being!"
You have now skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning, able to pose such a question for the sake of sentient beings.

You are capable of clearly understanding all Buddha-dharmas; you have already made offerings to and served immeasurable Buddhas of the past, having planted roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas; you have donned the armor of diligence and sought the Dharma without weariness;
with the staff of wisdom, you have emerged from the realms of Māra, and you always delight in benefiting all sentient beings.
You have transcended the eight worldly dharmas of praise and blame, and your mental conduct is as equanimous as space;
you have long since accumulated the wisdom of all-knowledge, and the limit of your merit is immeasurable;
you have already inquired about this meaning in the presence of past Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Therefore, noble son, listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall analyze and explain for you the merits obtained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, leading to the omniscience of the Great Vehicle.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja replied:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We are eager and desirous to hear it.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying: "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, their cultivation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) is like space."
What are the four? They are:
because the self is pure, sentient beings are pure;
Because sentient beings are pure, giving is pure;
because giving is pure, dedication is pure;
because dedication is pure, awakening is pure.
“Good son! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the practice of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) so that it is like empty space.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they are able to purify the practice of the perfection of generosity.”
What are the eight? They are as follows:
giving with a pure self;
The purity of my own self;
the purity of the cause;
the purity of the view.
Giving purified by its characteristics;
giving purified by its distinct characteristics;
and giving purified by not expecting a karmic reward.
Giving with a mind as equanimous as space and pure—
this is the eighth dharma by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the practice of the perfection of giving.
“Good son! Just as space has no boundaries, so too is the boundless practice of giving by a bodhisattva.
Just as space is vast, expansive, and unobstructed, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving through dedication.”
Just as space is formless, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving while detached from form.
Just as space has no recipient, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving while detached from reception.
Just as space is without any attachment, so too is the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving when free from attachment.
Just as space is without any conditioned activity, so too is the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving when free from the conditioned.
Just as space is devoid of conceptualization and perception, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving when free from conceptualization and perception.

Just as space pervades all buddha-fields, so too does the bodhisattva’s great compassion pervade all sentient beings throughout buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges when practicing giving.
Just as space is inexhaustible, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving dedicated to the uninterrupted lineage of the Three Jewels.
Just as space is free from darkness, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving free from the darkness of afflictions.
Just as space manifests without characteristics, so too is the essence of the Bodhisattva’s mind pure when practicing generosity.
Just as space contains all things, so too does the Bodhisattva’s practice of generosity universally embrace all sentient beings.

Furthermore, just as a conjured person gives to another who is conjured—without conceptualizing or hoping for a reward—the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving is likewise: all is like an illusion or a conjuration, transcending subject and object, and free from the hope for karmic fruition.

"Good son! When a bodhisattva practices generosity, he abandons all afflictions through superior wisdom, yet does not abandon sentient beings through the wisdom of skillful means. This is how a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the perfection of generosity is like space."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dīpāṅkara, who was present in the assembly, rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
by what characteristics does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice this perfection of giving?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice this perfection of giving with non-characteristic (animitta).”
Why is this? Because all dharmas lack the characteristic of a body, for the characteristic of a body is pure;
they lack the characteristic of a sentient being, for the characteristic of a sentient being is pure.
There is no characteristic of dharmas, because the characteristic of dharmas is pure;
there is no characteristic of knowledge, because the characteristic of knowledge is pure;
there is no characteristic of wisdom, because the characteristic of wisdom is pure.
There is no characteristic of mind, because the characteristic of mind is pure;
there is no characteristic of the world, because the characteristic of the world is pure;
there is no characteristic of form, because the characteristic of form is pure.
There is no perception of signs, because the perception of signs is pure;
thus, up to and including, there is neither darkness nor light, being free from all signs.

Having reached the ultimate limit of signlessness, one attains inexhaustible patience (*akṣayakṣānti*), receives the definitive prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of a Tathāgata, and dwells in the bodhisattva stage of *niyama*. Sealed with the seal of non-retrogression, one receives the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of a Buddha, accomplishes all equal Buddha-dharmas, and thoroughly knows the modes of conduct of all sentient beings.
"In this manner, the bodhisattva practices the perfection of generosity.

When this Dharma was spoken, sixteen thousand bodhisattvas perceived the nature of all phenomena within all phenomena as being like space, and they attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"With a mind always pure, one constantly practices giving; Seeking enlightenment, one expects no reward.
Having given, one rejoices without regret; This is the sublime giving that attains liberation."
The wise know that all phenomena are like illusions; They disregard their own bodies, lives, and wealth;
They harbor no craving for any other requisites, Their resolve upon the Buddha’s bodhi being firm and certain.
Bestowing gifts equally upon all without hatred or affection, they do not give rise to despondency but constantly practice with progress;
because they contemplate all phenomena as being like space, they have neither joy nor weariness.
Knowing that the nature and characteristics of phenomena are fundamentally pure, so too are awakening and giving;
because no greed arises toward what is given, one is thus able to constantly relinquish all conceptual proliferation.
Bestowing equally and universally, free from conceptual thought, they make no distinction between superior, middling, or inferior;
their intention is pure and ever stainless, and all their giving is free from expectation.
Knowing that the body is an illusion and entirely impermanent, and that wealth is as unsubstantial as a dream or a flash of lightning, they give rise to compassion for the world;
thus, they are able to constantly practice giving while remaining unstained by the worldly realm.
Giving with the practice of non-self purifies afflictions, and one is thus able to establish the Buddha’s teachings;
Māra finds no opportunity to exploit such a person— the merit of such a mind of giving is difficult to measure.
This mind of giving taught by the One of Ten Powers Should abide in the practice of pure ethical discipline;
Through this, one well-cultivates meditative concentration, And wisdom can then be swiftly perfected.
Generosity and precepts purify both body and mind; they burn away all fetters so they do not arise again.
Both self and others obtain benefit, and one is able to attain the bliss of unconditioned nirvana.
To eliminate the fetters of greed, one practices giving; therefore, one is neither defiled nor attached.
By bestowing gifts so that others are free from suffering, one personally accomplishes the cause for pure bodhi.
In the mind of one who practices giving, there is no retreat; through this, they come to see the nature of bodhi.
Having seen the pure virtues of bodhi, they are then able to deliver immeasurable multitudes.

By Imperial Decree: At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāākāśagarbha, saying:
