When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, their cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) is like space.
What are these four? They are as follows:
Knowing the body to be like a reflection;
knowing sound to be like an echo;
knowing the mind to be like a magical illusion.
Wisdom is like space.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), practicing it so that it is like space.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they are able to purify the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline.
What are the eight? They are:
the purity of precepts because one does not depart from the bodhicitta;
They attain an immeasurable mind by being free from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because their ethical discipline is pure;
they do not abandon any points of training, because their wisdom is pure;
and they take birth in all places, because their vows are pure.
It is effortless and spontaneous regarding the precepts because conduct is pure;
it is dedicated toward enlightenment because the mind of Māra is purified;
and it is free from feverish affliction because the defilements are purified.
Because their great vows are fulfilled and their awakening is pure.
These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
“Good son! Just as space is pure, so too is the purity of the bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts;
just as space is free from defilement, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts free from defilement.”
Just as space is tranquil and undisturbed, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts tranquil;
just as space has no boundaries, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts boundless;
just as space has no attachments, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts unattached.
Just as space is without attachment, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts free from attachment;
just as space cannot be accumulated, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts without accumulation;
just as space does not depart from its intrinsic nature, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts non-departing.
Just as the nature of space is eternally abiding, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts eternally abiding;
just as space is ultimately inexhaustible, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts inexhaustible;
just as space has no form or appearance, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts free from signs.
Just as space has no coming or going, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts unshakable;
just as space is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts free from proliferation;
just as space is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*), so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts without outflows.
Just as space is devoid of purposeful action, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts unconditioned;
just as space is subject to no change, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts immutable;
just as space is free from discrimination, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts without grasping.
Just as space pervades all places, so too does the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts pervade everywhere;
just as space cannot be destroyed, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts free from transgression;
just as space has no high or low, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts impartial.
Just as the nature of space is free from defilement, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of ethical discipline free from defilement. Noble son,
this is how a bodhisattva practices the perfection of pure ethical discipline, which is like space.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Guarding the precepts with a tranquil mind free from defilement, One can eliminate the feverish afflictions through non-attainment;
With no blemish in the actions of body, speech, and mind, All forms of restraint are fully perfected."
The wise do not become arrogant or heedless because of their precepts; their inner minds are ever tranquil and undisturbed.
The wise always rely upon the bodhicitta, remaining unstained by mental attachments.
Distant from all karma and free from discursive thought, one thus gives rise to no conceptual distinctions;
having departed from blue, yellow, red, and white, one likewise does not abide within name-and-form.
Without grasping, without abandoning, and with an undefiled mind, It is like space, free from all obstructions;
This precept is praised by the wise, Yet they do not perceive any referential meaning in that which is praised.
This precept can cause the mind to be tranquil, And it can also pacify all afflictions;
Fully attaining the ultimate limit of śamatha and vipaśyanā, It clearly manifests the attainment of liberation.
The noble ones who have liberated themselves from all bonds are entirely established in ethical discipline (śīla);
therefore, discipline is the supreme liberation and the fundamental word for awakening.
Those who observe the dhūta practices and dwell in forest hermitages, Having few desires and being content, they sever all greedy seeking;
Remaining in meditation far removed from bustle and clamor, Their minds attain pliancy and are freed from afflictions.
Such ethical discipline is the very root; it is the phrase for contemplating tranquility and liberation.
Therefore, śīla is an adornment, and in all places, it is the path to peace and happiness.
They also cause one to distance oneself from distraction, severing all afflictions and views;
with a mind of loving-kindness pervading like space, they are able to still extremist attachments and bring about purification.
Because they are determined never to forsake bodhi, they remain free from conceptual discrimination regarding bodhi;
if the wise possess such virtues, it is all due to their having reached the other shore through ethical discipline (śīla).
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, his cultivation of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) will be like space.
What are these four?
That is to say:
when others revile one, one does not retaliate, knowing that speech is like empty space;
when others strike one, one does not retaliate, knowing that the body is like empty space.
He does not retaliate against anger, knowing that the mind is like empty space;
he does not retaliate against restlessness or frivolity, knowing that the mental faculty is like empty space.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), practicing it so that it is like empty space.
"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they are able to purify the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
What are these eight? They are as follows:..."
The mind toward all sentient beings is unimpeded like space, because one attains purity through the practice of patience;
one does not give rise to greedy attachment toward any gain or honor like space, because one attains purity through the practice of patience;
and one’s benefit for all sentient beings is impartial like space, because one attains purity through the practice of patience.
Body and mind are indestructible, like space, because one attains purity through the practice of patience;
one is free from all fetters of affliction, like space, because one attains purity through the practice of patience;
one is free from the objects of observation, like space, because one attains purity through the practice of patience.
One contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing, being like empty space, because by practicing patience one attains purity;
one universally contemplates form and the formless with loving-kindness, being like empty space, because by practicing patience one attains purity.
"These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) so that it is like space. 'Good son!
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas by which one can thoroughly observe and practice the perfection of patience.'"
What are these eight? They are:
patience in the emptiness of nature, because it does not destroy various views;
patience in signlessness, because it does not discard signs;
Patience without aspiration, because it does not abandon bodhi;
patience without activity, because it does not exhaust the conditioned;
patience without arising, because it does not dwell in the unconditioned.
Patience without arising, because it does not abide in birth and cessation;
patience without sentient beings, because it does not destroy the essential nature;
patience as suchness (*tathatā*), because it does not destroy the three periods of time.
In this way, son of good family,
these are the eight kinds of patient acceptance through the thorough investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-kṣānti) by which one can cultivate the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Furthermore, son of good family:
When practicing the perfection of patience, if someone were to revile or abuse me, I would endure it; this is called my patience, but it is not the perfection of patience.
If one perceives the one who reviles and the method of reviling, and thinks, "I shall endure this," it is called my patience, but it is not the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Abiding in conduct free from contention is the patience of sound (*ghoṣa-kṣānti*), but it is not the perfection of patience.

When one performs such preparatory application, both "self" and "other" are empty; one contemplates and endures the impermanence of self and other. This contemplative endurance is termed the "provisional patience" (*prajñapti-kṣānti*), not the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
"Good son! One does not see at all a 'one who acts' or a 'that which is acted upon.

It is like a great sāl forest; if someone were to take a sharp axe and enter that forest to cut its branches and leaves, that tree would never give rise to even a single thought of mind, thinking, 'this one is the cutter' and 'this is what is being cut,' nor would it produce feelings of aversion or affection."

"Good son! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), it is likewise thus: there is neither hatred nor love; there is no capacity for discrimination and no object of discrimination. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the perfection of patience being like empty space."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Knowledge of exhaustion and the pure patience regarding non-arising, The mind achieves non-attachment toward objects;
Inner and outer tranquility without dependence, A pure mind and patience equal to space."
This body is like a shadow, like grass and trees; its form and mind are like illusions, lacking any reality.
This nature of phenomena is empty and nothing can be seen; the transformations of body and mind are equal to that.
Whether faced with slander or praise, there is neither joy nor anger; without discrimination, there is no sense of high or low.
Knowing patience to be like the earth and like a door-sill, one relies on the teaching of forbearance to deliver sentient beings.

Although one knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty—devoid of person, self, or life-span—one does not contradict causes, conditions, and volitional formations; this patience is the most authentic practice.
Hearing those evil words, do not give way to anger; know that the nature of speech is like space.
Cultivate the emptiness of body and mind in the same way; thus should one purify sentient beings by practicing this patience.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of diligence so that it is like space?
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they practice the perfection of diligence so that it is like space.”
What are the four? They are:
diligently cultivating roots of goodness, because one knows that all phenomena are not yet perfected;
They perform great offerings to all Buddhas because they realize the equality of the Tathāgatas’ bodies;
they constantly delight in bringing immeasurable sentient beings to fulfillment because they know that sentient beings are ungraspable;
and they receive and uphold the true Dharma from all Buddhas because they do not perceive any phenomena as objects to be weary of or renounced.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) so that it is like space.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they are able to purify the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). What are these eight?
By adorning the body, they practice diligence with vigor, knowing that the body is like a shadow, for it is unapprehendable like a reflected image.
One practices with diligent vigor by adorning speech, because one knows that speech is like dew and its nature is unattainable;
one practices with diligent vigor by adorning the mind, because one attains meditative concentration through knowing that the mind is unattainable;
and one practices with diligent vigor to fulfill the factors of the various pāramitās, practicing them progressively and contemplating their unattainability.
They practice with diligent vigor because they contemplate the nature and characteristics of bodhi as being unattainable, thereby accomplishing all factors conducive to enlightenment;
they practice with diligent vigor for the sake of purifying buddha-fields, knowing that all buddha-lands are equal to space and are ultimately unattainable;
they practice with diligent vigor to accomplish the retention of everything heard, knowing that the teachings heard are like echoes and are ultimately unattainable.

In order to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, one practices with diligent vigor, knowing that all dharma-realms are equal and of a single characteristic, because one contemplates their non-apprehensibility.
These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the practice of the perfection of diligence. "Good son!
Furthermore, there are two kinds of diligence for a bodhisattva, namely:
There is the diligence of application and the diligence of limitation.
By means of the diligence of application, one exerts the body, speech, and mind to cultivate and accomplish all wholesome dharmas, remaining without abiding because one contemplates non-apprehension.

By means of disciplined and balanced diligence, one should abide in neither emerging nor entering; following the dharma-realm without coming or going, one is like empty space because there is nothing to be attained.

Just as space, though devoid of form, accomplishes the tasks for all sentient beings, so too is the diligence of a bodhisattva; by relying upon the qualities of all Buddhas, it accomplishes all matters concerning sentient beings.
Just as space contains all forms, so too does the bodhisattva’s diligence contain all sentient beings while remaining free from all views.
Just as all grasses and trees grow in space without roots and without dwelling, so too does the bodhisattva’s diligence give rise to all Buddha-dharmas while not abiding in the view of a self.
Just as space pervades all places without being shaken, so too is the bodhisattva’s diligence in all wholesome dharmas, having no sign of movement.

Just as space manifests various forms and colors, so too it is with the bodhisattva’s diligence and other qualities: for the sake of sentient beings, they manifest the cultivation of equanimous contemplation, yet all these are without apprehension.
“Good son! This is how a bodhisattva practices the perfection of diligence so that it is like space.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Through the power of diligence born of valor, He is without stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth;
Able to practice the majestic Great Enlightenment, He constantly benefits all sentient beings.
The benefits of the merit cultivated in the past, one practices constantly without weariness;
loving and delighting in the liberation of all sentient beings, one always makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
May I travel through immeasurable Buddha-fields, Subduing all the māras;
Always delighting in giving to all people, Always delighting in upholding the pure precepts,
Always delighting in patience conjoined with great compassion, And always delighting in diligently accumulating all roots of goodness.
Contemplating the mind of immeasurable meditative concentration, Constantly observing with great wisdom,
Abandoning anger through immeasurable loving-kindness, One practices correctly for the benefit of merit;
Without stinginess regarding body or life, One is well able to liberate oneself from all afflictions.
Constantly cultivating the liberation of non-self and emptiness, possessing great majesty that is free from marks and signless;
forever departing from all views to cultivate bodhi, observing self-nature as being like an illusion or a mirage.
Delighting in preaching the dharma of emptiness without conceptual thought, one relies on pure worldly conduct to study the various sutras;
having abandoned both existence and non-existence regarding phenomena, one does not discard sounds or written characters.
One should constantly expound various sutras in the world, and praise the boundless merits of the Buddha;
since the mental activities of sentient beings are difficult to fathom, the wise should give rise to great diligence.
Awakened to the nature of immeasurable sentient beings, They do not linger in birth or non-birth;
With a mind of boundless diligence, They constantly practice the pure dharmas for delivering beings.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) so that it is like space?
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration so that it is like space.”
What are the four? They are:
settling the mind within, so that the inner mind perceives nothing;
Restraining the mind toward external objects, one finds nothing to be grasped externally;
because one’s own mind is equanimous, one knows that the minds of all sentient beings are likewise equanimous;
and both those minds and the contemplation of their equanimity are realized to be like illusions and transformations.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the practice of the dhyāna-pāramitā so that it is like space.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they are able to purify the practice of the dhyāna-pāramitā.
What are these eight?
They are as follows:
They do not practice meditative concentration by relying on the aggregates;
they do not practice meditative concentration by relying on the sense bases;
they do not practice meditative concentration by relying on the elements.
He does not practice meditative concentration based on the present world;
he does not practice meditative concentration based on other worlds;
he does not practice meditative concentration based on the realm of desire.
One practices meditative concentration without relying on the form realm;
one practices meditative concentration without relying on the formless realm.
These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration, making it like space.
"Furthermore, noble son, a bodhisattva purifies meditative concentration through a focused mind.
What is meant by 'focused'? "

Regarding the names and designations of phenomena, there is neither subtraction nor addition; there is no alteration and no differentiation; no loss and no gain; no grasping and no relinquishing; no darkness and no light; no conceptualization and yet not non-conceptualization; no perception and no mental engagement; no oneness, no twoness, and no absence of one or two; no movement, no volition, and no proliferation; no accumulation and no absence of accumulation; and without contemplating any signs, the mind has no place of abiding—this is called single-minded concentration.
With focused concentration, the mind does not wander; because it is detached from forms, the eye, and visual consciousness, its own characteristic is pure.
With focused concentration on contemplative practice, the mind does not wander; because it is detached from sounds, the ear, and auditory consciousness, its own characteristic is pure.
With focused concentration, the mind does not wander; because it is detached from odors, the nose, and olfactory consciousness, its own characteristic is pure.
With focused mind, not wandering, it is pure in its own characteristic through detachment from taste, tongue, and gustatory consciousness;
with focused mind, not wandering, it is pure in its own characteristic through detachment from touch, body, and tactile consciousness;
with focused mind, not wandering, it is pure in its own characteristic through detachment from mental objects, mind, and mental consciousness.
“Good son! For example, just as space is not burned during the conflagration at the end of a kalpa, nor moistened during the calamity of water;
so too, when a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration, he is not consumed by the fires of any afflictions.
He is swept away by the waters of all liberations, samādhis, meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and dhyānas.

Constantly and without interruption, he causes sentient beings who are distracted and agitated to dwell in dhyāna; yet he does not give rise to attachment to the flavor of those dhyānas, and likewise when emerging from them, he remains free from further hindrance.
He constantly manifests tranquility before all noble ones, yet this is not something achieved through the diligent efforts of those who are not noble.
He causes the concentrated mind to abide in equanimity, while for those who lack such equanimity, he teaches the Dharma to guide and transform them.
Not perceiving equality or inequality, and not being in opposition to the equal or the unequal,
their mind is unimpeded like space; for this reason, they are called practitioners of dhyāna-samādhi,
and are also called practitioners of dhyāna-samādhi with supreme wisdom.
They are also called those who practice meditative concentration by not abiding in consciousness.
By virtue of this concentration, those bodhisattvas attain such non-abiding meditative concentration that is like space.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Guarding the sense faculties well and practicing meditative concentration, Always settled in samādhi, unattached to sentient beings;
Abiding in equanimity and impartiality to cross over the world, Constantly dwelling in peace, both internally and externally.”
Not relying on the aggregates, sense bases, or elements, they dwell in tranquility, far removed from sensory objects;
the wise keep their minds constantly in meditative absorption, remaining equanimous toward both the equal and the unequal.
Reaching the Dharma-realm where there is no high or low, they see that both mind and intellect are utterly tranquil;
yet, for the sake of bringing accomplishment to the world, they manifest various dhyānas and transformations.
They are free from change and possess meditative concentration; their mastery of mental engagement is likewise so.
While manifesting within formless meditative concentration, they display the realm of desire in the same way.
All are for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, yet they do not become attached to those beings;
their spheres of experience are like space, like illusions, like mirages, like the moon in water, like dreams, and like clouds.
Having already known meditative concentration and the mundane world, one immediately transforms the worldly mind into wisdom;
because it can no longer obscure the mind, one attains the birth of a sovereign mind.
Thoroughly realizing meditative concentrations and supernormal powers, they travel throughout billions of lands;
they are able to universally make offerings to all Buddhas, and all ignorance, delusions, and hindrances are completely severed.
The faculties are subdued and the mind is serene; having crossed over *śamatha*, it is free from conceptualization.
Both the world and the mind are equally pure; the power of wisdom is likewise eternally tranquil.
Abiding in equanimity through non-apprehension, it is therefore called the universal signlessness of equanimity;
if one does not abide even in that equanimity, for this reason one is called an attainer of meditative concentration.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) so that it is like space?
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they practice the perfection of wisdom so that it is like space.”
What are the four? They are:
by virtue of the purity of space, one enters into the purity of all sentient beings;
Through the purity of wisdom, one enters the purity of all consciousnesses;
through the purity of the dharma-realm, one enters the purity of self, person, sentient being, and life-span;
through the purity of meaning, one enters the purity of all syllables and letters.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the practice of the prajñāpāramitā so that it is like empty space.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they are able to purify the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
What are these eight?
They are as follows:
Diligently gathering all wholesome dharmas without clinging to the view of eternalism;
diligently severing all unwholesome dharmas without clinging to the view of nihilism;
and knowing the dharma of dependent origination without contradicting the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
They manifest the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) without being attached to the four types of eloquence;
they are skillfully able to discern the four summaries (*uddāna*), yet do not perceive impermanence, suffering, selflessness, or tranquility;
they skillfully explain the results of karma while remaining unshakable.
Abiding in the absence of karmic fruition, they dwell in non-conceptualization;
their wisdom constantly elucidates the distinct characteristics of all dharma-terms;
and they have perfectly attained the radiance of all pure dharmas.
To teach the dharmas of both purity and defilement to all sentient beings—
this is the eighth dharma by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
“Good son! You should know that *prajñā* is the phrase for purity, because it can destroy evil conceptualizations;
it is the phrase for non-alteration, because its own characteristics are pure.”
This is the phrase of non-conceptualization, because it cannot be delimited;
this is the phrase of suchness, because its nature is true reality;
this is the phrase of truth, because it is unshakable.
This is a phrase of truthfulness, for it is free from falsehood;
this is a phrase of wisdom, for it releases all bonds;
this is a phrase of fulfillment, for it is the merit of the noble ones.
This is the phrase of thorough penetration, because it is well able to observe;
this is the phrase of the ultimate meaning, because there is nothing to be expressed;
this is the phrase of equality, because there is no differentiation.
This is the firm phrase, for it is indestructible;
this is the immovable phrase, for it has no basis;
this is the vajra phrase, for it can pierce through.
This is the phrase of deliverance, for that which was to be done has been accomplished;
this is the phrase of purity, for its nature is unstained;
this is the phrase of darknesslessness, for there is nothing to be apprehended in illumination.
This is the phrase of non-duality, because there is no establishment;
this is the phrase of exhaustion, because it is ultimately extinguished;
this is the phrase of inexhaustibility, because it is unconditioned and eternally abiding.
This is the phrase of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for it is not encompassed by arising or ceasing;
this is the phrase of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), for it is utterly pure;
this is the phrase of space (*ākāśa*), for it is without obstruction.
This is the phrase for the path of space, because it leaves no tracks;
this is the phrase for non-attainment, because its intrinsic nature does not exist;
this is the phrase for wisdom, because wisdom and consciousness are non-dual.
This is the phrase of non-destruction, because it is free from antidotes;
this is the phrase of bodilessness, because there is no transformation;
this is the phrase of the thorough knowledge of suffering, because it is free from conceptually constructed suffering.
This is the phrase for severing accumulation, because it eliminates craving;
this is the phrase for realizing cessation, because it is ultimately non-arising;
this is the phrase for cultivating the path, because it enters the non-dual path.
This is a phrase of the Buddha, for it gives rise to perfect enlightenment;
this is a phrase of the Dharma, for it ultimately transcends desire. Good son!

Regarding such distinctions of words and meanings, the light of wisdom does not depend on others; it enters even a small portion of the Dharma taught, being entirely free from both the conceptualizer and the conceptualized. This is called practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) like space.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Clear wisdom can sever the habitual tendencies of affliction; It manifests karma and its causal conditions.
It does not rely on the view of a self or sentient beings, Nor does it dwell upon the marks of a life-span or a person.”
Detached from both self and non-self, The Prajñāpāramitā is proclaimed as reaching the true source.
Prajñā can destroy all that exists; Prajñā can cross over the torrential flood;
Prajñā can act as the cause of purification; Prajñā can establish one in supreme liberation.
Pure wisdom can sever all entanglements and hindrances, Thoroughly knowing the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements.
Luminous wisdom shines upon the emptiness of the three realms, Attaining liberation from both subject and object;
Cultivating Prajñā-pāramitā to make it pure, One remains unattached to anything in all worlds.
Thoroughly penetrating, they are able to practice the conduct of Prajñā; Constantly cultivating pure wisdom, they illumine the true void.
The five eyes are purified and the five faculties are bright; They can eliminate the five destinies and purify the five aggregates.
Reaching the other shore, they dwell in constant peace; Their entry into the Dharma-realm is likewise so.
Equanimity is like the great void; lofty and vast, it perfectly accords with the Buddha’s wisdom.
Detached from both attainment and non-attainment, it can reveal the nectar-gate of the Middle Way;
following the conduct of the Sages, it skillfully distinguishes yet remains non-discriminative.
Able to know suffering and its origin, they sever craving; Cultivating the Path and demonstrating cessation, they manifest the unconditioned.
Having achieved the light of true wisdom, They thus understand that the three periods of time have neither coming nor going.
All buddha-fields are equal, and the tranquility of all phenomena is likewise so;
realizing that all sentient beings are devoid of self or person—this is the true cultivation of wisdom.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva cultivate merit so that it is like space? Good son!”
The nature of all phenomena is like space; taking the bodhicitta as its seed, the accumulation of merit cultivated therein is never separated from that bodhicitta.
One gathers roots of goodness and dedicates them all to the ocean of sarvajñā (omniscience); through this, one attains immeasurable merit that is equal to space.
"Good son! A bodhisattva should give rise to such a thought: because space is immeasurable, the accumulation of merit it engenders is likewise immeasurable. Why is this?
Because the mind is immeasurable, merit is also immeasurable;
the Bodhisattva should form this contemplation regarding that:
"O son of good family!..."
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of immeasurable adornments, which a bodhisattva should fulfill as such a mass of merit.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
Infinite adornment of body, because the marks and signs are perfected;
infinite adornment of speech, because the turning of the wheel of Dharma in all discourse is pure;
infinite adornment of mind, because of penetrating the minds of all sentient beings.
Adorned with immeasurable wisdom in practice, for the sake of maturing immeasurable sentient beings;
adorned with immeasurable aspects of practice, for the sake of purifying immeasurable Buddha-fields;
adorned with immeasurable merit, meditative concentration, and diligence, for the sake of perfecting the immeasurable majestic deportment of the Buddhas.
The adornment of the immeasurable great bodhimanda, because it fulfills all marks and practices;
the adornment of the immeasurable and unobstructed assemblies for giving, because it brings to perfection the immeasurable ūrṇā-kośa mark of the Buddha;
the adornment of immeasurable reverence and selflessness, because it brings to perfection the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown of the head.
Adorned with immeasurable and uninterrupted concentration of mind, because of fulfilling immeasurable, non-deceptive minds that accord with a pure intention.
Noble son, these are the ten kinds of immeasurable adornments.
If a bodhisattva can thus give rise to a vast mind like space, the merit they obtain will be like space. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva practice wisdom that is like space?"
If a bodhisattva universally takes all sentient beings as his object, he knows as they truly are minds with desire and minds without desire;
he knows as they truly are minds with hatred and minds without hatred;
he knows as they truly are minds with delusion and minds without delusion.
He knows with reality as it is whether the mind is afflicted or unafflicted;
having himself become free from desire, he is further able to teach other persons the Dharma for subduing desire;
having himself become free from hatred, he is further able to teach other persons the Dharma for subduing hatred.
Having personally become free from delusion, they are further able to teach other individuals the Dharma for subduing delusion;
having personally become free from defilement, they are further able to teach others the Dharma for subduing all afflictions.

They do not regard those who possess the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion as inferior-minded, nor do they regard those who are free from the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion as superior-minded.
Why is this? Because that bodhisattva has realized and known the pure dharma-gate of the non-dual dharma-realm;
such a dharma-realm is itself the realm of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Thus, the dharma-realm is itself the realm free from defilement.
Therefore, the dharma-realm and all phenomena interpenetrate one another; the dharma-realm is itself phenomena, and phenomena are themselves the dharma-realm, pervading everything without exception.
If one knows the realm of the self (*ātma-dhātu*), one knows the dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*), for there is no duality between the dharma-realm and the realm of the self.
Why is this so? Because the self is pure, the dharma-realm is pure; thus, all dharmas are pure.
It manifests radiance yet is without receptivity, for it is free from all marks due to its marklessness.
It is without any established foundation, like space; this is called unimpeded wisdom.
Because they comprehend all phenomena through unimpeded wisdom without any obstruction, this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of wisdom that is like space. "Good son!
What is the bodhisattva’s recollection of the Buddha as authorized by the Buddhas?
It is as follows:
to recollect untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) is the recollection of the Buddha through these precepts.
The non-dispersal of the equality of all phenomena is the recollection of the Buddha as concentration;
the absence of conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena is the recollection of the Buddha as wisdom;
and not abiding in dualistic states of mind is the recollection of the Buddha as liberation.
Not clinging to all-knowledge is the recollection of the Buddha as liberation-knowledge-and-vision;
being unmoving in the equality of the three times is the recollection of the Buddha as the powers;
not dwelling in any outflows is the recollection of the Buddha as the fearlessnesses.
In this way, one should recollect all the merits possessed by the Buddha’s body; these are all the recollection of the Buddha, for the *dharmadhātu* is equal and without differentiation.

Furthermore, in the recollection of the Buddha, one recollects that the self-nature of all the Buddha’s forms (*rūpa*) is pure. Because one perceives the purity of the self-nature of form, non-conceptual wisdom (*amanasikāra-jñāna*) follows accordingly. This extends to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); because one perceives the purity of the self-nature of consciousness, non-conceptual wisdom follows accordingly.
The same applies to the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

By means of the wisdom regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, the most excellent insight and all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) remain far removed from the entanglements of all views.
Being thus detached, one knows that form is free from defilement and that mindfulness is free from defilement; this is called the recollection of the Buddha as authorized by the Buddha.
Furthermore, the recollection of the Buddha consists of being mindful of all the Buddha’s modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—without giving rise to attachment;
it is not giving rise to attachment toward the Buddha’s preaching or his silence, nor is there attachment to mindfulness or non-mindfulness.

Why is this so? Because the Buddha is without recollection, without mental engagement, is not form, not characteristics, not phenomena, and not non-phenomena; for all conceptual objects of cognition do not manifest within him.
"Good son! This is called the recollection of the Buddha as authorized by the Buddha. Good son!"
What is the bodhisattva’s recollection of the Dharma as authorized by the Buddha?
The Dharma is called "freedom from desire," because there is no defilement regarding phenomena; thus, there is also no recollection of the Dharma.
The Dharma is called "the absence of the ālayavijñāna," because there is no concealment regarding phenomena; thus, there is also no recollection of the Dharma.
Dharma is named "quiescence," because it is free from the defilement of mind, thought, and consciousness; thus, there is no mindfulness that follows after dharmas.
Dharma is named "signless," because there is no consciousness that pursues signs within dharmas; thus, there is no mindfulness that follows after dharmas.
The Dharma is called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because there is no conceptual designation or abiding within the Dharma, there is also no recollection of the Dharma.

Furthermore, in the recollection of the Dharma, if one maintains mindfulness without interruption and does not give rise to the notion of "Dharma," one immediately enters the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). One contemplates that all dharmas are originally unborn and that there is no dharma to be realized; this is the very ground realized by all those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and perfectly awakened ones (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).
In this way, all these dharmas of liberation realized by the noble ones are likewise without intrinsic nature.
This is the bodhisattva’s recollection of the Dharma as authorized by the Buddhas. "Good son!
What is the bodhisattva’s recollection of the Saṅgha as approved by the Buddha?

The name "Saṅgha" signifies the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it cannot be produced through volitional construction, nor does it possess any manifest activity of body, speech, or mind, but exists only as a conventional designation for that which proceeds.
This is the unconditioned Sangha, which abides apart from conceptual designations and transcends all discursive speech. Noble son,
this is the recollection of the Sangha as authorized by the Buddha.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s recollection of renunciation as approved by the Buddhas?
It is the relinquishing of all supports and requisites, and the relinquishing of even the Dharma such that there is nothing to be relinquished; this is called the most supreme renunciation.”

Regarding all phenomena, there is neither grasping nor abandoning, nor is there anything sought; there is no discursive mental engagement, yet it is not without discursive mental engagement. Therein, there is no activity of mind and no conceptual designation, nor does one abide in consciousness, for one does not give rise to the mind because of this non-abiding mind.
This is called the recollection of relinquishment as authorized by the Buddha.

Furthermore, regarding the bodhisattva’s recollection of renunciation: they dedicate their practiced cultivation toward the wisdom of universal omniscience (*sarvajñā-jñāna*) that is equal and impartial, and do not perceive awakening as an object of recollection.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge (sarvajñā) and that nature of recollection are non-dual. Noble son!
Such mindfulness of relinquishment associated with the knowledge of phenomena is called the bodhisattva’s recollection of relinquishment approved by the Buddha. "Good son,
what is the bodhisattva’s recollection of ethical discipline approved by the Buddha?"

The name of this precept is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and unimpeded (*apratigha*). It eternally brings to rest all functional effort while accomplishing all prohibitive precepts. Being without consciousness and without marks, it does not dwell in the mind to produce *samādhi*. It is the supreme basis and also the root that gives rise to pure wisdom (*viśuddha-prajñā*).
Free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and the characteristics of liberation, it is also devoid of the two kinds of dualistic discrimination.

Praised by the wise, it manifests no forms; it can extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*) and is without any formal designation (*prajñapti*). It accords with the practice of peace and bliss, and is free from all antidotes to conceptualization.
A bodhisattva is always free from defilement regarding such categories of precepts; this is called the bodhisattva’s recollection of the precepts as authorized by the Buddha. "Good son!
What is the bodhisattva’s recollection of devas as authorized by the Buddhas?
One should recollect two kinds of devas:
first, the devas of the Five Pure Abodes, because they include noble beings; [and second, the devas of the desire realm].
Second, there is the Tuṣita Heaven, because a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood resides in that heaven.
Furthermore, when this Bodhisattva in his final birth dwells in that celestial palace, there are ten kinds of supreme dharmas.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
among all the pāramitās, the prajñāpāramitā is their crown;
Among all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the non-retrogressive supernormal power is the pinnacle;
among all stages (*bhūmi*), only the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-bhūmi*) is the pinnacle;
and among all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), the samādhi of superior right view that is non-retrogressive is the pinnacle.
Among all the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) is its crown;
among all forms of omniscience, unattached and unimpeded wisdom is its crown;
among all faculties (*indriya*), the unimpeded wisdom that knows superior, middling, and inferior faculties is its crown.
Among all the powers and fearlessnesses, the wisdom that shines forth and enters accordingly is its crown;
among all eyes, the Buddha-eye that observes all Buddha-dharmas as clearly as if they were in the palm of one's hand is its crown;
and while seated at the site of enlightenment, the right wisdom corresponding to the mind in a single kṣaṇa for the attainment of perfect awakening is its crown.
These are the ten characteristics of the stages of the summit (*mūrdhan*); one should keep them in mind.

Once a bodhisattva has attained this mindfulness, their vision will not be disturbed by underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) or active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), their mental attention (*manasikāra*) will not be disturbed by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and they will not be disturbed by such categories.
Mindfulness free from defilement and turbidity—thus should one practice mindfulness of those devas.
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva’s recollection of the devas as authorized by the Buddhas.
“Good son! How is it that the various practices performed by a bodhisattva are equal to nirvāṇa?

Nirvāṇa is called tranquility; it completely eliminates all afflictions, extinguishes all sensations, is detached from all objects of perception, and transcends the aggregates, sense bases, and elements. It is through this that such a noble being attains equality with nirvāṇa.”

By the power of their original vows, they sport in great compassion; through skillful means and wisdom, they obtain the empowerment of the Tathāgatas. Having well-cultivated wisdom and purified their mental dispositions, they abide in the wondrous samādhi that is like an illusion. Knowing that the afflictions and birth-and-death of sentient beings are all like illusory transformations, they manifest taking birth. By this, they are able to sever the bonds of all birth-and-death, remaining undefiled; this is called nirvāṇa.

Having attained mastery, they manifest birth though not born; there is nothing that is not born, yet there is nothing that is born. They eternally abide in nirvāṇa without severing saṃsāra, and they bring sentient beings to maturity without ceasing.
"Good son! This is called the gate of wisdom that unifies the great compassion and skillful means of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva dwells in this gate, they will attain the practice of equality within nirvana while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva thoroughly know the modes of conduct of all sentient beings? Good son!”
Bodhisattvas have eighty-four thousand modes of conduct; these constitute the fundamental *uddāna* verses.

The characteristics of the conduct of sentient beings are of immeasurable variety, inconceivable, and inexpressible; they can be known only by a Buddha, and are not understood by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor can they be fully understood even by Bodhisattvas.
That bodhisattva, through the empowerment of the Buddha and by the power of their own wisdom, comes to know the modes of conduct of all sentient beings as they truly are.
That is to say:

Thus, they know as they truly are all the modes of conduct of sentient beings: their characteristics of intrinsic nature, their characteristics of activity, their characteristics of causes, their characteristics of conditions, their characteristics of action, and their characteristics of conjunction; or various characteristics of separation, characteristics of desire, characteristics of hatred, characteristics of delusion, and characteristics of the equal proportions [of the defilements]; characteristics of hell-beings, animals, the realm of Yama, gods, and humans; or the *niyāma* of śrāvakas, the *niyāma* of pratyekabuddhas, or the *niyāma* of Buddhas; or distant causes, intermediate causes, and proximate causes. Knowing all such modes of conduct of sentient beings as they truly are, they remain unsubdued by anything except for omniscience.
"Good son! This is how a bodhisattva thoroughly knows the modes of conduct of all sentient beings.
