The Imperially Enfeoffed Lord of Three Thousand Households, invested with the purple robe and posthumously honored as Minister of Works, titled Dajian (Great Mirror), the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Bukong of Daguangzhi Daxingshan Temple, translated by imperial decree: “O son of good family!
"How does a bodhisattva maintain the precious treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma?
Son of good family!

The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas is inexhaustible. Because the dispositions, faculties, and characteristics of all sentient beings are immeasurably diverse, the World-Honored Buddhas, in order to lead them to enter [the path], preach a treasury of the Dharma that is likewise immeasurable and boundless according to those various diverse faculties. For this reason, it is called the 'Precious Treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma.'"

Furthermore, from the night the Tathāgata realized awakening until the night of his parinirvāṇa, all that he has spoken, speaks, and will speak is entirely called "spoken as it is," "not spoken otherwise," and "true speech."
What is meant by "speaking in accordance with reality"?
It is so called because it is spoken in accordance with that suchness (tathatā) in its state of equality; therefore, it is called "speaking in accordance with reality.
What is meant by "not speaking differently"?
The Dharma that is taught is based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is equal and non-dual; this is called "teaching without difference.
What is "true teaching"?
To accord with the intrinsic nature (*dharmasvabhāva*) of phenomena is called true teaching.
Furthermore, the Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas cannot be expressed through words.

Even if all sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm were like Ānanda, foremost in great learning, they would be unable to exhaustively explain even a single meaning within hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas.

In this way, bodhisattvas are able to receive and uphold the boundless Dharma-treasuries of all Buddhas according to the Dharma; they do not forget or neglect any of the words, nor do they differ in their understanding of any of the meanings. They cause all sentient beings to attain joy, make offerings to and serve all Tathāgatas, destroy all demonic adversaries, subdue all non-Buddhists, extinguish afflictions, and proclaim the True Dharma.
Thus it is, son of good family!
This is called upholding the precious treasury of the Buddha, the World-Honored One’s Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as we have awakened to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those phenomena, so too should a bodhisattva receive and uphold that very nature of phenomena.
What is meant by "the Tathāgata’s equal awakening to the intrinsic nature of those phenomena"?
That is to say, one knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely like an illusion, because they lack the characteristic of being established;
entirely like a dream, because they lack the characteristic of objective realms;
and entirely like a mirage, because they ultimately lack the characteristic of arising.
All are like reflections in light and shadow, for they lack the characteristic of movement;
they are also like images, for they lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature;
one knows that their empty intrinsic nature is ultimately like dew.
They know the self-nature of signlessness because it is free from conceptual discrimination;
they know the self-nature of wishlessness because the mind does not dwell anywhere;
they know the self-nature of detachment because all desires are far removed.
One knows the unconditioned self-nature because it transcends all numerical characteristics.
Son of good family!
Such verbal expressions are for the sake of enabling others to discern; I have personally realized the self-nature of these phenomena, yet the characteristics of that dharmic nature are ineffable.

If a bodhisattva wishes to receive and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, they should, like the Tathāgata, realize the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and then teach the Dharma to sentient beings in this manner by means of letters and language.
This is how a bodhisattva is able to uphold the precious treasury of the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva know that sentient beings are originally pure, and yet bring them to maturity?"
"Good son! The realm of sentient beings is originally pure; within that fundamental nature, sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
If a bodhisattva wishes to bring those sentient beings to maturity, they should understand this fundamental purity in such a manner."
Furthermore, one should reflect that there is no view of a self, no view of a sentient being, no view of a life-principle, and no view of a recipient.

Moreover, what is called the name "sentient being" arises merely from the entanglements of perverted views, ignorance, craving, and false discrimination among the various afflictions; it possesses no real nature.
That bodhisattva should sever all afflictions of false inversion and preach such a Dharma for sentient beings, without destroying their intrinsic nature.
In order to cause them to understand that sentient beings do not exist and that sentient beings are detached from existence, one should thus bring sentient beings to maturity.
Son of good family!
This is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the primordial purity of sentient beings and the subsequent bringing of them to maturity.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice the Buddha-dharma in accordance with reality?
‘In accordance with reality’ refers to entering into dependent origination.”
Why is this? Because according to various causes and conditions, various retributions are brought about.
That is to say:
Just as one obtains great wealth through the cause of giving, so too,
after a bodhisattva has practiced giving, they dedicate it entirely toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), thereby fulfilling and accomplishing the dānapāramitā.

Śīla is the cause for birth among gods and humans; the Bodhisattva universally causes sentient beings who have defiled their precepts to abide in pure morality, and having made a vow to dedicate this toward sarvajñā (omniscience), he fulfills and accomplishes the śīlapāramitā.

Patience and gentleness are the causes for adorning one’s body, speech, and mind; the Bodhisattva constantly practices for their own benefit and the benefit of others, dwelling in patience without causing harm or affliction. Having dedicated this toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they fulfill and accomplish the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Vigor is the cause for attracting and encompassing all Buddha-dharmas; a bodhisattva should arouse a mind of diligent vigor, accumulate all existing roots of goodness, and having dedicated them all toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience), fulfill and accomplish the perfection of vigor.

Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the cause of right knowledge; because the bodhisattva desires to seek right knowledge, they cultivate the provisions for *śamatha* and dedicate them all toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), thereby fulfilling and accomplishing the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Wisdom and extensive learning are the causes of great intelligence; when a bodhisattva does not grasp at nor cling to the characteristics of what has been heard, and dedicates this toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they fulfill and accomplish the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Thus, being able to understand that such causes produce such effects regarding all wholesome dharmas is called "attention according to reality" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) with respect to causes and conditions.
Furthermore, attention according to reality refers to attending to the self and all phenomena in accordance with reality.
Thus one knows that both self and non-self are such that all dharmas are entirely without self;
one knows that the self is empty, and all dharmas are likewise entirely empty;
the self is merely a name, and all dharmas likewise exist only as names.

When a bodhisattva attends to things in this manner according to reality, they are in harmonious accord with the equality of all phenomena; this is precisely to be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Buddha-dharmas through accordance with reality.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva attain non-retrogression in supernormal powers and achieve mastery over all phenomena? Good son!”
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, without having abandoned the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they will eventually fall away from them.

When a bodhisattva has already abandoned the view of a self-identity and is able to remain far removed from all views, such as the sixty-two [wrong] views, and gives rise to supernormal powers, he is said to be endowed with knowledge, endowed with wisdom, endowed with awakening, endowed with generosity, endowed with ethical discipline, and endowed with meditative concentration;

he is also said to be one whose body and mind are secluded. Having attained this knowledge, his mind is inwardly ever tranquil and outwardly inactive; it is a mind that pervades all that is known, a mind that acts according to its desires, a mind of skillful discernment, and a pure wisdom. Being free from the turbidity of afflictions, he attains luminous and unobscured knowledge. He accumulates the provisions of merit, accumulates the provisions of knowledge, accumulates the provisions of *śamatha*, and accumulates the provisions of *vipaśyanā*.

They are adorned with the ornaments of *dāna* (generosity) and pure precepts; they don the armor of patience and diligence; they rely upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and skillfully cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*); they accord with great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and dwell securely in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); they transcend through skillful means (*upāya*) to accomplish such dharmas; they give rise to wondrous supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and ascend loftily into the unobstructed; even until sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), by virtue of their supernormal powers, they attain mastery over all phenomena (*dharmas*), manifesting all forms, hearing all sounds, and entering all minds;

they recollect immeasurable eons and obtain all playful supernormal powers; they subdue and sever all outflows (*āsrava*) and even attain mastery in transforming things according to their will, such that regarding all phenomena there is no longer any further effort required.
"Good son! This is the non-retrogressive supernormal power of a bodhisattva, by which they attain mastery over all dharmas. Good son!"
"How does a bodhisattva enter the profound principle of the Buddha-dharma, which is difficult for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to fathom?
Good son, 'profound' refers to the principle of dependent origination."

That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.
With accumulation as cause and condition, this great mass of suffering arises, causing all sentient beings to wander in saṃsāra and become defiled.
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands this; this is called the principle of dependent origination.
What is called the principle of dependent cessation? It is as follows:

with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.
By this causal condition, with the cessation [of ignorance], the great mass of suffering ceases; thus, sentient beings attain purification. This is called the principle of the sequence of cessation.

If a bodhisattva understands it in this way, it is called entering the profound principle. That sentient beings can attain purification from affliction is not possible for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this is the domain of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
If a bodhisattva, through the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual sustenance (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is able to awaken to this according to their capacity.
Furthermore, "profound" refers to the view of a personal identity (*satkāya*); because the view of a personal identity is pure, all phenomena are pure.

Why is this? Because when one investigates the root of this *satkāya* (the view of a self-identity), nothing is found; that which is not found is profoundly deep. The Buddhas find no "self" whatsoever; I am fundamentally pure, and as I am pure, all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise pure.
For what reason is it called "pure"?
It is because those phenomena are originally unarisen, having neither origination nor cessation; therefore, they are called pure.
Furthermore, being without darkness, without light, and without the *ālayavijñāna*, this true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is called profound.
Therein, the eye ceases, and so on up to the mind which also ceases; there are no objective spheres. This absence of objective spheres is the reality.

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called "profound," for it is free from the mental attachments of the heart and mind regarding the supreme meaning, being difficult to fathom, difficult to see, and beyond conceptualization.

Regarding these various profound principles of the Dharma, one employs provisional names in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to analyze and reveal them to other sentient beings. This is how a bodhisattva gains entry into the profound principle of the Buddha-dharma, which is difficult for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to fathom.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva enter the skillful knowledge of dependent origination and remain far removed from all views of extremes? Good son!
Dependent origination is dependent origination because it is without an object of perception;
it is dependent origination because it is without a substantial entity and without accomplishment;
it is dependent origination because it is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and quiescent.
It is dependent origination that is without self, without sentient beings, without life-force, without nourishment, without a person (pudgala), without a human, and without a youth;
it is dependent origination that is without birth and without arising;

it is without anything existing, without effort, empty, signless, quiescent, without activity, and without conceptual proliferation; therefore, it is called the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
Such arising is what constitutes arising; such cessation is what constitutes cessation.

Furthermore, because there is no self, no sentient being, no life-span, no nourisher, no person (*pudgala*), no individual, and no youth (*māṇava*), there is no dharma that can arise through conditions; for in that regard, the designation "self" or "sovereign" does not exist.
Just as grass, trees, walls, and reflections are, so too are all phenomena.
When external phenomena arise, their arising is non-existent; when they cease, their ceasing is non-existent.
Internal phenomena are likewise: at the time of arising, there is no "arising" that exists; at the time of ceasing, there is no "ceasing" that exists.

Apart from dependently originated phenomena, there is nothing truly produced; lacking conditions, there is no cessation. When one accords with this principle, all extreme views are entirely abandoned.
What is the view of extremes?

The view of extremes refers to annihilationism and eternalism; it holds that things do not arise when they arise and do not perish when they perish. Being without arising and without perishing, one is naturally pure regarding the extremes of annihilation and eternity. Because of this natural purity, one attains purity regarding all views of extremes.
"Good son! This is the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom in entering dependent origination, which remains far removed from extreme views. Good son!"
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom that seals true suchness with the seal of the Tathāgata without interruption?

Son of good family, that which is sealed by the seal of the Tathāgata is the seal of non-interruption; it is without arising, without transformation, without grasping, without movement, and without being moved; it cannot be shaken by any in the world—humans, devas, or asuras.
Why is this? Because the world—including its humans, devas, and asuras—is sealed with that seal. Such is the Seal of the Tathāgata:

the seal of ultimate non-arising, the seal of ultimate emptiness, the seal of ultimate signlessness, the seal of ultimate wishlessness, the seal of ultimate unconditionedness, the seal of ultimate detachment from desire, the seal of ultimate suchness, the seal of ultimate reality-limit, and the seal of ultimate space.

"Good son! Just as no seal appears within empty space, so too the seal of the Tathāgata does not appear as a mark of radiance within the five eyes; rather, it seals them by means of its own characteristic seal."
Therefore, even when the Tathāgata establishes verbal designations for all phenomena, he seals them all with the seal of the Tathāgata; this is what constitutes a designation.
All consciousnesses and their objective spheres are merely established as conditioned phenomena, yet within those phenomena, he does not establish any marks of manifold differentiation.
It is sealed with the seal of suchness, without interruption.
What constitutes an interruption in suchness?
If one discriminates among phenomena and perceives them as superior, middling, or inferior, this is called an interruption.
If one does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena, this is called "uninterrupted.
Furthermore, even when conceptualization arises from manifold discriminations, it cannot disturb or corrupt that suchness.
Just as sentient beings may travel through space, yet that space is not destroyed;
so too do all sentient beings travel within suchness, yet that suchness is never interrupted or destroyed.
In this way, by means of wisdom, the bodhisattva seals form and all phenomena with the seal of *tathatā* (suchness), without interrupting or destroying that suchness;
this is the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom of sealing suchness with the seal of the Tathāgata without interruption.

“Good son! How does a bodhisattva enter the profound principle of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), seeing that all phenomena and the various dharma-realms are mutually pervasive, equal, and of one nature?”
The Dharma-realm is also called the realm free from desire, because it is detached from all defilements;
it is also called the realm of non-arising, because there is no accumulation;
it is the realm of non-contradiction, because it is fundamentally without birth.
There is no realm of going, because there is no equality;
there is no realm of coming, because there is no obstruction;
there is no realm of abiding, because there is no arising.
The realm of suchness, because it is equal throughout the three times;
the realm of selflessness, because it is primordially pure;
the realm of no life-principle, because of its ultimate nature.
There is no realm of discernment, because there is nothing upon which to dwell;
there is no realm of the ālayavijñāna, because there is no defilement;
there is no realm of origination, because its nature is fixed.
Like the realm of space, because its nature is pure;
like the realm of nirvāṇa, because it is free from conceptual proliferation—
this is called the principle of entering the dharma-realm.

If a bodhisattva enters into such a principle, every single word they utter is mutually pervasive with the principle of the dharma-realm; thus, they know that the desire realm and the dharma-realm are non-dual and without distinction.
Furthermore, the dharma-realm of the nature of desire and the dharma-realm of the nature of hatred are non-dual;
the dharma-realm of the nature of hatred and the dharma-realm of the nature of delusion are non-dual;
the dharma-realm of the nature of delusion and the dharma-realm of the nature of afflictions are non-dual.
The dharma-realm of the nature of afflictions and the dharma-realm of the nature of the desire realm are non-dual;
the dharma-realm of the nature of the desire realm and the dharma-realm of the nature of the form realm are non-dual;
the dharma-realm of the nature of the form realm and the dharma-realm of the nature of the formless realm are non-dual.
The nature of the formless realm and the dharma-realm are non-dual with the dharma-realm of emptiness;
the dharma-realm of emptiness and the nature of the eye-realm and the dharma-realm are non-dual;
the nature of the eye-realm and the dharma-realm and the nature of form and the dharma-realm are non-dual.
The nature of the realm of form and the nature of the realm of the dharma-dhātu are non-dual;

the nature of the realm of eye-consciousness and the nature of the realm of the dharma-dhātu are non-dual; and so on, up to the nature of the realm of mind and the nature of the realm of the dharma-dhātu being non-dual;
the nature of the realm of mind and the nature of the realm of mental consciousness and the nature of the realm of the dharma-dhātu are non-dual.
The nature of the consciousness element is the dharma-element; the nature of the aggregates and elements is non-dual with the dharma-element.
The nature of the aggregates and elements is non-dual with the nature of the earth, water, fire, and wind elements.
The nature of the earth, water, fire, and wind elements is non-dual with the dharma-element of emptiness.
Up to eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*), all phenomena and the *dharmadhātu* are non-dual;
this is the *dharmatādhātu* of all phenomena.
If a bodhisattva enters such a *dharmadhātu* by means of the wisdom of equality, they will be able to perceive the principle of the equality of all phenomena.
"Good son! This is the bodhisattva’s entry into the principle of the dharma-realm. Good son!"
"How is it that a bodhisattva’s resolve is as firm as a vajra, remaining unshakable while abiding in this Great Vehicle?
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes twelve kinds of dharmas, their resolve becomes as firm as a vajra and cannot be destroyed by the world of humans or devas."
What are the twelve? They are as follows:
the resolve of the mind of enlightenment and the superior resolve being indestructible;
Because they are unbreakable in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
because they are unbreakable in great loving-kindness and great compassion;
and because they are unbreakable in the four means of attraction.
Because maturing sentient beings is indestructible;
because purifying buddha-fields is indestructible;
and because not being weary of birth and death is indestructible.
Because the roots of goodness are never satiated and thus remain indestructible;
because the establishment of unobstructed assemblies for giving as an adornment for the primary and secondary marks remains indestructible;
and because the relinquishing of body and life to protect the true Dharma remains indestructible.
Because all roots of goodness are dedicated to all sentient beings so as not to be destroyed;
because all Buddha-dharmas are accumulated so as not to be destroyed. Noble son!
If a bodhisattva practices such dharmas without impairment, it should be known that at that time they are said to have accomplished a firm, adamantine, and indestructible intention;
just as a vajra jewel can destroy all other jewels while its own substance remains indestructible.
In this way, a bodhisattva who has accomplished a firm resolve is able to destroy all the latent tendencies of affliction in all sentient beings, yet their own person remains unimpaired. Good son!
This is how a bodhisattva achieves a vajra-like firm resolve, remaining unshakable within this Great Vehicle. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva purify their own sphere so that it is like the sphere of a Buddha?"

"Good son! The realm of the Buddha is a realm that has no realm; it is free from all realms and is entirely pure, because for that bodhisattva, both his own realm and the realm of the Buddha are completely pure.
Thus, the realm of the pure eye is the realm of the Buddha, yet there is neither a realm of the Buddha nor a realm of the eye; there is nothing near and nothing far."
Why is this? Because the realm of detachment and the realm of the Buddha are one; there is neither a realm of detachment nor a realm of the eye.
That which is the realm of the ear is the realm of the Buddha, and yet there is no realm of the Buddha; there is neither distance nor proximity.
Why is this? Because the realm of detachment and the realm of the Buddha are one; there is neither a realm of detachment nor a realm of the ear.
The realm of the nose is itself the realm of the Buddha, yet even that realm of the Buddha does not exist; there is neither distance nor proximity.
Why is this? Because the realm of detachment and the realm of the Buddha are one; there is neither the realm of detachment nor the realm of the nose.
The realm of the tongue is itself the realm of the Buddha, and yet there is no realm of the Buddha; there is neither distance nor proximity.
Why is this? Because the realm of detachment and the realm of the Buddha are one; there is neither a realm of detachment nor a realm of the tongue.
The realm of the body is itself the realm of the Buddha, yet there is no realm of the Buddha; there is neither distance nor proximity.
Why is this? Because the realm of detachment and the realm of the Buddha are one; there is neither a realm of detachment nor a realm of the body.
The realm of mind is itself the realm of the Buddha, and yet there is no realm of the Buddha; there is neither distance nor proximity.

Why is this? Because there is no separation from the realm of objects and the realm of the Buddha; nor is there a realm of objects or a realm of the mind. This is likewise true for the aggregates, the sense bases, the elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination.

Good son! If a bodhisattva enters the realm of the Buddha, remaining far removed from all realms, and if his own realm is pure and equal, this is precisely what is called entering the realm of the Buddha.
All such manifestations of these six kinds of objects enter into the realm of the Buddhas, for they give rise to no grasping and are entirely free from attachment.
Thus, the realm of the Tathāgata is without defilement or obstruction; likewise, all realms are neither defiled nor obstructed.
“Good son! One who understands in this way is a bodhisattva who has accomplished the entry into the purity of the Buddha-realm and the purity of one’s own realm. Good son!”
"How does a bodhisattva obtain the dhāraṇī of the practice of non-forgetfulness?
Good son! A bodhisattva should cultivate and perform the activities of this dhāraṇī."
How should one practice and uphold it? Good son,
there are thirty-two kinds of methods for practicing the dhāraṇī.
That is to say:
for the sake of seeking the Dharma;
and out of love and delight for the Dharma.
Because they delight in the Dharma garden;
because they follow the flow of the Dharma;
because they accord with the Dharma.
Because they revere the sublime Dharma;
because they serve and make offerings to those of great learning;
and because they are always free from pride toward their preceptors and ācāryas, honoring and making offerings to them with respect.
Because they seek the Dharma without weariness;
because they comply with and do not oppose their instructors;
and because they revere and love those who preach the Dharma as if they were the Buddha, seeking no faults in them.
Because they receive and uphold all the teachings they have heard;
because they are not indolent;
and because they are not stingy regarding the Dharma.
Because the Dharma-giving they practice is free from expectation;
because they apply correct mental attention to the Dharma they have heard;
and because they skillfully examine the Dharma they have heard.
Because they seek extensive learning without limit;
because they never cease in their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*);
and because they always delight in seclusion and the tranquility of mind.
Because they constantly and diligently cultivate the six recollections;
because they always abandon the six defiled dharmas;
and because they never relinquish the six points of harmonious respect.
Because they give rise to an unimpeded mind toward all sentient beings;
because they cultivate patient acceptance in accordance with dependently arisen phenomena;
and because they observe the three gates of liberation through mental attention without fear or trepidation.
Because they do not abandon the noble lineages or the virtues of the ascetic practices (dhūta-guṇa);
because their minds are free from inferiority in upholding the True Dharma;
and because they contemplate sentient beings and give rise to great compassion.
Because they seek the True Dharma without sparing even their own bodies or lives;
because they cultivate the practice of great wisdom to remain free from delusion and confusion;
and because they accomplish the welfare of sentient beings without weariness or indolence.
This is called the cultivation of the dhāraṇī that prevents forgetfulness.

Furthermore, son of good family, once a bodhisattva has attained this dhāraṇī, they are able to universally uphold all that the Buddha has spoken so as not to forget it; that is to say, there is no forgetting of the Dharma they have heard.
Through mindfulness, they do not forget;
through equanimity, they awaken; through wisdom, they illuminate and comprehend;
and they enter into all inexhaustible syllables.
The wisdom that skillfully understands all spoken sounds according to their respective types;
the wisdom that expounds with unimpeded eloquence without obstruction;
and the wisdom that enters into the principles of the sūtras of definitive meaning.
The wisdom that enters the principle of the *neyārtha* sūtras;
the wisdom that enters the inexhaustible discourse of the conventional;
and the wisdom that enters the uninterrupted discourse of the ultimate truth.
He attains non-retrogressive wisdom regarding diligence in the right efforts;
he gives rise to the wisdom of playful mastery regarding the four bases of power;
and he attains the wisdom of discernment regarding the faculties.
Among the powers, one attains unshakable wisdom;
among the seven factors of enlightenment, one attains the wisdom of awakening;
among the eightfold noble path, one attains the wisdom of entering into principle.
One attains the knowledge of mental abiding through śamatha;
one attains the knowledge of discerning phenomena through vipaśyanā;
and one attains the knowledge of conformity through the liberation of wisdom.
They attain profound penetrating wisdom regarding all forms of eloquent exposition;
they attain the wisdom of manifestation regarding all supernormal powers;
and they attain the wisdom of discernment regarding all perfections.
He attains the wisdom that accords with circumstances regarding the four means of attraction;
he attains the wisdom of linguistic expression regarding all sounds;
and he attains the wisdom of definitive discernment regarding the determined Dharma.
One attains uninterrupted wisdom regarding the meanings of all sūtras;
one attains inexhaustible wisdom regarding all syllables and letters;
and one attains the wisdom of bringing joy to all sentient beings.
Regarding those who seek the Dharma, they attain the wisdom of preaching according to their faculties;
regarding what has been taught by the Buddha, they attain the wisdom of mindfulness and dhāraṇī;
regarding all syllables, they attain the wisdom of entering into words and phrases.
They attain the wisdom of realizing impurity and purity as they truly are;
they attain the wisdom of awakening to the retribution of all karmic conditions;
and they attain the luminous wisdom free from obscuration regarding all phenomena.

This is called a dhāraṇī; one who attains the equality of body, speech, and mind through this dhāraṇī is able to rain down inexhaustible Dharma, is able to extinguish all afflictions, and is able to give birth to all the Buddha-dharmas.

Because they have attained the profound principle of this dhāraṇī, they are never subject to forgetfulness; therefore, it is called "the bodhisattva’s practice of attaining the dhāraṇī of non-forgetfulness."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva obtain the unimpeded eloquence empowered by the Tathāgata? Good son!”
If a bodhisattva is constantly sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgata, they attain twenty-four kinds of unimpeded eloquence.
What are these twenty-four kinds?
That is to say:
swift eloquence;
sharp and nimble eloquence;
Unimpeded eloquence;
unobstructed eloquence;
eloquence of skillful words;
The eloquence of profound depth;
the eloquence of intermingled manifold sounds;
the eloquence of supreme and wondrous adornment;
The eloquence that is free from despondency;
the eloquence that is fearless;
and the eloquence of various verses of praise.
The eloquence that analyzes the sūtras, the dependent origination, and the past events;
the eloquence that can subdue others;
and the eloquence of inexhaustible phrases for explaining distinctions.
The eloquence of manifesting subtle refinements;
the eloquence of majestic dignity and virtue;
the eloquence of uninterrupted discourse on the Dharma.
The eloquence of celestial adornments;
the eloquence that severs all doubts and delusions;
the eloquence regarding mundane and supramundane phenomena.
The eloquence of not losing [the teaching];
the eloquence that gladdens the hearts of the multitude through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
and the eloquence of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
The Buddha’s empowered eloquence:
"Good son! These twenty-four kinds of eloquence are accomplished by cultivating twenty-four kinds of karma."
What are the twenty-four kinds of karma?
They are as follows:
because one does not oppose the instructions and admonitions of teachers and elders, one obtains swift eloquence;
Because one’s coming and going is free from flattery, one obtains swift and sharp eloquence;
because one is free from all afflictions, one obtains unimpeded eloquence;
because one does not delight in dwelling among the mundane, one obtains unhindered eloquence.
Because they do not engage in divisive speech, they attain eloquence of excellent words;
because they have realized dependent origination, they attain profound eloquence;
and because they practice various forms of giving, they attain eloquence of diverse and harmonious sounds.
Because they have adorned the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgatas, they attain eloquence of supreme and wondrous adornment;
because they do not abandon the bodhicitta, they attain eloquence that never sinks;
because they skillfully protect the aggregate of ethical discipline, they attain fearless eloquence.
Because of giving various banners, pennants, bells, and canopies, one attains the eloquence to speak various verses of praise;
because of serving, honoring, and making various offerings to teachers and elders, one attains the eloquence to speak sūtras, nidānas, and itivṛttakas;
and because of not afflicting or distressing sentient beings who are impoverished, one attains the eloquence capable of subduing others.
Because they bestow inexhaustible treasuries of jewels to cause others to enter the Dharma, they attain the eloquence of inexhaustible phrases for explaining distinctions;
because what they speak is true and free from coarseness or harshness, they attain the eloquence that manifests the subtle and wondrous;
because they do not disparage the honored teachings nor cause schisms among others, they attain the eloquence of dignified majesty.
Because he maintains the Dharma he has attained himself, he obtains the eloquence of uninterrupted preaching;
because he does not slander or disparage others and joyfully gives away his own cherished possessions, he obtains the eloquence of celestial adornment;
because he does not harbor "teacher's fists" regarding the Dharma and preaches according to what he has heard, he obtains the eloquence that cuts through all doubts.
By regarding all beings as one's own teachers and refraining from causing them distress, and by bestowing medicine upon the sick, one attains eloquence regarding mundane and supramundane dharmas;
by not seeking out the faults of others and constantly examining oneself, one attains unerring eloquence;

and by observing all sentient beings with an impartial mind to establish them on the path to nirvāṇa, while remaining unattached to gain, honor, and fame, one attains the eloquence that delights the hearts of the multitude through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Because one’s speech is virtuous and gentle, because one practices according to what has been taught, and because the mind is free from turbidity and confusion, one attains the eloquence of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives;
because one does not slander the Mahāyāna, does not delight in the Hīnayāna, and possesses compassion for sentient beings, one attains the eloquence sustained by the Buddhas.
These are called the karmic factors for accomplishing the twenty-four kinds of eloquence.
Furthermore, it is called *pratibhāna* (eloquence) because it causes other sentient beings to reach the ultimate goal;
it is called *pratibhāna* because it is able to awaken others regarding their sustenance and maintenance.
Because one’s mental continuum is filled with joy for others, it is called eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Because one speaks to other sentient beings according to their minds and intellects, it is called eloquence. Good son!
To achieve such merit, wisdom, and dharmas as these constitutes a bodhisattva’s attainment of unimpeded eloquence through the empowerment of the Buddha. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva attain mastery within the cycle of birth and death?"
"Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes twelve kinds of dharmas, they attain mastery within birth and death.
What are these twelve?"
That is to say:
by distancing oneself from evil friends and by associating with virtuous friends;
Because they perceive purity as permitted by the Buddha;
because their aggregate of ethical discipline is purified through the arising of wisdom and skillful means from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*);
and because they have attained non-retrogressive supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Because they contemplate that all phenomena are unborn;
because they take birth within saṃsāra in order to fulfill their original vows;
and because they give rise to great compassion for sentient beings.
Because they observe all phenomena as being like illusions through the samādhi of great compassion;
because they know that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing;
and because they observe the nature of phenomena—which are like dreams—as being non-false in accordance with reality.
By the majestic empowerment of the Buddha, World-Honored One, he may manifest birth and death without being defiled by birth and death;
this is the twelfth.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these twelve dharmas, they can, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya lifetimes, manifest the taking of birth to bring vast benefit to all sentient beings.
Good son! All such things are established from two kinds of roots. Namely:
The wisdom of supernormal powers and the root of great compassion—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva attaining mastery over supernormal powers within the cycle of birth and death.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva subdue enemies and adversaries and transcend the four māras? Good son!
If a bodhisattva, by means of illusion-like wisdom, penetrates that all phenomena of the five aggregates are like magical illusions, they transcend the māra of the aggregates;
by penetrating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, they transcend the māra of afflictions;
and by penetrating dependent origination, they transcend the māra of death.
Because they do not regress from the bodhicitta, they transcend the celestial māras.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattva contemplates in this way, they are able to destroy all obstacles; regarding all demonic activities concerning enlightenment, the māras find no opportunity.
What are called the deeds of Māra? They are:
to delight in the Lesser Vehicle; this is a deed of Māra.
Failing to protect the bodhicitta is a work of Māra;
bestowing gifts with discrimination toward sentient beings is a work of Māra;
maintaining the prohibitive precepts while delighting in seeking rebirth in a specific realm is a work of Māra.
To practice patience for the sake of seeking physical marks is the work of Māra;
to apply diligence toward worldly affairs is the work of Māra;
to be attached to the flavor of dhyāna is the work of Māra.
To feel revulsion toward inferior dharmas through wisdom is the work of Māra;
to become weary of saṃsāra is the work of Māra;
to perform roots of goodness without dedicating them is the work of Māra.
To feel weary of and seek liberation from afflictions is the work of Māra;
to conceal one's own transgressions is the work of Māra;
and to harbor hatred and envy toward Bodhisattvas is the work of Māra.
To slander the True Dharma is the work of Māra;
to be ungrateful and fail to repay kindness is the work of Māra;
to not seek the various perfections is the work of Māra.
Disrespect for the True Dharma is the work of Māra;
stinginess regarding the Dharma is the work of Māra;
preaching the Dharma for the sake of gain is the work of Māra.
To fail to bring sentient beings to maturity through skillful means is the work of Māra;
to abandon the four methods of attraction is the work of Māra;
to violate the prohibitive precepts is the work of Māra.
To hold the precepts lightly is a work of Māra;
to follow the practice of the śrāvakas is a work of Māra;
to follow the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas is a work of Māra.
To demand the unconditioned is the work of Māra;
to feel weary of and seek to escape the conditioned is the work of Māra;
and to harbor doubts that fail to benefit sentient beings is the work of Māra.
To be fond of doubt regarding what one has heard and to lack skill in thorough comprehension and proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) is a work of Māra;
to be fond of harboring flattery and deception while feigning compassion is a work of Māra;
to be coarse and to utter abusive insults is a work of Māra.
To feel no revulsion toward transgressions is a work of Māra;
to be stained by attachment to one's own teachings is a work of Māra;
to consider mere learning sufficient is a work of Māra.
Not seeking the True Dharma is a work of Māra;
delighting in seeking what is not the Dharma is a work of Māra;
not delighting in the antidotes to hindrances, obscurations, and entanglements is a work of Māra.
Impure mind and speech are the work of Māra;
enduring the defilements of a śramaṇa is the work of Māra. Good son!
In this way, even up to the point of habitually practicing the ten unwholesome actions and abandoning wholesome dharmas—all such things are entirely the works of Māra.
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to transcend them."
What are the four? They are: not forgetting the bodhicitta;
Because they diligently cultivate the six perfections without negligence;
because they abide in skillful wisdom to bring sentient beings to maturity;
and because they abide in the profound principle to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
"Good son! If a bodhisattva accords with this Dharma, they will certainly be able to crush all Māras and hostile enemies; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to transcend the four Māras."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva accumulate immeasurable stores of merit and serve as a refuge for all sentient beings? Good son!”

If a bodhisattva, toward all sentient beings, gives rise to great compassion of a single essence and abides in meditative concentration, seeing those who come seeking, he gives to them all without exception; through inexhaustible merit, he attains the "jeweled hand" so that others may enjoy its benefits.

With pure intention, his mind is like level ground, free from high and low; whatever he hopes for is abundant benefit, and because his precepts are pure, he attains a mind free from attachment and well-guarded sense faculties.
Furthermore, he is able to accomplish all assemblies of giving, attaining dhāraṇīs and achieving eloquence.
By means of such accumulated roots of virtue, one dedicates them toward enlightenment and bestows them universally upon all sentient beings;
just as the four external great elements serve as the support for the entire world, so too do the four internal great elements serve as the support for all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"Of all the roots of goodness, dharmas of wisdom, and skillful means that I have accumulated, there is not a single dharma that does not serve as a basis and support for sentient beings."
“This is how a bodhisattva acquires immeasurable stores of merit and serves as a refuge and dwelling place for all sentient beings.
‘Noble son, how does a bodhisattva perform the work of a Buddha for sentient beings when appearing in a world where no Buddha exists?’”
"Good son! If a bodhisattva, for the sake of giving rise to the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, cultivates the karma of the ten powers;
and for the sake of giving rise to the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, cultivates the karma of the four fearlessnesses;"
To give birth to the thirty unimpeded knowledges, one cultivates the karma of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
to give birth to the attainment of the radiance of the Buddha-eye, one cultivates the karma of fully knowing through the five eyes;
to give birth to all supernormal powers, one cultivates the karma of recollecting past lives.
In order to attain the fulfillment of enlightenment, one cultivates the complete perfection of all wholesome dharmas and severs the afflictions and karmic actions of body, speech, and mind;
in order to give rise to the marks and signs of physical adornment, one cultivates and accumulates the karma of all merit-provisions;
in order to give rise to the ten stages and obtain the empowerment of all Buddha-dharmas, one cultivates and accumulates the karma of all wisdom-provisions.
In this way, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva fully cultivates such deeds as these, they will be able to extensively perform the Buddha-work for sentient beings and bring it to fulfillment even in an age when no Buddha exists.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva attain the ocean-seal samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) and remain unstained by the mental activities of all sentient beings? Good son!”
For what reason is it called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi?
Just as the various classes of sentient beings in Jambudvīpa all manifest their reflections within the great ocean, it is therefore named the Great Ocean.

In this way, all such categories of sentient beings—including their minds and forms, up to their voices—appear as reflections within the ocean-like mind of the bodhisattva; therefore, it is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi).
Just as the great ocean has but a single salty taste, so too is the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of liberation through the single flavor of the Dharma.

Just as the great ocean does not overstep its tidal limits, so too is it with the Bodhisattva who, observing the proper and improper times, does not overstep the time for attaining enlightenment when sitting at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Just as the great ocean does not harbor a dead corpse, so too the Bodhisattva does not coexist with any habitual tendencies, afflictions, or the minds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Just as the great ocean contains the myriad streams without increasing or decreasing, so too it is with the Bodhisattva, who receives all dharmas without increase or decrease.
Just as the great ocean is vast and boundless, so too is the application of a bodhisattva’s wisdom limitless.
Just as the great ocean is deep and its bottom difficult to reach, so too is the ocean of a bodhisattva’s knowledge difficult for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to fathom.
Just as the great ocean serves as the support for immeasurable worlds, so too does the bodhisattva serve as the support for all sentient beings. Good son!
This is how a bodhisattva, having skillfully entered the ocean-seal samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), remains unstained by the mental activities of any sentient beings. "Noble son,
how does a bodhisattva attain a mind free from attachment, like the wind in space, without any obstruction?"

"Good son! If a bodhisattva remains far removed from the entanglements of views regarding all phenomena, with a mind free from attachment— just as a great wind has no defilement or attachment within space—
in this same way, a bodhisattva’s mind is likewise free from attachment toward all phenomena."
This is how the bodhisattva attains freedom from defiled attachment, with a mind like space or wind, free from all obstructions.

Translated by the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, Tripitaka Master of Daixingshan Monastery, who held the rank of Fourth Rank, Court Gentleman with the same Privileges as the Minister of State (Kaifu Yitongsan Si),

Special Advance (Tejin), Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Shi Honglu Qing), Duke of Sushan with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works (Sikong), and bestowed the posthumous title of Great Mirror (Dajian), and the honorific name of Great Universal Wisdom (Dayangzhi), by Imperial Decree: “O son of good family!

How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the proper conduct, practice so as to leave behind darkness and attain illumination, achieve spontaneous wisdom without depending on external conditions, and swiftly reach the omniscience of the Great Vehicle?

"Good son! If a bodhisattva, regarding all the practices and modes of conduct therein, attains light that is non-retrogressive and immovable, this is called the light of the self-knowledge of the True Dharma;
it is also called the unobstructed knowledge regarding phenomena."
They are able to leave behind darkness and attain illumination; they do not rely on external conditions but attain spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). Why is this?

When those bodhisattvas abide in the light of spontaneous wisdom, they clearly perceive and ascertain both other sentient beings and this Dharma without relying on external conditions, and they are swiftly able to realize the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajña-jñāna*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The wise one who has already been liberated from all views Possesses merit within the cycle of birth and death;
Abiding in yoga and free from all signs, They dedicate [their merit] toward the inexhaustible state of Bodhi.”
One should fully equip oneself with the provisions for omniscience, Which is the nature of infinite wisdom like space;
Being formless, signless, and without phenomena, One is then able to fulfill all-knowledge.
One should mindfully recollect the Buddha’s body, the supreme birth of a son;
with the mind and thoughts undisturbed therein, one does not grasp at physical marks or lineage—therefore, this is called "mindfulness of the Tathāgata."
The essence of the Dharma is far removed from all desires; it is profoundly tranquil, quiescent, and eternally signless.
If one can remain detached from all objects of perception, this is therefore called the true mindfulness of the Dharma.
Unconditioned, unstained, and eternally liberated—therefore it is called mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
Regarding all material requisites and things, one is able to relinquish them all without attachment;
being free from thought, pure, and non-conceptual—therefore it is called mindfulness of relinquishment.
Unconditioned ethical discipline is free from all outflows; detached from body, speech, and mind, it does not circulate.
Not arising within the three realms of existence and having no basis, this is right mindfulness and the untainted precept.
The deities of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens are by nature stainless, And those dwelling in Tuṣita succeed as Dharma Kings;
One should contemplate such pure deities as these, Thinking: "Before long, I too shall always be like them."
If one upholds the True Dharma of all Buddhas, one should not cling to the affairs of affliction;
liberated from both what is dharma and what is non-dharma, one is thus able to uphold the teachings of all Buddhas.
Just as the characteristics of the Bodhi attained by the Buddha, so too it is for those who uphold the Dharma;
if one knows that the primordial limit is free from defilement, this is called upholding all the Buddhas' teachings.
Through the purity of the self, sentient beings are pure; The wise who follow this path are pure in their Dharma.
Knowing that the nature of the minds of all sentient beings is pure, They achieve accomplishment through such practice.
He does not bring about the annihilation of the realm of sentient beings, nor does he perceive them as increasing or decreasing;
to teach the eradication of perverted views, he transforms immeasurable multitudes and brings them to purity.
One should say that the various realms of the world are not different from the realm of the Tathāgata;
the realm of the Buddha is like space, and the realms of the world are likewise so.
All speech and written characters are entirely like echoes in an empty valley;
there is no one within them who hears. Having understood this, one attains dhāraṇī.
By upholding, practicing, and reciting it, one is able to fully proclaim the principles of the Dharma;
free from the notions of self, person, or phenomena, one thus dwells securely in the dhāraṇī.
Able to uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas, Skillfully expounding them so that all who hear rejoice;
With right mindfulness never departing from samādhi, One thereby attains certainty in dhāraṇī.
Unwavering in the Dharma with an undistracted mind, and free from doubt regarding all phenomena;
just as a dragon king sends down a great rain, so too does that person preach the Dharma.
Unattached, unbound, and without obstruction, They can expound billions of koṭis of scriptures;
Regarding all sentient beings, they have no notion of "dharmas"— Such is their attainment of the supreme merit of eloquence.
Relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall preach the wondrous Dharma, remaining forever unimpeded for thousands of koṭis of kalpas;
may all sentient beings have their hearts filled with joy, and may they dwell securely in eloquence and the merits of the Buddhas.
If one knows the principles of all phenomena, Their essential nature being like empty space;
Without a person, without a life-force, and without a soul— That person is said to uphold the Buddha’s true Dharma.
The nature of sentient beings is primordial quiescence; Ultimately, all phenomena are entirely unborn.
This realm of patience is stainless and pure; Attaining this is called non-negligence.
Seeing that all aggregates are like illusions, one then perceives the true nature of all phenomena;
knowing the six sense bases to be like an empty village, one is thus able to transcend the māra of the aggregates.
Just as floating clouds arise in the sky, so too are all delusions;
by constantly and diligently observing the true principle, one can transcend the demon of afflictions.
If one knows that there is no arising and is eternally unarisen, Then one knows that in quiescent extinction there is likewise no cessation;
The Dharma has neither past nor future worlds, And is certainly not invaded by the Mara of Death.
Unmoving and without thought regarding all phenomena, Abiding neither in bodhi nor in conceptual cognition;
Arising compassion to rescue others without self or person— This is the subduing of the host of celestial Māras.
Seeing the equality of consciousness and wisdom, they do not dwell in the unconditioned nor in the conditioned;
knowing the world to be like an illusion, such a one is called brave, steadfast, and invincible.
Unattached to this shore or the other, teaching the Dharma and practicing in accordance with it;
rescuing sentient beings while free from the notion of a person—such a one is called a guide of Bodhisattvas.
He contemplates the three realms of existence as a wilderness, And as emptiness, unchanging;
Without paths, without people, and without rescue— Such is the Great Caravan Leader who preaches the Dharma.
Skillfully expounding the true nature of existence and non-existence, They realize that all phenomena are primordially and eternally pure;
Their compassion accords with the principle of cessation— Such a one is called a Bodhisattva guide.
The preceding and succeeding moments of the flowing mental continuum—these two minds do not coalesce;
to thoroughly understand the essential nature of this streaming mind is called the valor of a bodhisattva.
Knowing that the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally pure, like space or the moon reflected in water,
and remaining unattached to any afflictions— this is the Pure Being (Śuddhasattva) who is ever praised.
If one knows that a single phenomenon is identical to all phenomena—like a phantom or a mirage, devoid of anything to be grasped;
unreal, empty, quiescent, neither permanent nor eternal—that person will before long realize true awakening.

When this definitive Dharma-gate was being taught, seventy-two thousand nayutas of devas, humans, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In this trichiliocosm, the earth shook in six ways, a great light shone everywhere, hundreds of thousands of devas rained down various flowers, played various musical instruments, and together praised him with udānas:
"All these sentient beings have now been sealed by the Dharma-seal of the Tathāgata."

If there are those who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, are able to give rise to resolute faith, receive and uphold it, expound it, and practice according to the Dharma as omniscient ones, all such persons within this Buddha-field should pay them homage as a means of self-adornment.

Why is this? It is because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world and expounded this secret, definitive Dharma-gate for us to hear, which is not something heard or seen by other sentient beings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, having heard these words from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, immediately attained six gates of stainless and pure samādhi. He then offered worship to the Buddha by covering him with a net of maṇi jewels, worth as much as a trichiliocosm, and with palms joined in single-minded devotion, he spoke these words:

“The Tathāgata now, through his unimpeded wisdom, skillfully observes the preceding and succeeding capacities of all sentient beings and proclaims the profound principles of the Dharma free from obstacles; because of this, the entire assembly is filled with great joy and praises the Mahāyāna.”
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had gathered from the worlds of the ten directions again emitted light and all said:
"Because the Tathāgata has preached such a Dharma-gate for us to hear, we feel profound joy and there is none among us who is not delighted."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Śīghrapratibhāna, who addressed the bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
“O Noble Being!
"Your name is Gaganagañja; do you perhaps take empty space as your treasury?
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja replied, "Noble son!..."
"I am both space and a treasury.
The Bodhisattva Swift Eloquence said, "Noble son!"
"I wish to see the various characteristics of your treasury of space.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja said, "Noble son!
"Whatever object you conceive in your mind, I shall cause it to rain down for you from the sky.
The Bodhisattva Swift Eloquence said:

"In the past, I once beheld the world-system called Lotus Adornment belonging to the Tathāgata Red Utpala Śrī. Therein was a lotus named All-Pervading Universal Radiance; its size was one krośa, possessing many thousand petals that were fragrant, pure, and soft like kācilinda cotton, such that when the body touched them, one experienced supreme bliss."
The fragrance of these flowers pervades immeasurable hundreds of thousands of worlds; upon smelling the scent and seeing the flowers, the bodhisattvas therein all attain meditative concentration.
We pray that you, O Benevolent One, will cause this rain of flowers to fall within this assembly.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Swift Eloquence focused his mind with pure intent; before long, through the power of the great majestic spiritual sustenance of the Bodhisattva Great Space Treasury, such flowers rained down from the midst of the sky.
At that time, when the assembly in this gathering saw these flowers, each attained the *samādhi* called "Delighting in Flowers.
Emerging from their concentration, they praised the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Noble One!
By the power of your sustaining wisdom (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*), may all sentient beings likewise obtain such power.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva in the assembly named Ratnavyūha, who addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
“O Mahāsattva! I pray that you will cause fine gold dust to rain down from the void for my sake and for the sake of all sentient beings.
Before these words had even concluded, immeasurable gold dust descended from the void like rain.
The Bodhisattva Ratnavyūha spoke again:
"May all manner of jewels rain down from the sky.
Before he had finished speaking, immeasurable and innumerable varieties of mani-jewels—of various names, various colors, and various kinds—rained down from the sky like a torrential shower.
That is to say: gold, silver, crystal, vaidūrya, agate, red pearl, musāragalva treasure,
auspicious-store treasure, uṣṇīṣa-vimalaprabha treasure, and moonlight treasure.
...the sun-light jewel, the illuminating jewel, the supreme light jewel, the Jambū-river light jewel, the fire-light jewel,
the mother-of-pearl, jade, coral, and sapphire jewels, the virtue-treasury jewel,
the tranquil light jewel, the jewel that clarifies turbid water, the indestructible radiance jewel, and the eye-establishing jewel...
Jewels: the Revolving Jewel, the Śākalanka Jewel, the Victorious Jewel, the Greatly Victorious Jewel, the Jewel of Blazing Majestic Power,
the Jewel of the King of Auspicious Treasuries, the Vajra-stamen Jewel, the World-Illuminating Jewel, the Light-Taste Jewel,
the Holding-Light Crescent-Moon Jewel, the Jambūnada Jewel, and the Jambudvīpa-Light Jewel.
The Jewel of Thousandfold Radiance, the Jewel of Torch-like Flame, the Jewel of Supreme Adornment, the Jewel that Quells Heat, the Jewel Free from Torment,
the Jewel that Eliminates Disease, the Jewel of Pure Eyes, the Jewels of Pure Ears,
Nose, Tongue, Body, and Mind, the Jewel of Illuminating Limbs, the Jewel of Illumination, the Jewel of Blue Light, and the Jewel of Yellow Light.

Crystal jewels, white crystal jewels, and net-jewels—to summarize, a rain of all such immeasurable varieties of jewels fell; the names of such boundless treasures could not be fully recounted even in an eon.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Time addressed the Bodhisattva Great Space Treasury, saying: "O Mahāsattva!

In this Sahā world, there are immeasurable sentient beings undergoing suffering; they are destitute and famished, lacking all food and drink; they wear tattered and worn-out clothes, or are even naked."
As for the various hungry ghosts who wander with naked bodies, tormented by hunger and thirst, their hair covering their forms as they constantly crave discarded mucus,
saliva, pus, and blood— may you conceive compassion for such beings as these, raining down food and clothing to satisfy and sustain them.

Then, by the power of his empowerment, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha caused a rain of various foods and drinks, diverse garments, and hundreds of thousands of colors and forms—immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable—to fall from the sky. These were supremely exquisite, fine, and soft, surpassing even kācilinda cotton; when they touched the body, they brought forth the utmost bliss.
Within this trichiliocosm, all sentient beings who are impoverished, destitute, and orphaned, as well as all hungry ghosts, shall be fully satisfied by these sublime foods and excellent garments.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva in the assembly named King of Physicians, who addressed the Bodhisattva Great Space Treasury, saying: "O Mahāsattva!

In this world, immeasurable sentient beings are afflicted by various diseases; moreover, they have no relatives to care for them, and being entangled by illness, they undergo great suffering and distress."
"I pray that for the sake of these sentient beings, you may rain down these supreme medicinal herbs, so that all those who are afflicted may be completely healed.
Before he had finished speaking, immeasurable ambrosial and wondrous medicines immediately rained from the void;
by virtue of these medicines, all those who were ill took them and were entirely cured.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Destroyer of Evil Realms who addressed the Bodhisattva Great Space Treasury, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!
We pray that you will, through great compassion, pacify all sentient beings in the three evil realms who are undergoing various intense sufferings."

Before these words had even been finished, a great radiance immediately issued forth from the sky, illuminating the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; all those sentient beings therein were relieved of their manifold sufferings and attained peace and happiness.

Furthermore, from the sky there rained down various flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, banners, pennants, parasols, canopies, lamps, music, male and female servants, wives and concubines, youths, and court ladies.

Elephants, horses, chariots, dwellings, cities, towns, villages, kingdoms, palaces, towers, gardens, windows, couches, precious jewels, litters, and vehicles drawn by four oxen, sixteen oxen, or even up to a thousand oxen—all these descended from the void like rain;
this was entirely due to the power of the empowerment of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja.
He addressed the assembly again, saying:
"Sons of good family!
You should all take such items as these and give them away according to your needs, so that you may fulfill the dāna-pāramitā."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Śīlālaṃkāra who addressed the bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
"O son of good family!
You have already rained down the *dānapāramitā*; why do you not further rain down the *śīlapāramitā*?"
Before these words had even been finished, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all together praised the merit of the adornment of the *śīlapāramitā*.
Thus, the sound praising the merit of ethical discipline issued from the sky;
likewise, the sounds praising the merits of the adornments of patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom issued forth in the same manner.
Furthermore, I have heard that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas utter hundreds of thousands of phrases praising all phenomena as neither increasing nor decreasing;
by this sound of the Dharma, the trichiliocosm is awakened, causing immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to cultivate and study the three vehicles and thereby attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabha who addressed the bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
"O Gaganagañja, does your treasury of space manifest benefits for sentient beings only within this world-system, or can you likewise manifest such deeds in other world-systems as well?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, saying:
"Son of good family!
You have attained the stainless, wondrously pure divine eye; you should now observe the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—what do you see?"

When these words had been spoken, the Universal Radiance then used his divine eye to observe the immeasurable, incalculable worlds of the ten directions; the rain of precious objects, food, drink, and clothing was exactly like that in this world, without any decrease.
Furthermore, he heard the sounds of all the subtle and wondrous Dharma being proclaimed in the air, likewise neither increasing nor decreasing.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance, having witnessed these events, was filled with profound wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He praised the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja with an udāna:
"Inconceivable and immeasurable is your power, yet you are able to suddenly manifest such various treasures throughout all worlds!

We pray that by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the sustaining power of your own virtue, all sentient beings in this assembly and in other worlds may universally behold these myriad jewels and universally hear the Dharma-sound of space."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, acting in accordance with those words, again rained down such various kinds of jewels that all sentient beings in this assembly and in lands of other directions were able to see them, and each of them gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, there were five hundred women in the great city of Rājagṛha who went together to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha was.
Having arrived, they addressed him, saying:

"We have heard, O Noble One, that you are able to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings. Yet now our husbands have all died, and we do not know their destination; we only pray that the Great Being will show us so that we may see them."

At that time, by the power of his majestic spiritual authority, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja caused each of the five hundred women to manifest the form of their respective husbands before the Bodhisattva.
Then Ākāśagarbha addressed the women, saying:
"Sisters! You should consider whether this is your original husband or not."
Each of those women beheld her own husband, and a mixture of sorrow and joy welled up within them.

Then those men each followed their respective wives back to their original homes. During the seven days, he preached the Dharma for the women, causing them all to achieve realization and resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, abiding in the stage of non-retrogression.
Then the five hundred women went together to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha was, and with one mind and in unison, they praised him with these verses:
“We now understand this nature of phenomena, Which is like an illusion or a phantom, having the nature of space;
He has manifested as our husband, And now we have accomplished the most supreme deed.”
Since all these phenomena are mere transformations, fundamentally empty, mindless, and unmoving;
by means of this, one penetrates the outflow-free dharmas and never again follows after the various afflictions.
Therefore, we all resolve upon bodhicitta, Vowing to deliver and rescue the multitudes of sentient beings;
May you grant us our prophecy, That we shall attain buddhahood and save sentient beings.
The Tathāgata named Suvinita extensively cultivated all practices in future ages;
we have obtained this wondrous rain of Dharma, and for this reason we praise the Great Guide.
At that time, there were also five hundred men who were about to be harmed by bandits when they heard a voice from the sky saying:
"You should know that there is a bodhisattva named Mahāgaganagañja, who is able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings who are in a state of terror."
"You all should take refuge and prostrate yourselves; you shall certainly suffer no harm.
Then, out of fear, those people all became single-minded and, with different mouths but one voice, spoke these words:
"Namo to the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja!"
As these words were spoken, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja manifested five hundred people who descended from the sky and stood before those men, saying to the bandits:
"These people are impoverished; why do you seek to harm them?"
"It would be better to kill us;
we shall now provide you with clothing, necklaces, and all necessary things so that you lack for nothing—do not take his life.

Thereupon, those bandits killed the emanated person. Those five hundred people were all freed from their fear and became profoundly at ease. Together they went to the place of the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated themselves at his feet, and spoke these words:

“We have all now preserved our lives and spirits through the Great Master; therefore, we have come to pay our respects. We do not know how to repay such vast kindness; we only pray that you will preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for us, so that we may together uphold it and accomplish the practice of the two benefits.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed them, saying:
"Sons of good family!
Since you now have nothing to fear, each of you should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; thus shall you achieve the fulfillment of both self-benefit and the benefit of others."

When these words had been spoken, they all simultaneously gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immediately offered exquisite garments worth hundreds of thousands to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja as an act of worship.
Having thus made offerings to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, one has thereby made offerings to all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed upon them all the prediction of enlightenment:

"In a future age, after immeasurable kalpas have passed and they have cultivated the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), they shall attain Buddhahood, all bearing the same title: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Fearless."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, saying: "Noble son!
Since you attained this treasury of space, how much time has passed until now, such that it remains neither parched nor exhausted, providing for all beings without end?"
Gaganagañja said, "Venerable One, what do you think?"
"How could there ever be an exhaustion of space? "No, Great Being! said Ākāśagarbha.
“In this way, Venerable Śāriputra!
Just as the intrinsic nature of space is inexhaustible, so too are all the roots of goodness and merits that I now possess.”

Why is this so? For the sake of Bodhi, I have accumulated immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness throughout countless eons and dedicated them all; like that space, they are inexhaustible. Therefore, they provide for all beings without depletion or exhaustion.

"As you have said, regarding how long these treasuries have been established in this space: from the time I first gave rise to the bodhicitta until now, the treasuries in the sky have existed for exactly that length of time."
Then Śāriputra spoke again: "How much time has passed since you first resolved to attain bodhicitta? He replied:
“The Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows [their] proximity and distance.
Śāriputra then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“After how long has this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha been resolved upon bodhicitta?
The Buddha said, “Good son!...”
"If I were to explain it in full detail, those among gods and humans who hear it would all give rise to doubt and confusion. Śāriputra said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and reveal this to me;
furthermore, there are immeasurable multitudes in this assembly who all look up to you with longing thirst, so I pray that you will explain it for them so that they may attain pure faith.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Suppose there were as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; let every single grain of dust therein constitute one kalpa. Such kalpas of dust would constitute one lakṣa."

Furthermore, for immeasurable nayuta-koṭi atoms of kalpas—indeed, for as many kalpas as there are in all those atoms—the Ākāśagarbha bodhisattva gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and has passed through that much time.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When that Ākāśagarbha first resolved his mind on enlightenment, what was the name of the Tathāgata he encountered?”
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"At that time, a Tathāgata appeared in the world named Sarvavijayapraṇidhānaratnatejorāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. The world was named Sarvabuddhakṣetrasaṃdarśana, and the eon was named Ratnavyūha."
Śāriputra! As for all the meritorious adornments achieved by those manifested Buddha-fields and worlds, I could not exhaustively describe them even with a lifespan of an eon.
Śāriputra! The site of enlightenment where that Blessed One sat extended for a thousand worlds, and he was further attended by a retinue of bodhisattvas whose number transcended all calculation.
Śāriputra! At that time, there was a universal monarch named Sarvadevābhiṣikta who ruled over a trichiliocosm.
That king also possessed inconceivable treasuries of jewels and had thirty-six thousand sons, all of whom were born through transformation and possessed great majestic power.
In that Buddha-world, even the name of "woman" does not exist. Śāriputra!

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, has a lifespan of one hundred thousand kalpas. All the consecrated kings among the devas served that Buddha for forty intermediate kalpas; within a single day, they used a thousand koṭis of supreme and exquisite requisites, piling them as high as Mount Sumeru as an offering—the mass of merit thus accumulated is inconceivable.
The king’s sons and all his retinue all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra, do not view that Universal Sovereign King of All Devas at that time as anyone else; he was none other than the present Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
