This Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha has donned inconceivable armor, and having dwelled in the Mahāyāna for so long, he is able to realize such majestic and virtuous dharmic practices."
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja has made offerings to Buddhas exceeding the number of sands in immeasurable Ganges Rivers; under those Buddhas he purified his bodhicitta, and because his bodhicitta was purified under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, his resolute intention (āśaya) became pure.”
When the intention is purified as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the application becomes purified;
when the application is purified as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the superior intention becomes purified;
when the superior intention is purified as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) becomes purified.
When the *dānapāramitā* is purified as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the *śīlapāramitā* is purified;
when the *śīlapāramitā* is purified as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the *kṣāntipāramitā* is purified;
when the *kṣāntipāramitā* is purified as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the *vīryapāramitā* is purified.
The purification of the perfection of diligence as numerous as the sands of the Ganges results in the purification of the perfection of meditative concentration;
the purification of the perfection of meditative concentration as numerous as the sands of the Ganges results in the purification of the perfection of wisdom;
the purification of the perfection of wisdom as numerous as the sands of the Ganges results in the purification of the perfection of skillful means.
When the *pāramitā* of skillful means, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is purified, then the unimpeded mind and unimpeded light of all sentient beings are purified;
when the unimpeded mind and unimpeded light of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are purified, then great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is purified;
and so on, until great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the wisdom of great supernormal powers are purified, whereby body, speech, and mind are purified.
Through the purification of a mind as vast as the sands of the Ganges, one mark of a Great Man is purified;

thus it is explained in detail that from the thirty-two marks of a Great Man up to all the marks of a Great Man, the purification of their roots of goodness results in the purification of the Treasury of Space.
Śāriputra! Because it is thus, this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is able to manifest all the practices of bodhisattvas within space. Śāriputra!
Just as space is without end or limit;
so too, son of good family, are all the vows and practices of a bodhisattva pure and inexhaustible. For this reason, it is called the "Treasury of Space."
When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly attained inexhaustible wealth and treasures, and fulfilled their vows through the patience of the treasury of space.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva in the assembly named Dharmarāja, who addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
"I vow to hear the sound of the sublime Dharma from the midst of space."
Gaganagañja said: "Good son! Generate the utmost reverence;
dwelling with a mind focused on space as if it were the Great Teacher, I shall cause you to hear the sound of the sublime Dharma."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmarāja, together with the great assembly, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, paid homage toward the sky, and remained gazing up at it. Through the power of the empowerment of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, there emerged from mid-air these verses:
"The mind and all phenomena Are all like space;
I shall now speak of a small portion— Listen to me in due order."
Because space has no height, its lowliness is likewise unattainable;
all phenomena are also thus—their nature has neither high nor low.
Space has no arising, and its cessation is likewise unattainable.
All phenomena are likewise thus: their arising and ceasing cannot be apprehended.
Within emptiness there is no diminution, nor is there any nature of increase;
all phenomena are like space, equal and without increase or decrease.
In space there is no darkness, nor is there anything to be defiled;
the nature of the mind is likewise, being neither darkened nor defiled.
Just as with the light of the sun and moon, space remains free from attachment and defilement.
The mind is likewise like space, Without craving and without defilement.
Just as in space, A spear or a halberd cannot cause injury;
so too, when a Bodhisattva contemplates all sufferings, there is no heart of sorrow or fear.
Just as when the sky rains down ambrosia, the void remains without attachment or delight;
so too, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to stained or affectionate thoughts toward fame and profit.
Unmoved by slander or praise, their mind remains ever tranquil amidst suffering and joy.
Though the great earth may tremble, the nature of space remains eternally constant.
So too, the Bodhisattva remains far removed from the conceptual mind regarding worldly phenomena;
just as fire does not burn empty space, the Bodhisattva is untainted by delusion.
Space is free from arising and ceasing; the dharma-realm has no coming or going.
All forms appear within space; all phenomena abide dependent upon the mind.
Space is formless and not material; the nature of the mind is likewise so.
Space is merely a provisional name; the mind, intellect, and consciousness are just the same.
Because space is boundless, the virtues of the wise are such as this.
Just as tracks in the sky are difficult to form, so too is the practice for enlightenment signless.
As space has no prior limit, the nature of the five aggregates is likewise;
the four great elements of the past and present are empty, and the future is also thus.
Just as the realm of space cannot be filled by the conflagration at the end of an eon,
so too the mind, into which the stream of the five desires pours, is difficult to satisfy.
The Buddha has taught the great verses of the Dharma, which transcend the world and are free from desire.
The Dharma teachings are vast and boundless, Like space, there is nothing to be apprehended.
To thoroughly understand the true Dharma Is its indestructible and non-abiding nature;
Knowing that this nature is itself no-nature, Right view abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The nature of sound is empty and non-existent; the nature of speech is likewise so.
The essence of phenomena is fundamentally beyond words; there is neither sound nor speech.
All dharmas are like illusions and mirages; dreams, shadows, and echoes are all empty.
Quiescent and beyond comparison, it is metaphorically illustrated for the sake of guidance.
The Dharma is signless, yet signs are spoken of; both the subjective and objective signs are absent.
The Bodhisattva realizes suchness, which, like space, is without anything to be apprehended.
Without attachment and without anything possessed, without conceptualization and without proliferation;
because there are no sentient beings to deliver, suchness itself is the bodhisattva.
Sentient beings are fundamentally in nirvāṇa; those who hear this and are not terrified, donning the armor of valor, are called those who abide in bodhi.
They are like a master of illusions who destroys many illusory beings.
In reality, there is nothing that is harmed, and the same applies to the beings who are delivered.
Illusions, magical transformations, and sentient beings—the Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise so.
If one realizes their identical nature, that which lacks intrinsic nature is itself the nature.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has attained the treasury of space;
He suffices all sentient beings, yet this treasury is inexhaustible.
A mass of boundless merit, he has attained this pure treasury.
Observe the nature of all phenomena: its nature is without movement.
You should know that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
because they are inexhaustible, this treasury of Dharma is inconceivable.
The World-Honored One constantly proclaims that four things are inexhaustible:
sentient beings, space, the bodhicitta, and the Buddha-dharma.
Just as worldly objects can be said to have an end, [these four do not].
There is no thing and nothing that can be exhausted; therefore it is called inexhaustible.
As for the dharma of ultimate extinction, the dharma of extinction cannot itself be exhausted.
There is neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion; therefore it is called inexhaustible.
"If a person hears this Dharma, they are called a Bodhisattva who has attained awakening;
one should know that such a person will swiftly abide in the path to Bodhi.

At that time, having heard these verses, eight thousand Bodhisattvas within the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and twelve thousand devaputras dwelling in the air gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, Scroll Four;
The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, Scroll Five.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Da Guangzhi Daxingshan Monastery, who held the rank of Kaifu Yitong Sansi, was specially promoted to the position of Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, was a Duke of Suku with a fief of three thousand households, was granted purple robes, was posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and was given the title Dajian (Great Mirror). By Imperial Decree: At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva named Chang Xiqi (Ever-Curiosity), who rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I do not know from where this sound has emerged?”
The Buddha said, "Good son!
You should question that Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha; he shall explain it for you."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ever-Seeking the Extraordinary addressed the Bodhisattva Great Space Treasury, saying: "O Mahāsattva!
I do not now know from where such a sound of the Dharma has emerged?"
"I only pray that you, O Benevolent One,
will explain this for me. Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva said,
"O son of good family!
"What do you think?
From what does that echo within the valley arise?
The Bodhisattva Constantly Seeking the Extraordinary replied:
"It is manifested through the sound of others.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha said: "Noble son!"
Is that echo the body? Is it the mind? Or is it form?
"Is this sound real?
Does it exist as a substantial entity? "No."
"O Mahāsattva!
An echo has no intrinsic nature; it is manifested due to sound. How could it have any reality?
"O Son of Good Family!"
Just as an echo is not real and exists only because of sound;

so too is the Dharma-sound produced from space: it is manifested by inconceivable wisdom and arises from the emptiness of the mind itself through its grasping. Thus, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), yet it is not the case that cyclic existence itself can manifest that sound.

"Good son! Observe the profound principle of what is produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions: although effects are elicited in dependence upon causes, there is no inherent nature of cause or effect that undergoes transmigration, for these two phenomena lack self-nature and lack an agent.
If one knows that causes and conditions cannot elicit an effect, then one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally without conjunction."
Why is this so? As the Blessed One has said:
"If one knows that defilement is itself purity, then even without abandoning defilement, it is naturally pure."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of afflictions is fundamentally pure.

These two dharmas—namely, defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*)—are called "provisional designations" (*prajñapti-pada*), for they are established based upon the limit of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-koṭi*).
Within the limit of ultimate reality (*paramārthakoṭi*), neither affliction (*saṃkleśa*) nor purification (*vyavadāna*) can be apprehended.

The limit of ultimate reality is called the "limitless" (*ananta*); that very limitlessness is called the "actual limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*). This actual limit is the limit of emptiness (*śūnyatākoṭi*); this limit of emptiness is the limit of self (*ātmanakoṭi*); and this limit of self is the limit of all phenomena (*sarvadharmakoṭi*).

If one knows the limit of all phenomena, the limit of emptiness, the limit of tranquility, the limit of supreme tranquility, and the gateways of all limits, then one will have no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena and will attain unimpeded wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the bodhisattva Sadāścarya: "Good son,
for what reason are you named Sadāścarya?"
He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
Regarding all dharmas, I constantly apply myself with diligent vigor and give rise to a sense of wonder; yet though I desire to fulfill them, I am unable to understand them."

Furthermore, regarding all the practices of bodhisattvas, they give rise to a sense of wonder, wishing to enter the wisdom that understands the mental activities of all sentient beings yet being unable to fully comprehend it; they wish that all afflictions and demonic deeds may find no opportunity against them yet being unable to fully comprehend this. For this reason, they constantly give rise to a sense of wonder toward the Dharma;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, they are called "Ever-Wondrous."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
This noble being possesses such clear eloquence; he is unstained by any of the dharmas of all Buddhas, and he does not grasp at the dharmas he preaches."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ratnaśrī who addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying: "Noble son,
I pray that you will explain to me a samādhi, so that I may practice it according to your instructions."
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī, saying: “Noble son!
There is a samādhi called ‘The Pure Intention of a Bodhisattva,’ which can remove obstacles on the path and lead one to enlightenment.”
There is a samādhi named "Unobstructed Radiance of All Sentient Beings," because it provides illumination for sentient beings;
there is a samādhi named "Protecting Self and Others," because it transcends all harm and affliction from others;
there is a samādhi named "Stainless," because it enables the attainment of mental purity.
There is a samādhi named Universal Illumination, because it can increase all wholesome dharmas;
there is a samādhi named Majestic Beauty, because it can attain the nature of clarity and purity;
there is a samādhi named Lofty and Vast, because it can attain the state of having an invisible crown of the head.
There is a samādhi named "Detachment," because it can subdue all afflictions;
there is a samādhi named "Revolution," because it can turn to the right and enter the true path;
there is a samādhi named "Reversal," because it can overturn the heterodox views of external paths regarding false causes.
There is a samādhi named "Creating Joy," because one experiences happiness while wandering through the gardens of all dharmas;
there is a samādhi named "Reaching the Ultimate," because one plants pure conduct and reaches the subsequent stages;
there is a samādhi named "Majestic Power," because one attains mastery over the mind and is free from weakness or inferiority.
There is a samādhi named Entering Equality, because the mind is equal toward all sentient beings;
there is a samādhi named Knowing Deeds, because one can know the fruits of karma according to what has been done;
there is a samādhi named Lion Banner, because one is free from fear and the hair on the body does not stand on end.
There is a samādhi named Courageous Mind, because it can eliminate all afflictions and māras;
there is a samādhi named Puṇḍarīka, because it attains freedom from defilement within all worlds;
there is a samādhi named Padma, because it is said to attain the adornment of the mind.
There is a samādhi named Radiant Adornment, because it can illumine all Buddha-fields;
there is a samādhi named Skillful Action, because it can forever eliminate hatred and attachment;
there is a samādhi named Banner Adornment, because it can illuminate the teachings of all Buddhas.
There is a samādhi named "Possessing a Torch," because it can illuminate all habitual tendencies;
there is a samādhi named "Sun Lamp," because it can eliminate all darkness;
there is a samādhi named "Solar Revolution," because it can observe the minds of all sentient beings.
There is a samādhi named "Treasury of Merit," because all dharmas of merit arise in accordance with it;
there is a samādhi named "Nārāyaṇa," because it can subdue all challenges from other disputants;
there is a samādhi named "Firmness," because it can obtain an indestructible body like a vajra.
There is a samādhi named Endowed with Firmness, because it can transcend all worldly wisdom;
there is a samādhi named Maṇḍala, because it can attain non-retrogressive supernormal powers;
there is a samādhi named Vajra-field, because it signifies the ability to proceed to the site of enlightenment.
There is a samādhi named Vajra-like, for it is well able to pierce through all phenomena of outflows;
there is a samādhi named Endowed with Practice, for it can know the various mental activities of sentient beings;
there is a samādhi named Purifying the Ground, for it can cause one to remain far removed from the faults of craving and desire.
There is a samādhi named "Crushing," because it can crush the four māra-enemies;
there is a samādhi named "Sun-like Contemplation of the Body," because it can contemplate all the characteristics of the physical body;
there is a samādhi named "Unblinking," because it can cause one-pointed concentration on a single object.
There is a samādhi named Entering Space, because it can purify all minds of diligence;
there is a samādhi named Non-contention, because it can transcend all objects of perception;
there is a samādhi named Stainless Wheel, because it can turn the pure and wondrous wheel of Dharma.
There is a samādhi named Lightning Flash, because it can observe that the mind perishes moment by moment;
there is a samādhi named Skillful Creation of Excellent Conditions, because it can swiftly bring all wholesome dharmas to fulfillment;
there is a samādhi named Capable of Purification, because it can sever all unwholesome dharmas.
There is a samādhi called Adornment of the Body, because it fulfills the primary marks and secondary signs of a Great Man;
there is a samādhi called Adornment of Speech, because it delights the multitude by proclaiming the Dharma with the Brahma-voice;
there is a samādhi called Adornment of the Mind, because it prevents all wholesome dharmas from being lost or destroyed.
There is a samādhi named Fearlessness, because it enables one to attain firmness and non-retrogression;
there is a samādhi named Equal Giving, because it makes no distinction among sentient beings;
there is a samādhi named Accumulation of Precepts, because it causes all vows to be completely fulfilled.
There is a samādhi named Armor of Forbearance, because it is able to disregard one’s own body and life;
there is a samādhi named Firmness of Diligence, because it is able to swiftly attain all supernatural powers (abhijñā);
there is a samādhi named Immeasurable Treasury, because it is able to cause even the Brahma Kings to be subdued.
There is a samādhi named "Non-existence," which renders the formless realm capable;
there is a samādhi named "Lofty Banner," because one cannot be overwhelmed or subdued by sentient beings;
there is a samādhi named "Lofty Lamp," because it skillfully observes the ten directions.
There is a samādhi named Wisdom Torch, because it can destroy all hindrances, veils, and entanglements;
there is a samādhi named Ocean Seal, because it can manifest the various karmic actions performed;
there is a samādhi named Infinite Revolution, because it can sever all evil views.
There is a samādhi named "Emptiness," because it is able to leave behind all perceptions of signs;
there is a samādhi named "Signlessness," because it is able to sever all conceptualizations and discriminations;
there is a samādhi named "Wishlessness," because it is well able to purify all characteristics of wishes.
There is a samādhi named "Immovable," because it can destroy all moving thoughts;
there is a samādhi named "Endowed with Sound," because it can skillfully attain unimpeded eloquence;
there is a samādhi named "Universal Retention," because it can retain all the teachings one has heard.
There is a samādhi named Pure Mindfulness, because it enables one to skillfully uphold all the Buddha-dharmas;
there is a samādhi named Inexhaustible, because it causes all sentient beings to give rise to joy;
there is a samādhi named Jewel Adornment, because it enables all to obtain the "jewel-hand."
There is a samādhi named "Following Along," because it enables one to follow sentient beings and attain the wisdom of their minds;
there is a samādhi named "Knowing the Destination," because it causes those who proceed toward existence to awaken;
there is a samādhi named "Entry of the Mind," because it can cause both the mind and its mental factors to be completely purified.
There is a samādhi called "Dharma Cloud," because it rains down the rain of Dharma according to one's resolute conviction;
there is a samādhi called "Recollection of the Buddha," because it can realize the pure Dharma of ambrosia;
there is a samādhi called "Recollection of the Dharma," because it can realize all wholesome dharmas that are free from desire.
There is a samādhi called "mindfulness of the Saṅgha," because it causes one not to regress from the Buddha-dharma;
there is a samādhi called "mindfulness of relinquishment," because it enables one to relinquish all requisites;
there is a samādhi called "mindfulness of the precepts," because it establishes the root of all Buddha-dharmas.
There is a samādhi named "Recollection of the Devas," because it causes one to be without fault regarding pure dharmas;
there is a samādhi named "Entry into the Dharma Realm," because it knows that all dharmas mutually enter one another;
there is a samādhi named "Nature of Space," because it causes all dharmas to be entirely without obstruction.
There is a samādhi named "Unarisen Nature," because it enables one to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
there is a samādhi named "Similar and Dissimilar," because through skillful wisdom one is able to maintain mastery over all distinctions of words and phrases;
there is a samādhi named "Stainless Seal of Sublime Speech," because by attaining this samādhi, a bodhisattva is able to realize great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) through wisdom in a single instant.
"Good son! These eighty-three samādhi-gates each have five hundred samādhi-gates as their retinue; when calculated in total, they constitute forty thousand samādhi-gates."
Purity and defilement together constitute eighty thousand gateways to samādhi.

Each of these—along with their prior, subsequent, and intermediate limits, as well as inexhaustible knowledge—possesses five hundred gateways to samādhi. Together with purity and defilement, these form eighty-four thousand gateways to samādhi. To such an extent do these samādhis serve as the *udāna* for that many dharmas, further forming the eighty-four thousand distinct aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*) of the Tathāgata, due to the eighty-four thousand different mental dispositions of sentient beings.
"Good son! The fundamental *udāna* causes all sentient beings to enter the practice of the Buddha’s wisdom, for it gives rise to awakening.

Furthermore, the entire wisdom of all Buddhas enters the mental activities of all sentient beings; the treasury of Dharma thus taught is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, such that it could not be fully expounded even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas."
"I have now briefly explained a small portion of this samādhi gate.

When he spoke these words, sixteen thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) regarding the samādhi gate, and eighty-four thousand humans and devas resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"

"Quickly speak this Dharma-gate of the merits of such samādhi, which proclaims the subtle and supreme wisdom of the Tathāgata; for you have personally realized this Dharma-gate through your own body, awakening to it without depending on another."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions is the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja able to rain down various jewels from the void before the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī, saying: "Good son!

I recall that in the past, immeasurable and incalculable eons ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vimalajvālānantaprabhārāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world was named Mekhalā, and his eon was named Guṇaprabha."

"Good son! That world of Mikhalā is a land of peace and happiness where the population is flourishing. Its ground is composed of the seven treasures and is as level as the palm of a hand; it is pure and soft like kācilinda cotton, and when one walks upon it, one experiences supreme bliss at every touch. It is covered with Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with various kinds of jewels; it is demarcated by eight paths lined with rows of precious trees.
Like the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, whatever is enjoyed there accords perfectly with one's wishes."
All the hosts of humans and devas dwell together in palaces and towers; whatever food or drink they think of appears before them according to their wishes. Good son!
That Tathāgata Vimalajvālānantaprabhā-rāja has a community of sixty nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, there was a wheel-turning sage king named Puṇyavibhūṣaṇa (Adorned with Merit), who possessed the seven treasures. His royal city and palace were like those inhabited in Jambudvīpa; extending four yojanas in each of the four directions—east, west, south, and north—it was adorned with an interlacing array of the seven treasures.
Furthermore, there were five hundred gardens, magnificently decorated and reflecting one another's splendor.
"Good son! This King Puṇyavipāka-alaṃkāra had eighty-four thousand court ladies, all of whom were upright and exquisite;
he had forty thousand sons, all of whom were dignified and handsome, possessing strength and valor beyond compare."
He had two precious daughters:
the first was named Śrītejas and the second was named Śrīprabhā.
Surrounded by his court ladies and princes, the king proceeded to the Garden of Lovely Adornments (*Priyavyūha-udyāna*), where he enjoyed himself with sightseeing, singing, and dancing.

From the wombs of these two precious women, each gave birth to a son through miraculous transformation— of incomparable beauty, radiant in appearance, having planted roots of goodness in past lives and perfected the power of their vows, and aspiring toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— one named Siṃha,
the other named Siṃhavikrāntagāmin.
Immediately after being born through transformation, they raised their voices in unison and addressed the Father King with these verses:
"Past deeds of both good and evil do not perish; Offerings made to the Tathāgata are likewise never lost.
Because the aspiration for Bodhicitta has not been abandoned, One's firm and extensive learning shall also not be forgotten."
Not failing in generosity and pure precepts, Accomplishing the practice of patience and gentleness;
Recognizing kindness and repaying it by performing virtuous deeds, Diligently never forsaking the vow for enlightenment.
Through single-minded meditative concentration one attains liberation; with both concentration and wisdom, the mind is free from delusion.
By being able to cultivate the work of wisdom and remaining ever unmoving, one swiftly realizes Bodhi.
Having extinguished all afflictions, one remains unstained; Because of this, one is not born from a womb.
One is born by transformation upon a lotus flower, Just as a lotus in water remains unsullied.
In the east there is a Buddha named King of Physicians; we have come from there to seek the Dharma.
Having approached and made offerings to the Stainless Buddha, we have accomplished the unimpeded wisdom of the three periods of time.
"Father King, you should go together with me to the Buddha's presence, to serve, pay homage, and cultivate merit;
for it is extremely difficult to encounter a Tathāgata appearing in the world, like the blooming of an udumbara flower."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with supreme joy;
together with his wife, children, and attendants, and accompanied by a retinue of one thousand koṭis, he went to that place to behold the Tathāgata.
He paid respectful homage to that Blessed One with great earnestness, making offerings of exquisite flowers and fragrant ointments;
bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he circumambulated him to the right, and stood before the Buddha with palms joined and body upright.
Siṃha and Vīrapada likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; having paid homage to the Buddha’s feet, they praised him with these verses:
“May you be our supreme refuge for deliverance, And act as a lamp for those blinded by the world.”
Skillfully penetrating the mental dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings, you are able to bring them to awakening according to their respective convictions.
Now my father, the King, relying on his noble status, is entangled by the five desires;
he does not go to approach the Tathāgata, nor does he lose the opportunity to make offerings or hear the Dharma.

Excellent, World-Honored One, give rise to compassion; We pray you will proclaim the most supreme path to enlightenment, So that all who have heard the Dharma May never regress from the Buddha Vehicle.
Then the Buddha leaped into the air, rising higher than eighty tala trees, and said:
"O King, now listen to my most supreme Dharma; having heard it, practice according to what has been taught."
The five desires are impermanent and life is difficult to preserve; the body is like morning dew or a bubble upon the water.
Sensual pleasures are like dreams or playful frolics—who among the wise would give rise to craving and attachment?
Those who indulge in sensual desires are never satisfied; they only cause them to blaze more fiercely and increase their craving.
The foolish follow after sense objects without ceasing; only the sages of wisdom are able to know contentment.
The five aggregates are like illusions and lack solidity; one should skillfully examine how they deceive the world.
The elements are like venomous snakes, and the six sense bases are like an empty village.
There is no king, no country, and no wife or children; one's companions are nothing but impermanence.
Only generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and diligence serve as one’s companions in this life and in lives to come.
Behold the power of my supernormal faculties and majestic virtue; My marks and signs are sublime and I possess eloquence.
If you desire such karma in future lives, You should resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta.
Having heard the Dharma, King Puṇyavipāka, together with a multitude of seventy koṭis—
including his wife, children, attendants, and all his kinsmen— aroused the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta.
All have declared that they have already resolved upon the supreme mind, vowing to extensively deliver all classes of sentient beings;
they pledge to practice the extraordinary conduct of bodhi, aspiring to attain Buddhahood as the Honored One of the world.

“Good son! At that time, King Puṇyavipāka-vyūha, having heard these verses from the Buddha, together with his retinue, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘World-Honored One!...’”
"I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and accept my offerings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, giving rise to a heart of pity, immediately accepted his request.

Thereupon, King Puṇyavanta-vyūha provided various kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—all of which were supreme, exquisite, rare, and faultless treasures—for eighty-four thousand years as an act of worship.

At that time, Siṃha and Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, together with twenty thousand other princes, gave rise to pure faith and renounced their worldly positions of honor to leave the household life and become monks under that Buddha’s Dharma.

At that time, the two sons of the king practiced with diligent vigor; before long, through their cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), they attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

By means of the power of *ṛddhi* (supernatural transformation) and the power of wisdom and vows, they were able to perform the Buddha-work in all Buddha-worlds, extensively preaching the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, and causing immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya numbers of sentient beings to abide in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Good son! After eighty-four thousand years had passed, King Puṇyavipāka-vyūha, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, went to the presence of the Tathāgata Vimalajvālāpramāṇaprabhā-rāja;
there he saw two youths who had left the household life to practice the Way, and he thought to himself:”
"What has this youth gained by leaving the household life?
It is not equal to the merit of my providing him with all manner of musical instruments and articles of enjoyment for eighty-four thousand years."
"Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata Vimalajvālānantaprabha, knowing the king’s thoughts, addressed the youths Siṃha and Śūramati, saying: 'Good sons!'"

"You should manifest the supernormal power of wisdom, the supernormal power of merit, and the supernormal power of strength, so as to eclipse all the majestic splendor of this great assembly, as well as all the light from the palaces of Māra. Reveal the signs of Bodhi, causing this great assembly to give rise to a sense of wonder, to attain right view, and to subdue heterodox arguments. Kindle the great torch of the Dharma to extinguish all afflictions, and sport with the sovereign supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva."
At that time, the Bodhisattvas Siṃha and Śūramgama immediately raised their hands and stroked the great void; the three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways.

Again they raised their hands and stroked the void, whereupon hundreds of thousands of koṭis of celestial music arose in the air, sounding spontaneously without being struck, its tones harmonious and elegant.

Again, raising their hands and stroking as before, there immediately rained down immeasurable, most wondrous celestial flowers never before heard of or seen; they were as soft as *kācilinda* cotton, and when touched by the hand, they brought forth supreme bliss.

Along with various jewels, powdered incense, ointments, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, food, and drink—all manner of requisites for enjoyment and adornment—they filled the entire trichiliocosm, such that the entire assembly experienced what they had never known before.
At that time, the Tathāgata King of Immeasurable Light and Undefiled Radiance addressed King Puṇyavibhūṣaṇarāja, saying:
"Is it possible to know the measure of such vast and extensive giving as this rain of jewels?"
The King said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
The rain of jewels bestowed is like space; its measure cannot be known.”
The Buddha said,

“Great King! If these Bodhisattvas Siṃha and Śūramgama were to employ the power of their supernormal knowledges and wisdom, they could, in a single kṣaṇa, rain down such jewels throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
"May all sentient beings receive whatever they desire according to their wishes, so that all may obtain fulfillment and be made joyful. "Good son!
At that time, there were earth-dwelling devas who proclaimed these words:"
"In a future age, this bodhisattva will surely achieve the treasury of space, able to rain down such jewels from the sky according to whatever is sought by the minds of sentient beings."

In this manner, the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Heaven of Mahābrahmā each informed one another, and all did so in this way.
At that time, the Tathāgata King of Immeasurable Light of Undefiled Radiance immediately confirmed him, saying:
"In this way, you shall become the Treasury of Space.
Having spoken these words, all the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, simultaneously raised their voices and confirmed it in the same manner.
"Good son! When King Puṇyavipāka-vyūha saw such miraculous transformations of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
'World-Honored One!'"
"The power of a bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledges and merit is indeed thus inconceivable.

He then established Prince Jñānavijaya as his successor to the throne, personally relinquished the sovereignty of the kingdom, shaved off his hair, and went forth into homelessness within that Buddha's Dharma to pursue the path.
Having already left the household life, he reflects thus:
"That which is given in renunciation and charity is for the sake of benefiting body, speech, and mind; whereas one who has left the household life causes body, speech, and mind to be entirely pure.
That which is given in renunciation and charity is to relieve lack and deprivation; whereas one who has left the household life has no lack or deprivation whatsoever."
Those who practice giving obtain rewards that are precarious and fragile; those who have left the household life obtain fruits that are firm and solid.
Those who practice giving are possessed by the notion of "mine"; those who have left the household life have nothing to grasp.
Those who practice giving harbor the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); those who have left the household life are free from all views.

Those who practice giving are like infants, playing with joy and possessing no knowledge; whereas those who have left the home life possess the wisdom of tranquility that fully understands all things.

Having reflected thus, he dwelt in seclusion and tranquility; without giving rise to negligence, he applied himself diligently to the cultivation of the Path. Not long thereafter, he attained the five supernormal powers.
"O son of good family!
At that time, do not regard King Puṇyavipāka-alaṃkāra as anyone else; he was none other than Tathāgata Krakucchanda.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃha was my very self;
and the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin was the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja.

This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, has been able to constantly rain down jewels from the treasury of space without ever ceasing.
“Good son! At that time, the prince Jñānavara was none other than the present Bodhisattva Maitreya. Good son!”
"Know that these pleasing and pure teachings of the Dharma, heard through the planting of roots of goodness in past lives, are all the basis for sentient beings.

When this account of the former causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja was spoken, there were one hundred and twenty thousand people who all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the supramundane path of a bodhisattva?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
"Good son! That which is called the supramundane path is as follows:"

The six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, śamatha and vipaśyanā, the four means of attraction, the four immeasurable minds, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.
Good son! This is called the supramundane path of a bodhisattva.
As for "the mundane," it refers to:
Regarding the five aggregates:
in order to seek awakening, the bodhisattva employs wisdom and skillful means to know that form is impermanent, and thus practices giving;

knows that form is suffering, knows that form is selfless, knows that form is tranquil, knows that form is empty, knows that form is signless, knows that form is wishless, knows that form is without activity, knows that form is unarisen, knows that form does not originate, knows that form arises through conditions, knows that form is detached, knows that form is without grasping, knows that form is without the *ālayavijñāna*, knows that form does not manifest, knows that form is like an illusion, knows that form is like a dream, knows that form is like a mirage, the moon in water, an echo, a reflection of light, knows that form is like a reflected image, and like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles—and thus practices giving.
When a bodhisattva practices giving in this manner, they know the suchness of form;
by knowing the suchness of form, they know the suchness of giving;
and by knowing the suchness of giving, they know the suchness of dedication.
Because one knows the suchness of dedication, one attains the suchness of bodhi;
because one attains the suchness of bodhi, one knows the suchness of sentient beings;
because one knows the suchness of sentient beings, one knows the suchness of the self.
Because one knows the suchness of the self, one knows the suchness of all phenomena;
because one knows the suchness of all phenomena, it is the non-false suchness, the unerring suchness, and the non-differentiated suchness. Knowing thus, one practices giving accordingly.
Good son! This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva.
Having thus understood that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one practices giving.

Thus, knowing that consciousness is selfless, knowing that consciousness is quiescent, knowing that consciousness is empty, knowing that consciousness is signless, knowing that consciousness is wishless, knowing that consciousness is without activity, knowing that consciousness is without birth, knowing that consciousness is without arising, knowing that consciousness is dependently originated, knowing that consciousness is detached, knowing that consciousness is without grasping, knowing that consciousness is without the *ālayavijñāna*, knowing that consciousness does not originate, and knowing that consciousness is like a magical illusion, a dream, a mirage, the moon in water, an echo, a reflection in light, and a reflected image—having known that consciousness is without form or characteristics, one practices giving.
When practicing generosity in this manner, because one realizes the suchness of knowledge, one attains the suchness of generosity;
by attaining the suchness of generosity, one attains the suchness of dedication;
and by attaining the suchness of dedication, one attains the suchness of bodhi.
Because one attains the suchness of awakening, one attains the suchness of sentient beings;
because one attains the suchness of sentient beings, one then attains the suchness of the self;
because one attains the suchness of the self, one then attains the suchness of all phenomena.
Because they have realized the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, they practice giving by means of that which is non-suchness, non-false suchness, and non-differentiated suchness. Good son!
This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva.

Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhisattva, having realized that form is impermanent, guards the precepts; even unto realizing that form is like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles, he guards the precepts.
When a bodhisattva thus guards the precepts, they know the suchness of form;
by knowing the suchness of form, they know the suchness of the precepts;
and by the suchness of the precepts, they attain the suchness of dedication.
Because one dedicates toward the suchness of true reality (tathatā), one attains the suchness of awakening;
because of the suchness of awakening, one attains the suchness of sentient beings;
because of the suchness of sentient beings, one realizes the suchness of the self.
Because my suchness is suchness, I attain the suchness of all dharmas;
because the suchness of all dharmas is non-suchness, non-delusory suchness, and non-different suchness, I thereby accord with and protect the precepts.
"Good son! This is called the supramundane path of a bodhisattva.
Having thus understood that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one guards the precepts."
In this way, having realized that consciousness is without form or characteristics, one guards the precepts.
When guarding the precepts in this manner, because of the realization of the suchness of consciousness, one attains the suchness of the precepts;
because of the suchness of the precepts, one attains the suchness of dedication.
Because of dedicating toward suchness, one attains the suchness of awakening;
because of the suchness of awakening, one attains the suchness of sentient beings;
because of the suchness of sentient beings, one knows the suchness of the self.
Because my suchness is such, I attain the suchness of all phenomena;
because the suchness of all phenomena is non-suchness, non-delusory suchness, and non-different suchness, I thereby follow and protect the precepts.
"Good son! This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva. Furthermore, good son!"

Having realized that form is impermanent, the bodhisattva practices patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; even unto realizing that form is like grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles, he practices wisdom.
When a bodhisattva practices prajñā in this manner, they know the suchness of form;
by knowing the suchness of form, they attain the suchness of prajñā;
and by the suchness of prajñā, they attain the suchness of dedication.
Because of dedicating toward suchness, one attains the suchness of bodhi;
because of the suchness of bodhi, one attains the suchness of sentient beings;
because of the suchness of sentient beings, one knows the suchness of the self.
Because my suchness is suchness, I know that all dharmas are suchness;
because all dharmas are suchness, I practice prajñā through a suchness that is not non-suchness, a non-delusive suchness, and an undifferentiated suchness.
"Good son! This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva.

Having thus known that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one practices prajñā; likewise, up to having known that consciousness is without form or characteristics, one practices prajñā."
When practicing prajñā in this manner, by virtue of knowing the suchness of consciousness, one attains the suchness of wisdom;
by virtue of the suchness of wisdom, one attains the suchness of dedication;
and by virtue of the suchness of dedication, one attains the suchness of bodhi.
Because of the suchness of bodhi, one attains the suchness of sentient beings;
because of the suchness of sentient beings, one knows the suchness of the self;
because of the suchness of the self, one knows the suchness of all phenomena.
Because all dharmas are suchness—neither non-suchness, nor falsely such, nor otherwise than such—one practices prajñā.
O son of good family!
This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,

having known that form is impermanent, the bodhisattva contemplates the body within the body to cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of the body, up to knowing that form is like grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles, thereby cultivating the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
When a bodhisattva thus cultivates the application of mindfulness of the body, they know the suchness of form;
because they know the suchness of form, they know the suchness of the body;
and so on, until they know the suchness of all phenomena.

Because all phenomena are suchness, one cultivates the application of mindfulness of the body as non-suchness, unerring suchness, and non-differentiated suchness; it does not function together with vitarka and vicāra associated with the body.
"Noble son! This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva.

Having thus understood that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body; likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
In this way, up until one has realized that consciousness is without form or characteristics, one cultivates the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

When cultivating the application of mindfulness to the body in this manner, because one realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness, one attains the suchness of the application of mindfulness to the body;
and because of the suchness of the application of mindfulness to the body, one attains the suchness of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Because one dedicates toward the suchness of true reality (tathatā), one attains the suchness of awakening;
because of the suchness of awakening, one attains the suchness of sentient beings;
because of the suchness of sentient beings, one realizes the suchness of the self.
Because my suchness is such, I know the suchness of all phenomena;
because all phenomena are such, I cultivate the application of mindfulness of the body as non-suchness, non-false suchness, and non-different suchness.
This is likewise true for the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness of sensation, mind, and phenomena, wherein there is no discursive thought or investigation accompanying those phenomena.
"Good son! This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva.

Having thus known that form is impermanent, one cultivates the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, śamatha, the four means of attraction, the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers; it is likewise for all these."

Having known that form is suffering, form is non-self, form is tranquility, form is empty, form is signless, form is wishless, form is without activity, unborn, unarisen, dependently originated, and detached—up to knowing that form is like grass, wood, tiles, and pebbles—one brings forth the knowledge of supernormal powers.

Having thus known that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one draws forth the knowledge of supernormal powers; even until having known that consciousness has no defining characteristic, one draws forth the knowledge of supernormal powers.
Thus, because of the suchness of the aggregates and the suchness of the supernormal powers, it extends to the suchness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-tathatā*).
Because of the suchness of all phenomena, there is the non-suchness, the non-false suchness, and the non-different suchness; the induction of the wisdom of supernormal powers is likewise so.
"Good son! This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva. Why is this so?"

Because this path transcends mundane paths, one knows that the suchness of form does not destroy that form; it is neither annihilated nor eternal, arising from conditions and possessing a nature of non-arising.

In this way, one knows the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; without destroying that consciousness, one sees it as neither annihilated nor eternal—a nature of non-arising born from conditions.

Transcending the aggregates, the world, as well as the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and being free from attachment—because it is unstained—it is for the sake of sentient beings taking birth within the five destinies that this is called the supramundane path.
Because the Buddha provisionally designates these as existing in the world, they are therefore not destroyed.

Why is this? Because the characteristic of impermanence does not destroy the world; likewise, the characteristics of suffering, non-self, tranquility, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-activity—up to and including the characteristic of suchness—do not destroy the world.
“Good son! This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva; this path is pure.
If a bodhisattva abides in this pure path, they are able to act as a great light for sentient beings in those evil realms.”
By attaining this radiance, one is said to dwell securely in the supramundane path.
This path is most excellent, for it enables one to proceed toward the site of enlightenment;
this path is pure and superior, for it allows one to abandon all unwholesome states of mind.
This path is preeminent, for it can reach the summit of the Buddha’s wisdom;
this path is unsurpassed, for it can cross over the various torrents of birth and death;
this path is peerless, for it can transcend all deviant and divergent paths.
This path is peerless, for there is not a single dharma that can be compared to it;
this path is equal to the unequaled, for it does not depart from the causal path of the Buddhas of the past;
this path is secure and peaceful, for it is well able to subdue all demonic adversaries.
This path is unimpeded, for it is the playground of the wisdom of the supernormal power of mastery over the mind;
this path is without darkness, for it possesses the radiance of wisdom;
this path is level and upright, for it is free from all guile and crookedness.
This path is straight, for it is free from all crookedness;
this path is level, for it is equal toward the minds of sentient beings;
this path is vast, for it accommodates all sentient beings.
This path is broad and vast, for its elements do not encroach upon one another;
this path is capable of growth, for it is free from weariness;
this path is the provision of merit, for it is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
This path is free from feverish affliction because of the perfection of ethical discipline;
this path is free from fear because of the perfection of patience;
this path is non-retrogressive because of the perfection of vigor.
This path is detached from all objects because it is the perfection of dhyāna;
this path pervades empty space because it is the perfection of prajñā;
this path accords with wisdom because it is able to effect transformations.
This path is eternally fulfilled because it gathers all wholesome dharmas;
this path follows the wheel of Dharma because it does not forget what has been heard. Good son!
This is the supramundane path of the bodhisattva; it is thus exceptionally sublime, pure, and peerless.
"If a bodhisattva wishes to abide in this pure path, they should don the great armor to accomplish the Mahāyāna, for by means of this, they shall proceed to the site of enlightenment."
What is meant by "donning the great armor"?
These bodhisattvas don the armor of causing those who have not crossed over to cross over, because they repair and prepare the great ship;
they don the armor of causing those who are not yet liberated to be liberated, because they liberate them from the bonds of afflictions and various views.
They don the armor that brings peace to those who are not yet at peace, because it causes them to relinquish all grasping and fear;
they don the armor that leads those who have not attained *nirvāṇa* to attain *nirvāṇa*, because it causes those who are inverted to obtain the true path;
they don the armor of liberating all sentient beings, because it causes them to find nothing to be grasped as a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, or a person.
They don the armor of upholding the True Dharma because they do not crave their own bodies or lives;
they don the armor of purifying Buddha-fields because they never tire of cultivating roots of goodness;
they don the armor of adorning the marks and signs of excellence because they accumulate various provisions of merit.
They don the armor of subduing all the māras and the doctrines of external paths, because they have attained the power of supernatural faculties;
they don the armor of causing all sentient beings to rejoice, because they have attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge;
they don the armor of seeking the true Dharma of all Buddhas, because they have attained the wisdom of dhāraṇī.
They don the armor of observing the minds of all sentient beings, because they have attained the wisdom of supernormal powers;
they don the armor of knowing the prior and subsequent faculties of all sentient beings, by means of skillful means and wisdom;
they don the armor of fulfilling the ten powers, through the accumulation of the power of wisdom.
They don the armor of fearlessness, because their minds never retreat or sink in any circumstance;
they don the armor of fulfilling the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because they cultivate all wholesome dharmas and sever all unwholesome dharmas;
they don the armor of hearing all dharmas without being startled, terrified, or afraid, because they know all dharmas to be like illusions, dreams, reflections, echoes, and the moon in water.
They don the armor of great compassion, because they know that all sentient beings are originally in nirvāṇa and are fully accomplished therein;

they don the armor of skillful means, because although they hear that all phenomena—emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the absence of activity—are unborn, they are nevertheless able to manifest within the cycle of birth and death;

they don the armor of the immovable prior empowerment, because although they hear it said that they have transcended the characteristics of *niyama* (the limit of existence), that all phenomena are unborn and all activities are unceasing, they do not take up the realization of the fruit.
This constitutes the great vehicle armor of the bodhisattva.
Once the bodhisattva has donned these twenty great armors, they mount the Great Vehicle and reach the further shore.
Furthermore, as for "mounting," the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) serve as the wheels, for they are skillfully able to gather in all sentient beings.
The ten pure wholesome actions serve as the spokes, for they skillfully enable penetration into all correct practices;
the roots of virtue of pure intention serve as the axle, for they skillfully act as the foundation for profound conduct;
and the vast wisdom of dependent origination serves as the hub, for it is capable of bearing the burden of benefiting sentient beings.
Great compassion serves as the rim, for it gathers and sustains the retinue of the Dharma-jewels as adornment;
steadfast power serves as the binding, for supreme merit is never lost;
and prior vows together with skillful wisdom serve as the movement, for great compassion and skillful means can be practiced in tandem.
It takes śamatha as its shaft, because it induces right wisdom that is well able to fully know the Four Noble Truths;
it takes unobstructed generosity as its spokes, because it serves as the requisite for provisions;
and it takes the bases of psychic power as its means of travel, because it journeys through the buddha-fields.
"By means of the rope of right mindfulness, one maintains the bodhicitta so that it is not lost.

Furthermore, 'vehicle' (yāna) refers to that which is vast and capacious enough to accommodate all sentient beings; it subdues those of the two vehicles and restrains all non-Buddhists; it destroys the hosts of Māra and manifests clear wisdom; it is able to reach the ultimate goal, for it is what all Bodhisattvas ought to study;
and it is that which Brahmā, Śakra, and all the devas praise and revere."
It is like a lion throne because it provides a secure seat for all who preach the Dharma;
it can manifest subtle and exquisite forms that one never tires of beholding;
and its adamantine hook and chain represent a firm resolve that is forever indestructible.
With the bodhicitta as the precursor, so that the merit of physical conduct and vows may be fulfilled;
with the pure divine eye for constant observation;
and with pure radiance to illumine the ten directions.
Because it constantly rains the flowers of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) that are pure;
because it constantly performs the music of the Dharma that is unimpeded;
and because it skillfully expounds the teachings that accord with correct principle (nyāya).
Because it skillfully transforms all sentient beings of a similar kind;
because all bodhisattvas serve as its retinue;
and because it is adorned with immeasurable merits.
Because it flows forth from the unsurpassed *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Son of good family!
Thus, the bodhisattva dons those twenty pure armors, mounts this Great Vehicle, and abiding in the supramundane path, performs the work of a Buddha and establishes sentient beings [in liberation].
When this adornment of the Great Vehicle armor was spoken, seventy-two thousand devas and humans conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained purification regarding the supramundane path and realized the patience of non-arising.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of the Great Xingshan Monastery—Grand Master with the Rank of Kai-fu Yitong Sansi, Special Advancement, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Sui, with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, with the posthumous title Dajian (Great Mirror), and the epithet Dayangzhi (Great and Vast Wisdom)—by imperial decree. At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying:
"O Virtuous One!..."
"Have you already purified the supramundane path?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied, "Noble son!"
"In this way, it is already purified.
He asked again: "In what way is it already purified?"
He replied, “Because I am pure, I have already attained purity.
He was asked again:
"How is it that I am pure? He replied, "Because the world is pure, I am pure."
He asked again: "What is the purification of the world? He replied:
“Good son! The prior limit of form is pure because there is no going;
the posterior limit of form is pure because there is no coming.”
Form is pure in its middle limit because it does not abide;
so too are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
Consciousness is pure in its prior limit because it has no going.
Consciousness is pure at its future limit because it has no coming;
consciousness is pure at its middle limit because it does not abide.
O son of good family!
"Therefore, it is called 'worldly purity.
He asked again: "Virtuous one!"
"In this way, what is it that the purity of the world is intended to manifest? He replied, "Good son!"
"It reveals that all phenomena are entirely pure.
He asked again:
"In what way does it reveal that all phenomena are pure?"
He replied: "It is because of wisdom that one knows the demarcation between the prior limit and the posterior limit of all phenomena.
He asked again:
"What is the delimitation of the prior and posterior limits of all phenomena?
He replied: "Because they are neither annihilated nor eternal."
He asked again:
"Regarding that which is neither annihilated nor eternal, what is the expression for it? He replied:
"Neither discontinuity nor permanence is a discourse on non-arising and non-ceasing.
He asked again:
"Regarding that non-arising and non-ceasing, what is it a discourse upon?"
He replied, “Non-arising and non-ceasing are beyond verbal expression.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'dharmas are ineffable'? He replied,
"Because these dharmas are innumerable."
He spoke again:
"Virtuous one! If dharmas are without number, how can they follow after names and numbers?"
He replied: "Good son!

For example, space does not follow names and numbers; it is only by means of names and numbers that 'space' is provisionally designated. Thus, these names and numbers are not, in themselves, names and numbers."
He asked again:
"What is the gate of the calculable and the incalculable? He replied:
"The category of calculation refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), while the category beyond calculation refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Furthermore, both calculated and non-calculated phenomena are unconditioned; therefore, the Buddha taught that one should use wisdom to distance oneself from all phenomena of measurement and calculation.

When one calculates conditioned phenomena with consciousness and observes them according to reality, at that time one does not perceive any phenomenon as something to be abandoned or something not to be abandoned."
"This dharma should be realized and this should not be realized;
this dharma should be cultivated and this should not be cultivated";
yet one does not perceive any dharmas, nor does one form any conceptual limitations.
If one is without views and without measure, at that time one immediately attains non-attachment and achieves freedom from expectation.
If there is no expectation, then there is no object of focus; if one attains the absence of an object of focus, one attains non-self; and if one attains non-self, then there is no grasping.
What is meant by "being without grasping"?
It is not grasping at form as permanent or impermanent;
it is not grasping at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent or impermanent.
One does not grasp at form as being suffering or happiness;
one does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being suffering or happiness;
one does not grasp at form as being self or non-self, and so on, up to not grasping at consciousness as being self or non-self.
One does not grasp at form as pure or impure, nor even up to consciousness as pure or impure;
one does not grasp at form as empty or non-empty, nor even up to consciousness as empty or non-empty;
thus, one attains the samādhi of non-attachment.
Having attained this samādhi, one constantly gives rise to great compassion to deliver all sentient beings, yet perceives no afflictions within the cycle of birth and death. Why is this so?

Because the natures of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-different, one perceives the nirvāṇa of all sentient beings and likewise knows that one’s own self is primordially in nirvāṇa; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s practice of parinirvāṇa?
Parinirvāṇa is defined as the absence of conceptual observation and the dedication [of merit] toward sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).”
Regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one does not seek it through form, nor does one seek it through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

dwelling with a mind free from seeking in the pure precepts, one fulfills one's original vow, perceives neither increase nor decrease in any phenomena, attains equanimity, and abides in the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).
By abiding in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and practicing the bodhisattva path, one does not take any practice as an object of practice.
Noble son! This is the bodhisattva’s practice of parinirvāṇa.
He asked again:
"How does one observe nirvana through non-practice and practice? "Good son!
When a bodhisattva attends to and contemplates nirvāṇa, it is called "realizing the non-active through the active"; because it is non-active, it is named nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding verbal expressions and designations, it is named nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, nirvāṇa is called the "other shore," and that other shore is devoid of all marks; when the mind does not grasp or cling to those marks, it is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, "the other shore" is called non-conceptualization; because one does not give rise to a conceptual mind therein, it is named *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, "the other shore" is without the *ālayavijñāna*; because one does not give rise to the *ālayavijñāna* mind therein, it is named *nirvāṇa*.
"Good son! Practicing in this manner is called the bodhisattva’s practice of parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, O noble son!
You have eloquently expounded this Dharma, which accords with the practice of the parinirvāṇa of bodhisattvas.”
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas in the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is because the Tathāgata’s wisdom-light shines upon us that we have obtained this eloquence; it is not due to our own ability.

Just as the light of the sun illuminates all forms and images within Jambudvīpa, so too is it through the power of the wisdom-light of the World-Honored One, the Great Tamer, that we are able to clearly understand all dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying: "Noble son!
Why do you now conceal your own wisdom and claim that all of this is solely the empowerment of the Tathāgata?"
Gaganagañja said, "The eloquence attained by all bodhisattvas is sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgata; it does not belong to me alone."
“Good son! If there were no dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata, from what would the bodhisattva’s eloquence arise? Ratnaśrī replied:
"If the eloquence of a bodhisattva arises because of the Tathāgata, should one know that the Buddha’s eloquence can be transferred?
Ākāśagarbha replied, "The eloquence of the Tathāgata is not subject to transfer; it merely serves as its cause."
By means of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the eloquence of a bodhisattva arises.
For example, ignorance does not transfer into formations; it merely acts as a cause for formations, giving rise to them.
In the same way, the Buddha’s eloquence does not shift or transfer anywhere; it merely acts as a cause, giving rise to the eloquence of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, just as the voices of elephants, horses, or humans do not travel to the valley, yet an echo arises in the valley because of those sounds, so those sounds merely act as the cause for the echo;
likewise, the Buddha’s eloquence does not undergo any displacement, yet it acts solely as the cause for the eloquence of bodhisattvas.
Ratnaśrī said: “The Tathāgata has always taught profound dependent origination, and has also taught that all phenomena are without arising.
O son of noble family!
"Is it not the case that all phenomena arise from conditions? Akāśagarbha replied,
"If there were an agent within conditions, then those phenomena would have an arising."
"Because the dharma of causes and conditions has no creator, all dharmas are said to be without arising.
Ratnaśrī asked, "The Tathāgata has now appeared in the world; is this not an arising?"
Ākāśagarbha said: "If true thusness were subject to arising, one could say that the Tathāgata has an arising.
However, if it is admitted that true thusness is without arising, then one should not question or demand that the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world constitutes an arising."
Therefore, non-arising is taught as the Tathāgata.
As for the Tathāgata, he is called the Tathāgata because he has awakened to all phenomena in accordance with their true nature.
O son of good family, why do you further say that the Tathāgata is born?
"This should be answered by setting it aside. He asked again:
"What is meant by answering by setting it aside?"
He replied, “To abide in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is what is called ‘setting aside.
He asked again:
“How does the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abide? Gaganagañja replied:
“It abides in neither arising nor ceasing, neither abiding nor not abiding; this is called the abiding of the nature of phenomena.”
As the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abides in non-abiding, so too do all phenomena abide in non-abiding.
The Tathāgata is likewise: he abides in non-abiding;
neither born nor extinguished, neither abiding nor not abiding—this state of neither abiding nor not abiding is called the dwelling place of the Tathāgata.
Good son! To say that the Tathāgata is born is to cling to one extreme;
to say that he is not born is likewise to cling to an extreme.
To be free from these two extremes is called the Middle Way.
Good son, one who contemplates the Tathāgata should contemplate him in this way; if one contemplates otherwise, it is not correct contemplation.
Ratnaśrī said: "The meaning of the Tathāgata’s birth is thus profound: he abides in non-abiding, neither arising nor ceasing. Gaganagañja said:
“Good son! If one understands this meaning of the Buddha’s birth, no further [conceptual] arising will occur.
He asked again:
“Good son! What is meant by ‘superior’? Akāśagarbha replied:
"Superiority is called the phrase of augmentation; that is, to falsely produce augmentation where there is none, for dharmas are without augmentation.

If one can not produce augmentation regarding dharmas, it is called the phrase of equality, the phrase of non-equality, the phrase of no-phrase, the phrase of the phraseless, the phrase of no-syllables, and the phrase of no-cognition. Regarding those, it is the phrase of no-action by mind, thought, or consciousness;
as for that phrase of no-action, it is like how in the sky there is truly no bird-track, yet one uses conventional speech to utter the sound of 'bird-track'."
In this way, the Tathāgata truly has no birth; it is only by means of conventional expression that one speaks of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
Only those possessed of wisdom are able to understand the meaning of the phrase "non-arising."
Why is this so? This meaning of the phrase "non-arising" is the very self-nature of all dharmas.
That which is called "non-arising" likewise lacks self-nature.

That which lacks intrinsic nature has no place of abiding; the limit of non-abiding is the limit of all phenomena. Abiding in the limit of all phenomena is called the "actual limit" (bhūtakoṭi) and is also called the "extreme limit" (paryanta), because this limit pervades all places.
By this, one realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena, which is equal to space, without limit or boundary; that limit of reality is likewise without limit or boundary.
If it were limited by the boundary of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it would not be called the "limit of reality of all phenomena.
Such equality—the limit of reality of all phenomena—is the limit of the self; knowing the limit of the self, one knows the limit of all sentient beings.
If one knows the limit of all sentient beings, then one knows the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena;
this limit of reality is my own limit, the limit of all sentient beings, and the limit of all phenomena—this is called the limit of exhaustion.
Now, that which is the limit of exhaustion is what is termed *nirvāṇa*.
One who realizes this principle is said to have attained nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, all dharmas are without mutual dependence and are free from relative opposition;
just as space has nothing that can oppose it, so too do these dharmas have no opposites.
If one says that there is a nirvāṇa to be entered or sought, this is a view of arising and ceasing; it implies that "this dharma should arise" and "this dharma should cease.
Such a person is thus practicing within arising and ceasing, and does not know the equal, single nature of nirvāṇa.

Because of ignorance, one becomes attached to various phenomena and gives rise to false disputes; as the World-Honored One has said, if one understands my teaching, one should know that this constitutes the fulfillment of the most supreme merit of a śramaṇa.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!
“Only one with the unimpeded eloquence of the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha could, having realized it through his own experience, speak in such a manner.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Venerable One!...”
One should not say, "I have personally realized this. Why is that?
My own body is itself empty space; because my body is empty space, I know that all phenomena are entirely empty space.
"How is it, Venerable One, that you say 'I have realized it with my own body'? Ānanda said,
"If the body were empty, with what body would you perform the Buddha-work?"
Ākāśagarbha said: "By virtue of the Dharma-body;

for the Dharma-body is without transition or change. The aggregates, bases, and elements are neither born nor extinguished. It is not a body of inversion that appears at will, but rather a mind-made body that performs the work of a Buddha."
Ānanda said: "O Great Being! Have you realized the Dharma-body?"
Ākāśagarbha said: "Venerable sir!
As I understand it, apart from dharmas there is no body; my body is itself the dharma, and the dharma is itself my body."
"Whether it be dharmas or the body, because they lack two distinct characteristics,
one speaks of 'bodily realization'. Ānanda said, "O Great Being!"
"If you have realized this through bodily witness, have you attained arhatship? He replied,
"I have attained it by way of non-attainment."
"Why is this? Because an Arhat has thoroughly mastered the dharma of non-contention (araṇā), and is thus neither defiled, nor angry, nor deluded.
He spoke further:
“O Mahāsattva! If this is so, should you not enter final parinirvāṇa? Akāśagarbha replied:
“Venerable sir! An Arhat does not enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Knowing that all phenomena are ultimately *nirvāṇa*, one abandons the conceptualization of *nirvāṇa*;

yet ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) engage in such discrimination, saying "I am attaining *nirvāṇa*," and even further discriminate and calculate various distinctions among different types of *nirvāṇa*.
Ānanda said: "O Great Being!
As you have stated, a bodhisattva is not an arhat, nor an ordinary person, nor one in training, nor one beyond training, nor a pratyekabuddha, nor a bodhisattva, nor a tathāgata."
Gaganagañja said: “Excellent, excellent, Venerable Ānanda!”

Because they are neither arhats, nor ordinary beings, nor those in training (śaikṣa), nor those beyond training (aśaikṣa), nor pratyekabuddhas, nor bodhisattvas, nor tathāgatas, bodhisattvas are able to manifest in all places, yet they do not abide in any stage or level.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred arhats in the assembly each removed the upper robes they were wearing and offered them as a gift to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"May all sentient beings attain eloquence such as that of Gaganagañja."
