At that time, by the power of his empowerment, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja caused the exquisite Dharma robes he had offered to enter entirely into space, becoming hidden and no longer visible.
Those arhats and bhikṣus asked the bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"O Mahāsattva! Where are robes such as these?"
Gaganagañja replied, “They shall all enter my treasury of space. At that moment,
the World-Honored One smiled with a serene and joyful countenance.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do you manifest a smile?"
“The Tathāgata’s smile is not without cause or condition; I pray that you will explain it.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:

“The robes offered by those bhikṣus, through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, have been entirely placed within the treasury of space. They shall go to the world-system called Kāṣāyadhvaja, to the presence of the Tathāgata Śailendrarāja, where they will perform the work of a Buddha.”
The sounds of the Dharma preached by the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja all flowed forth from his saffron robes in that world.
Having heard this Dharma, immeasurable bodhisattvas all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Ānanda, you should know!
The Bodhisattva’s wisdom of supernormal powers is supreme; by means of such various sounds and voices, he brings sentient beings to maturity.
It is for this reason that I smile!
When this Dharma was being spoken, suddenly there fell from the sky immeasurable flowers of sun and moon light, all the color of fire, such as had never been seen before.
From within these flowers, a voice issued forth, saying:

"If any person hears this Seal of the Non-retrogressive Dharma taught by the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja and attains faith and understanding, they will certainly proceed to the site of enlightenment."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From where do these flowers come?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There is a Brahmā king named Prabhālaṃkāra, who is the lord of a hundred thousand worlds.
It was that Brahmā who, in order to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, rained down such flowers."
Ānanda said: "World-Honored One!
We all wish to see that Brahmā King."
The Buddha said, "Wait but a moment; you shall see for yourself.

At that time, the Brahma King Prabhālaṃkāra, surrounded before and behind by a retinue of six hundred and eight thousand Brahmās, vanished from that heaven and appeared before the Buddha. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, withdrew to sit on one side, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“Most marvelous, World-Honored One!

This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is inconceivable, being fully endowed with the majesty of pure ethical discipline, the majesty of samādhi, the majesty of supernormal powers, the majesty of wisdom, the majesty of fulfilling vows, the majesty of skillful means, the majesty of superior intention, the majesty of mastery over the Dharma-body, the majesty of physical adornment, the majesty of verbal and mental adornment, and the majesty of mastery over all phenomena.”
“World-Honored One!

This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha does not manifest any of his various transformative deeds through the diligent exertion of physical, verbal, or mental karma; rather, it is solely by the power of his past cultivation, having accumulated roots of goodness and fulfilled the profound practices of all Buddhas, that he is thus able to let out the great lion’s roar.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is!
Brahmā King!”

As you have said, all bodhisattvas, by the power of their past roots of goodness and through the accumulation of the provisions of merit and wisdom, vow not to regress from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and are thus able to manifest such miraculous transformations.
At that time, the Brahma King Prabhālaṃkāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What constitutes the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva?”
"What is merit? What is wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the Brahma King, saying:
"Roots of goodness" refers to when sentient beings first give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Merit" refers to having given rise to that mind, surpassing all *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and practicing giving and maintaining the precepts for the sake of all sentient beings, as well as all meritorious deeds accomplished through cultivation.
"Wisdom" refers to dedicating the roots of goodness one has accumulated toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to pure intention (*āśaya*) free from hypocrisy and deceit;
"merit" refers to the accumulation of all merit through application (*prayoga*).
Because the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) of the wise is entirely preeminent.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*) refers to the firm resolve toward all wholesome dharmas;
"merit" (*puṇya*) refers to the insatiable accumulation of the provisions for goodness.
Because the wise regard all their roots of goodness as being like illusions.
Furthermore, roots of goodness consist in obtaining virtuous friends;
merit consists in not abandoning virtuous friends.
The wise frequently consult with virtuous friends.
Furthermore, those with roots of goodness joyfully seek the Buddha-dharma;
those with merit do not forget what they have heard.
The wise find delight in the joy of the Dharma.
Furthermore, those with roots of goodness constantly seek the Buddha-dharma;
those with merit preach the Dharma without harboring any expectations.
The wise have no stinginess regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, those with roots of goodness always delight in hearing the Dharma;
those with merit investigate according to reality.
The wise practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, those with roots of goodness always delight in seeing the Buddha;
those with merit constantly make offerings to the Buddha.
The wise person accords with the Buddha’s teachings.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to attaining the life of renunciation;
"merit" refers to cultivating the practices of the noble lineages.
The wise delight in dwelling in the araṇya.
Furthermore, those with roots of goodness are well able to cultivate few desires and contentment;
those with merit spontaneously lack greed regarding all food and clothing.
The wise person is spontaneously unstained regarding that which they enjoy.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the cultivation of the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness;
"merit" refers to fulfilling the four right efforts.
The wise attain the bases of supernormal power.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to entering the faculty of faith;
"merit" refers to cultivating diligence and mindfulness.
The wise one contemplates the wisdom of samādhi.
Furthermore, roots of goodness abide in the five powers;
merit accords with the factors of enlightenment.
The "wise" refers to the knowledge that enters the noble path.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the mind abiding in the sublime principle;
"merit" refers to seeking the provisions for *śamatha*.
The wise attain skill in vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the meritorious action consisting of giving;
"merit" refers to the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline.
The wise call the bases of meritorious action accomplished through cultivation "wisdom.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the training in higher ethics;
"merit" refers to the training in higher mind.
The wise cultivate the training in higher wisdom.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the confession of all transgressions;
"merit" refers to rejoicing in the various virtues of others.
The wise exhort and entreat all Buddhas.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" consist of relinquishing all that one possesses;
"merit" consists of not hoping for a reward.
The wise dedicate [their roots of goodness] toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the formal commitment to the precepts;
"merit" refers to maintaining the precepts without deficiency.
The wise uphold the precepts and dedicate them [toward enlightenment].
Furthermore, roots of goodness consist in harboring no intent to harm sentient beings;
merit consists in being able to endure harsh words when heard.
The wise are able to sacrifice their own bodies and lives to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to diligently seeking wholesome dharmas without becoming weary;
"merit" refers to dedicating all one's roots of goodness toward sentient beings.
The wise accumulate roots of goodness and dedicate them toward enlightenment.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the ability to cultivate the various factors of dhyāna;
"merit" refers to the attainment of all roots of goodness through meditative concentration.
The wise emerge from various meditative concentrations to manifest birth in the desire realm.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to wisdom, power, and extensive learning;
"merit" refers to the contemplation of what has been heard.
The wisdom of the wise becomes perfected.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to regarding all sentient beings with equanimity;
"merit" refers to realizing the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
The wise person’s mind of loving-kindness is impartial, like space.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to cultivating the provisions for the three stages;
"merit" refers to accumulating the provisions for the fourth stage.
The wise one fulfills the provisions for the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds;
"merit" refers to bodhisattvas abiding in and practicing the stages.
The wise are bodhisattvas who do not regress.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the practice of equanimity;
"merit" refers to the adornment of the primary and secondary marks.
The wise possess the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to the adornment of Buddha-fields;
"merit" refers to the mental intention of giving.
The wise benefit all sentient beings.
Furthermore, those with roots of goodness hear the teachings on the deeds of Māra;
those with merit discern the deeds of Māra.
The wise are able to transcend the activities of Māra.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to being endowed with great compassion;
"merit" refers to skillful means.
The wise are those who cultivate *prajñā*.
Furthermore, roots of goodness adorn the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
merit is that which is well able to destroy all Māras.
The wise say that perfect enlightenment is achieved through the wisdom associated with a single moment of mind.
Brahmā King!
These are what are called roots of goodness, merit, and wisdom.
At that time, the Brahma King Prabhālaṃkāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous, World-Honored One!
You are able to explain all dharmas by means of the meaning of three phrases.”
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed the Brahmā Prabhālaṃkṛta, saying: “Brahmā!
There is a single phrase that can encompass all dharmas.”
What is this one? It is the phrase "emptiness of intrinsic nature. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are identical in their emptiness, this is called "one phrase.
Furthermore, there is another phrase that encompasses all phenomena: the phrase of signlessness and the phrase of wishlessness; both encompass all phenomena.

Thus it is explained at length, up to the phrase "non-activity," the phrase "detachment from desire," the phrase "tranquility," the phrase "absence of the ālaya," the phrase "dharma-realm," the phrase "suchness," the phrase "the limit of reality," the phrase "non-arising," the phrase "non-origination," and the phrase "nirvāṇa"; in each case, the inclusion of all phenomena is likewise.
Furthermore, Brahmā King!
Desire is a phrase for the transcendence of desire, because the very nature of the transcendence of desire is itself desire;
all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Hatred is a phrase for the transcendence of hatred, because the nature of the transcendence of hatred is itself hatred;
all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Delusion is a phrase for the transcendence of delusion, because the nature of the transcendence of delusion is itself delusion.
All Buddha-dharmas are likewise of this same nature.
Even the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) is a phrase for the absence of a view of a self, because the nature of the absence of a view of a self is itself the view of a self;
all Buddha-dharmas are likewise of this same nature.
Form is a phrase for formlessness, because the nature of formlessness is itself form;
all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: consciousness is a phrase for non-consciousness, because the nature of non-discrimination is itself consciousness.
All Buddha-dharmas are likewise of this same nature.

Thus it is explained at length regarding the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the twelvefold dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the phrase for clarity (*vidyā*), because the nature of clarity is itself ignorance;
all Buddha-dharmas are likewise of this same nature.
Even "that which arises" is a phrase for non-arising, because the nature of non-arising is itself arising;
all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
The phrase "all dharmas" is a phrase for the absence of dharmas, because the nature of the absence of dharmas is itself the Buddha-dharmas.
All Buddha-dharmas are likewise of this same nature.
Brahmā King!
This is the single phrase that encompasses all dharmas.
If a bodhisattva enters this Dharma-gate, they enter all Buddha-dharmas within a single phrase.
Brahmā King!
Just as the great ocean receives and contains all flowing streams, so too does each single phrase encompass all dharmas.
Just as empty space can encompass all phenomena, so too does each and every one of these phrases subsume all dharmas.
Therefore, these phrases are inexhaustible, unfolding infinitely through their mutual interpenetration.

It is like a mathematician who uses counting sticks to calculate by arranging them upon a board; yet, although there are no counting sticks within the board and no board within the counting sticks, they can produce immeasurable numbers through their mutual interaction. In this same way, a single phrase gives rise to immeasurable phrases.
Brahmā King!

Such comparisons of the Buddha-dharma spoken throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas—whether regarding body or mind—are entirely without anything to be apprehended, nor can they be known by means of number.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are the Buddha-dharmas, and that which is the Buddha-dharma is itself no-dharma. Why is this so?
Because they are spoken of as conventional designations through conceptualization and thorough knowledge by means of conceptualization;
therein there is neither sign nor non-sign, neither dharma nor non-dharma, for it is ultimately signless.
"These marks are pure and devoid of their own characteristics, just as space has a single, identical nature;
the Buddha-dharma is likewise, for both its nature and its characteristics are empty.
When the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja spoke this Dharma, twenty-two thousand Brahmā deities among that assembly of Brahmās all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, five thousand Brahma kings, having planted roots of goodness in past lives, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The Great Collection Sūtra, the Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, Fascicle Six. Engraved by imperial decree at the State Printing Office of the Tripitaka in the Kingdom of Goryeo during the Bingwu year.
The Great Collection Sūtra, the Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, Fascicle [Six].
Translated by the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery— who was the seventh [rank of] Kaifu Yitongsisi, Teshen, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,

Duke of Sushan with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and bestowed the title Dajian (Great Mirror) and the epithet Dayangzhi (Great Vast Wisdom)— by imperial decree. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi addressed the Bodhisattva Mahākāśyapa-garbha, saying:
“Good son! By means of which dharmas is the bodhicitta sustained so that one does not fall back?
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja replied:
“Good son! The bodhicitta is sustained by two dharmas and abides in non-retrogression. What are these two?
That is to say:
"aspiration and superior aspiration. He asked again:
“Noble son! By what are this resolve and the superior resolve subsumed? He replied:
“Good son! They are gathered by four dharmas. What are the four?
That is to say:
the intention (*āśaya*) is comprised of being without guile (*akuhanā*) and without deceit (*amāyā*);
the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) is comprised of an unmixed mind and the practice of progressive advancement (*viśeṣa-gamana*).
"These four dharmas are subsumed within two dharmas.
He asked again:
"And these four dharmas are subsumed within how many dharmas?"
He replied: "They are subsumed by eight factors. What are these eight?"
That is to say:
being without flattery is subsumed by uprightness and right abiding;
being without deception is subsumed by the absence of pretense and pure intention.
The undistracted mind is subsumed by the mind that does not sink back and by non-retrogressive diligence;
superior progress in practice is subsumed by the equipment of merit and the equipment of wisdom.
"These eight dharmas are subsumed within four dharmas.
He asked again: "Good son!"
Furthermore, by how many dharmas are these eight dharmas subsumed? He replied,
“They are subsumed by sixteen dharmas.”
What are these sixteen? They are as follows:
being upright, which is comprised of tranquility and gentleness;
Abiding correctly is comprised of selflessness and the absence of hypocrisy;
being without pretense is comprised of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
and pure intention is comprised of purity of body and purity of mind.
The non-retrogressive mind is encompassed by steadfastness and power;
non-retrogressive diligence is encompassed by acting according to what has been taught and by correct practice;
the accumulation of merit is encompassed by application and intensified application.
"The equipment of wisdom is subsumed by extensive hearing and reflection upon what has been heard.
These are the eight dharmas subsumed by sixteen dharmas.
He asked again:
“By how many dharmas are these sixteen dharmas subsumed? He replied: “Good son!
These sixteen dharmas are subsumed by thirty-two dharmas.
What are these thirty-two? They are as follows:
Tranquility is subsumed by a sense of shame and a dread of blame;
gentleness is subsumed by pleasant speech and dwelling in happiness;
selflessness is subsumed by humility and immovability.
Absence of hypocrisy is comprised of stainless speech and unharmed speech;
great loving-kindness is comprised of an impartial mind toward all sentient beings and an unobstructed mind;
great compassion is comprised of tirelessness and the performance of all services for sentient beings.
Purity of body is comprised of non-harming and contentment with one’s own possessions;
purity of mind is comprised of flexibility and the nature of tranquility;
and steadfastness is comprised of not failing in one’s commitment and the certainty of deliverance.
Power is comprised of well-established wisdom and immovable wisdom;
as it is said, that which is performed is comprised of the nature of acting according to what was taught and the capacity to act;
correct practice is comprised of correct application and correct diligence.
Application is comprised of transcendence and non-retrogression;
superior application is comprised of hearing from others and proper mental attention;
extensive learning is comprised of associating with virtuous friends and following virtuous friends.
Reflecting upon what has been heard is comprised of right practice, vigor, and contemplation through meditative concentration. Noble son,
this is how the thirty-two dharmas subsume the sixteen dharmas.
He asked again:
"Good son, by how many dharmas are these thirty-two dharmas subsumed?"
He replied: "These thirty-two dharmas are subsumed by sixty-four dharmas.
What are these sixty-four?"
That is to say:
shame (hrī) is comprised of internal observation and the restraint of the sense faculties;
while remorse (apatrāpya) is comprised of guarding against external objects and revering those with virtue.
Skillful speech is comprised of seeking the Dharma and delighting in the Dharma;
dwelling in peace and happiness is comprised of tranquility of body and tranquility of mind;
humility is comprised of freedom from arrogance and speaking in accordance with the Dharma.
Immovability is subsumed by the absence of physical crookedness and the absence of mental crookedness;
stainlessness is subsumed by the removal of the three stains and the cultivation of the three gates of liberation;
non-harming speech is subsumed by the absence of harshness and the absence of divisive speech.
The unimpeded mind is subsumed by protecting oneself and protecting others;
the impartial mind toward all sentient beings is subsumed by non-discrimination and the nature of a single flavor;
and freedom from weariness is subsumed by the dream-like intrinsic nature and the illusion-like intrinsic nature.
Providing for all the needs of sentient beings is encompassed by supernormal powers and skillful means;
non-harming is encompassed by a sense of shame and faith in the ripening of karma;
and knowing contentment with one’s own wealth is encompassed by fewness of desires and being easily satisfied.
Suppleness is comprised of non-agitation and non-deception;
the nature of tranquility is comprised of relinquishing the self and what belongs to the self;
and the integrity of one’s commitment is comprised of contemplating the bodhicitta and conforming to the stages of enlightenment.
Resolute deliverance is comprised of awakening to the deeds of Māra and being sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas;
well-established wisdom is comprised of being neither frivolous nor agitated;
immovable wisdom is comprised of a mind like a mountain and being unshakable.
As it is said: nature (*dhātu*) is comprised of wholesome action and the absence of regret;
capability (*sāmarthya*) is comprised of real nature (*bhūtatā*) and true nature (*tattvatā*);
correct application (*samyak-prayoga*) is comprised of accordance with dependent origination and the avoidance of the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Right effort is subsumed by application and that which is governed by correct reasoning;
non-retrogression is subsumed by right abandonment and lack of indolence;
and transcendence is subsumed by valor and diligence.
Hearing from others is comprised of [relying on] spiritual friends and seeking the Dharma;
appropriate mental attention is comprised of the requisites for śamatha and the requisites for vipaśyanā;
and attending upon spiritual friends is comprised of compliance and reverence.
Conformity with virtuous friends is comprised of physical agility and mental agility;
right practice with vigor is comprised of nirvāṇa and dispassion;
and meditative observation is comprised of the non-destruction of causes and the non-destruction of results.
"Good son! These thirty-two dharmas are subsumed within sixty-four dharmas.
He asked again:
“Good son! By how many dharmas are these sixty-four dharmas subsumed? He replied:
“Good son! These sixty-four dharmas are subsumed by one hundred and twenty-eight dharmas. Namely:”
Internal observation is comprised of the contemplation of emptiness and the contemplation of intrinsic nature;
the gathering of the sense faculties is comprised of right mindfulness and right situational awareness;
and the guarding of external objects is comprised of the restraint of the sense faculties and the absence of mental distraction.
Reverence for those with virtue is comprised of observing one’s own faults and being wise without seeking the faults of others;
seeking the Dharma is comprised of self-vowing to be courageous and non-retrogressive, and not dwelling on the evil deeds of others;
delighting in the Dharma is comprised of seeking the Dharma and conforming to the Dharma.
Physical tranquility is comprised of being free from lethargy and being free from the nature of delusion;
mental tranquility is comprised of thorough knowledge and the abandonment of afflictions;
freedom from arrogance is comprised of the absence of pride and the cessation of violence.
Speaking according to the Dharma is subsumed by the abandonment of unwholesome phenomena and the fulfillment of all wholesome phenomena;
bodily uprightness is subsumed by the absence of harsh speech and the absence of malicious speech;
mental uprightness is subsumed by right mindfulness and right samādhi.
The removal of the three stains is subsumed by the contemplation of impurity and the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion;
the cultivation of the three doors of liberation is subsumed by the [absence of] grasping at a personal entity and the ultimate truth;
and the absence of harshness is subsumed by speech that benefits others and speech that brings happiness.
Non-divisive speech is subsumed by non-destructive speech and reconciliatory speech;
self-protection is subsumed by refraining from all misdeeds and accumulating all merit;
protecting others is subsumed by patience and gentleness.
It is subsumed by the mind of equanimity that makes no distinctions and by the mind that is like the wind;
it is subsumed by the nature of a single flavor through true suchness (*tathatā*) and the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
and it is subsumed by the dream-like intrinsic nature through phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and known, as well as the objects experienced and utilized.
The nature of illusion is comprised of deception and pervasive conceptualization;
supernormal powers are comprised of accomplishing benefit and conforming to wisdom;
skillful means are comprised of the light of wisdom and observing sentient beings.
Shame is comprised of remorse for what has already occurred so that it does not arise again, and the non-concealment of one’s own faults;
faith in the ripening of karma is comprised of the direct realization of the non-arising of all phenomena and the dread of suffering in future lives;
fewness of desires is comprised of pure enjoyment and the abandonment of the mind of insatiability.
Contentment is subsumed by being easy to satisfy and easy to support;
lack of agitation is subsumed by ultimate exhaustion [of defilements] and non-contention;
lack of deception is subsumed by truthful speech and gentleness toward the Dharma.
Abandoning the notion of "self" is comprised of not calculating causes and destroying evil views;
the state of selflessness is comprised of the absence of pride and the absence of craving;
contemplating the bodhicitta is comprised of not aspiring to inferior vehicles and having compassion for sentient beings.
Proceeding toward the site of enlightenment is comprised of the subduing of all māras and the manifest realization of the Buddha-dharma;
awakening to the activities of māras is comprised of the instructions of spiritual friends and the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and the empowerment of all Buddhas is comprised of acting according to what has been taught and not abandoning any sentient being.
It is comprised of being free from frivolity through a mind like the earth and the severing of love and hatred;
it is comprised of being free from agitation through the abandonment of remorse and the contemplation of impermanence;
and it is comprised of a mind like a mountain through neither exaltation nor depression.
It is comprised of non-deviation through the vow of non-retrogression and non-destruction, and the vow of superior progress;
it is comprised of skillful action through the activity of wisdom and the non-recollection of demonic deeds;
and it is comprised of freedom from regret through the purity of ethical discipline and the purity of meditative concentration.
The nature of reality (*tattva*) is subsumed by the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
the true nature (*bhūtatā*) is subsumed by suchness (*tathatā*) and reality (*bhūta*);
and that which accords with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādānuloma*) is subsumed by causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*).
Detachment from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism is subsumed by non-arising and non-ceasing;
application is subsumed by faith in the causality of karma and the eradication of karma;
and accordance with reality is subsumed by the path of distancing and the path of non-arising.
Right abandonment is comprised of the abandoning of the unwholesome and the non-abandoning of the wholesome;
non-laxity is comprised of the power of mind and the power of body;
and valor is comprised of thorough investigation and the non-loss of practice.
Diligence is subsumed by an undistracted mind and non-retrogression;
spiritual friends are subsumed by respect and making offerings;
the quest for the Dharma is subsumed by seeking correct knowledge and seeking liberation.
The provisions for śamatha are comprised of physical seclusion and mental seclusion;
the provisions for vipaśyanā are comprised of tireless hearing of the Dharma and appropriate mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra);
and compliance is comprised of prostration and joining the palms.
Reverence is comprised of truthful speech and non-deception;
physical agility is comprised of moderation in eating and the practice of rousing oneself from sleep during the first, middle, and last watches of the night;
and mental agility is comprised of freedom from desire and right reflection.
Nirvāṇa is subsumed by the departure from impermanence and suffering;
the departure from desire is subsumed by non-self and non-appropriation;
and the indestructibility of causes is subsumed by the cause of tranquility and resolute conviction.
The fruit is characterized by non-destruction because it is not deceptive according to yoga, and because it is comprised of the praise of the fruit according to resolute conviction.
Noble son, these sixty-four dharmas are subsumed within one hundred twenty-eight dharmas.

"Good son! Thus have I briefly explained that which encompasses all dharmas. If I were to explain the increasing enumeration of these dharmas by doubling them again and again, even with my uninterrupted eloquence, it could not be exhausted in one kalpa or even more than one kalpa."

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi heard the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha speak of how all these dharmas are subsumed, he attained what he had never experienced before and was immeasurably elated. He then covered this trichiliocosm with his right palm; in a single kṣaṇa, all flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, banners, pennants, robes, and various exquisite musical instruments throughout the worlds of the ten directions descended from within the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi’s right palm like rain, filling the entire trichiliocosm. The flowers reached up to the knees, while the banners, pennants, and robes pervaded the void, their adornments intermingling and reflecting one another, as hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
From within that sound, a verse was uttered:
“Holding virtue and manifesting excellence, filled with a hundred blessings; Subduing Māra, endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and practice;
A great śramaṇa who skillfully expounds the essential Dharma, Capable of destroying all tainted formations throughout the ten directions.”
The sublime practice is auspiciously fulfilled; it subdues fear and removes the dust of delusion.
It can deliver humans and devas to nirvāṇa; with the ten powers and the exhaustion of outflows, the mind is signless.
He expounds the Dharma with a subtle and wondrous voice; without error or confusion, he has eliminated the three defilements.
Peerless among humans and devas, the Honored One of the Three Realms, he accords with the world and is able to bestow happiness.
Mindfulness, wisdom, and cultivation are all perfected; with the supreme ten powers, he destroys the armies of Māra.
Thus he is able to open the gate of the Deathless (amṛta); free from worldly dust and burdens, he is the sublime Tamer.
Wandering without wavering, he emerges from the multitude; with the ten powers, he tames and benefits humans and devas.
His wondrous wisdom is like space, having no dependence; the dharma-realm is unmoving, as stable as the earth.
The sound and light can destroy all the darkness of the sensory realms; therefore, I offer sublime praise to the Stainless Honored One.
The light of wisdom shines forth, replete with auspiciousness; it illuminates the Muni and eclipses the hosts of Māra.
Following sentient beings and devas throughout the three realms of existence, he manifests both composure and agitation while remaining free from攀缘 (pariṣaṇḍa/ālambana);
as the world is unimpeded and entirely like space, the Buddha thus tames the multitudes of humans and devas.
The volume of the three thousand great oceans may be fully measured; The voids of the ten directions may even be traversed on foot;
The minds of all sentient beings may be known; But the merit of the Tathāgata is difficult to conceive or fathom.

While this verse was being spoken in praise of the Buddha, the Māra Pāpīyas arrayed his fourfold army and came to where the Buddha was staying before the assembly. Manifesting himself in the form of an elder, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These two noble beings, the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha and the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, have accomplished immeasurable and boundless merit, and are further able to manifest such various extraordinary supernormal powers for the benefit of others.
"In future ages, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing this sutra, attain awakening, develop faith and understanding, and engage in contemplation?
The Buddha told Pāpīyas:
"In future ages, those who believe in this sutra will be very few in number."
Suppose a single hair-tip were divided into a hundred thousand parts, and from one such part, a single drop of water were taken from the great ocean. Noble son!
Those who believe in this sutra are like the water on the hair-tip; those who do not believe are like the waters of the great ocean.
When Māra Pāpīyas heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy; he leaped for joy, sang and danced, and departed from the assembly.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Who is this person who emerges from the assembly with such joy and exultation?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"This is the Māra Pāpīyas, who has manifested in the form of an elder and come to me, desiring to obscure the True Dharma. Hearing that those who believe in the sutras in future ages will be few, he felt joy in his heart and thus proclaimed:
'The followers of the śramaṇa Gautama are diminishing, while my own followers are many.'"
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, having conceived joy, departed from the assembly and intended to return to his celestial palace.
He thought to himself:
"The merit of this Gaganagañja, as well as that of the other bodhisattvas, and all the qualities belonging to Gautama, have all been diminished."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja immediately used his supernormal powers to restrain Māra Pāpīyān and his retinue, causing them to remain suspended in mid-air so that they could not depart.
Then he addressed Māra, saying: "Pāpīyān!
Space is unimpeded; why do you not depart quickly and return?"
At that time, Māra in the celestial palace replied:
"You see the void as being without obstruction;
yet when I look into the sky, it is entirely and only pitch-black, and I know not where to turn."
"Looking only downward, one sees the World-Honored Buddha’s light shining everywhere.
Then, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed Pāpīyas, saying: "Pāpīyas!..."
"How could it be that one whose internal mental disposition and white dharmas are pure should externally manifest darkness?
Such a principle does not exist.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, realizing that his own inner mind was constantly harboring jealousy and affliction, felt deep shame and addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer perform the deeds of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja said, "Pāpīyan!..."
This is truly rare; this is a difficult feat, to be able to give rise to such firm vows.
Pāpīyān! You and your retinue should descend to the presence of the Tathāgata to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
"Why is this? Because a Buddha of the world is difficult to encounter.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān’s mind returned to his own palace and he had no desire to listen; yet, because of the command issued by Gaganagañja, he descended from the sky with his retinue, looking up and down as he came.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O virtuous ones, are you able to proclaim the dharma-gate that transcends all māras?"
"Each of you should speak according to what you delight in.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Śailendra who spoke these words:
"If there is one who seeks to escape the realm of Māra, this itself constitutes falling into the realm of Māra."
If one knows that all objective realms are the realm of the Buddha and that there is no realm of Māra, such a person is said to follow the realm of the Buddha.
One who enters the realm of the Buddha does not even perceive the existence of a "Buddha-realm," much less any other realm.
"By means of this, a bodhisattva transcends the path of Māra; therefore, it is called the Dharma-gate of Transcending Māra.
The Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī said:

"That which the mind takes as an object of thought is the realm of Māra. If, moreover, one does not take any dharma as an object of thought, and knows that all dharmas are unobtainable, then one attains the state of being without an ālayavijñāna."
"How could there be any activity of Māra therein?
This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:

"If there is attachment, one falls into the realm of Māra; if there is no grasping or attachment, there is no contention. One does not share the same mind with either one or two [beings], let alone with all the Māras."
"If a bodhisattva realizes this dharma-gate of non-duality, they transcend the realm of Māra;
this is the bodhisattva’s dharma-gate for transcending Māra.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Ratnavīra.
"If one falls into emptiness or existence, this constitutes contention; because of such contention, one dwells within the realm of Māra.

If one does not fall into emptiness or existence, but accords with the consciousness of signs without being subject to their transformation, dwelling at the limit of signlessness, then one transcends the realm of Māra."
“This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra. The Bodhisattva Ratnacintin said:

“The Tathāgata has taught that all delusive thoughts and afflictions are like light and shadow, like reflections; they do not revolve, nor do they cease to revolve; they do not come, they do not go, and they do not abide within or without. If one knows them thus, then one does not give rise to afflictions through discrimination, nor does one extinguish afflictions through discrimination; thus one severs pervasive conceptualization and transcends the realm of Māra.”
"This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha said:
"If there is defilement or non-defilement, then there is love and hatred; [if there is no defilement or non-defilement, then there is no love or hatred]."
Because there is attachment and aversion, one falls into the conduct of Māra;
if one is free from aversion and attachment, it is called abiding in equanimity;
if one abides in equanimity, then one is detached from the various characteristics of all phenomena.
"By contemplating with equanimity because of being free from all marks, one attains this equanimity, which is called transcending the realm of Māra.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate for Transcending Māra.
The Bodhisattva Free from Treasures said:
"That which arises from 'self' is the work of Māra.
If the self were pure, how could there be any Māra? Why is this so?"

Because of the purity of the self, afflictions are pure; because of the purity of afflictions, all phenomena are pure; because of the purity of all phenomena, space is pure. One who dwells in this purity of space transcends the realm of Māra;
this is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Dharmarāja said:

“For example, when a great king has received the consecration, he possesses a vast retinue and has nothing to fear; likewise, a bodhisattva who has received the consecration takes the many jewels of the Dharma as his retinue and has no fear of any māras.”

Why is this? Because at that stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one fulfills the retinue of the Dharma-jewels—the infinite qualities of all Buddha-dharmas—and is able to uphold all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions; if a bodhisattva abides in such a mind, they transcend the realm of Māra.
This is the Dharma-gate for bodhisattvas to transcend the realm of Māra.
The Bodhisattva King of Mountain Collisions said:
"It is like when wind enters through a gap or opening and causes objects to move back and forth."
It is the same for the bodhisattva: if the mind has gaps, the mind wavers; because it wavers, Māra gains an opportunity.
Therefore, the bodhisattva guards the mind so as not to allow it to have gaps.
If the mind is without interval, then all marks are perfected; because the marks are perfected, emptiness is perfected.
This is the bodhisattva’s dharma-gate for transcending Māra.
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
“Among all views, the view of the Buddha and the view of the Dharma are the most supreme.
Herein, viewing the Buddha is not by means of form, nor by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
To see nothing at all in any phenomena is to truly see the Buddha.
To see the Dharma is to be free from mental engagement regarding all phenomena; not seeing words and not giving rise to attachment—this is truly seeing the Dharma.
"Because one attains accomplishment through seeing the Buddha and seeing the Dharma, one is able to transcend the realm of Māra.
This is the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate for transcending Māra.
The Bodhisattva Indra-net said:

"To give rise to thoughts and reflections is called the work of Māra; if a Bodhisattva, regarding those causes and conditions, should have any movement of thought or reflection that constitutes improper mental attention, all such things are the workings of Māra."
If one is unmoving and without recollection, not giving rise to discursive thought and not producing contact, then one transcends the realm of Māra.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Puṇyarājaprabha said:

"If there is an antidote, that constitutes the work of Māra; if there is no antidote, that is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). All phenomena accord with the Dharma-realm; if one enters the Dharma-realm, there is no realm of Māra."

Why is this? Because apart from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), Māra cannot be found; the dharma-realm and the realm of Māra are identical in their true suchness (tathatā) and do not differ in the slightest. When a bodhisattva understands this, they enter the single path and transcend the realm of Māra.
"This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Gandhahastin said:
"Those who lack power provide an opportunity for Māra; those who possess power do not provide an opportunity for Māra."

Those who lack power are those who experience alarm and fear upon hearing of the three gates of liberation; those who possess power are those who do not experience alarm or fear upon hearing of the three gates of liberation. Why is this?

If one realizes liberation, one will not be terrified; one who penetrates this does not give rise to terror, and the practitioner of skillful cultivation likewise does not fear. Because there is no terror, one transcends the realm of Māra.
"This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya said:
"Just as the great ocean has but one single salty taste, so too is it with the ocean of wisdom of the Buddha-dharma, which likewise has but one single flavor of the Dharma."
Whether it be the Buddha or the Dharma, all are equally empty, signless, and wishless; they are non-arising and non-originating, equal in their single characteristic and equal in their single flavor.
If a bodhisattva thoroughly understands this characteristic of the single flavor, they transcend the realm of Māra.
"This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja said,
"O worthy one!..."

Just as space transcends all objective domains and possesses no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind, so too does the Bodhisattva know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure like space.
Equalizing body, speech, and mind, they enter the light of wisdom; having attained this light of wisdom, they transcend the realm of Māra.
"This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"O worthy one!"
"Everything you have said is entirely the realm of Māra. Why is this?
The establishment of written characters is all the work of Māra; even the words of the Buddha are likewise the work of Māra."
Being without verbal expression and free from all letters, Māra can do nothing.

If there is no conceptual designation, then there is neither the view of self nor the view of letters; because there is no self, there is neither loss nor gain regarding any phenomena. One who enters in this way transcends the realm of Māra.
"This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed Māra Pāpīyān, saying:
"Have you not heard this teaching on the Dharma-gate of the realm of transcending Māra?"
Pāpīyān replied, "Indeed, I have heard it. Ākāśagarbha said:
“Pāpīyān! Do you dare to perform demonic deeds regarding this Dharma-gate on the Transcendence of the Realm of Māra, as expounded by these great bodhisattvas? He replied:
“O Great Being!

Whether I have heard in the past, or shall hear in the future, the sublime Dharma-gate that transcends the realm of Māra, I would never dare to engage in the deeds of Māra, let alone manifest its realization.”
At that time, there were four deities among the retinue of guardians of the Bodhimaṇḍa in the assembly:
first, named Uccakalī; second, named Samudgakalī;
[third, named Śvetakalī; fourth, named Mahākalī].
The third was named Gandhamādana;
the fourth was named Śraddhā.
Then these four devas addressed Pāpīyas, saying:
"In the past, when I saw you at the foot of the Bodhi tree as the Tathāgata sat upright at the site of enlightenment to attain perfect awakening, you led your retinue to create obstacles for him."

At that time, the World-Honored One, through his compassion, gentleness, precepts and learning, concentration and wisdom, steadfastness, valor, diligence, merit, and knowledge, struck the earth with his precious hand; immeasurable worlds shook at that very moment.
The World-Honored One has already subdued you and your retinue through his supernormal powers; you should bear witness to this yourself.
Why do you now further seek to perform demonic deeds against the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
"Pāpīyān! From this day forward, you and your retinue should respect the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and cultivate various offerings.

At that moment, Pāpīyān immediately manifested eighty-four thousand koṭis of precious parasols that completely covered the great assembly. Furthermore, he took various immeasurable celestial flowers, unguents, and powdered incense, scattering them over the Buddha and the entire congregation, and spoke these words:

"Whatever adornments there are in the entire realm of desire, as well as all the adornments of all Buddha-fields, even including the exquisite and rare jewels that adorn my own palace and all the wondrous articles of enjoyment in the heavens and among humans—I offer them all to the Buddha and the assembled multitude;
I also offer them as an act of worship to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja."
Then, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha said to Pāpīyas:
"You and all your retinue should each resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, Pāpīyān, together with his eighty-four thousand retinues, all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Among that assembly was a son of Māra named Durmukha, who was the foremost leader among the māras; his mind lacked reverence and faith, and he delighted in what is contrary to the Dharma, saying these words:
"What is the use of resolving one's mind upon this *bodhicitta*?"
"We shall employ various skillful means to cause such a sutra as this to disappear into the earth so that it may not be circulated.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha, saying:
"O son of good family!
Have you now heard these words of Māra?
You should proclaim the mantra syllables of the True Illumination that crush, subdue, and restrain the retinues of all Māras, rendering them powerless;
and by means of these mantra syllables of the True Illumination, you shall cause the Māra hosts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to all attain abiding in unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja then spoke this vidyā-mantra:
*Tadyathā | ambe jīve | sambe sahitānusandi-nurudra-nai-nirga-tani-namai-trayugatikāruṇi-sandhi-pati-dya* || 1 ||
Vatīti-pada-ākṣa-dharma-nirvṛti-dharmākṣi-ti uccari-nikṣi-hulu hulu hulu hulu tatkṣaṇi tathā-vanitī-śīla-nu-vatī-akṣaya-nirvāṇi-śe-kleśa-prakleśa.
namo bhūtebhyaḥ dharmāvalokanī saṃghanugame anudhye anatikramaṇīye | nīrāhaṇi mārapakṣasi yuktihṛd hṛdyaṇḍale aśvastare saviśayanugame aryya-guṇakare siddhe siddha ||
*tadānimukṣaṇu kule nīlāhani paravānināṃ dṛśanimāraprīṣṇo 'vyaśantu tadvā*.
At that time, that evil Māra, whose mind lacked pure faith and who took no delight in the Dharma, heard a voice from the sky saying:

"If there be any māras, male māras, female māras, or māra subjects who, upon hearing these mantra-words of illumination, do not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and do not abandon their demonic activities, then the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi shall shatter the crowns of their heads with a vajra-staff of great flaming fire."

At that time, the hosts of Māras were struck with terror and their hair stood on end; they all simultaneously gazed upward into the void and saw five hundred great Vajrapāṇis, each poised above the head of an evil Māra, about to strike them down.
Filled with total dread, they all at once gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a joyful countenance.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with single-minded devotion, joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The World-Honored One does not smile without cause or condition; I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Did you see these five hundred hosts of Māras give rise to the bodhicitta out of fear?”
Ānanda replied, “Indeed, I have seen it.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"When this Māra Pāpīyān attains Buddhahood, he and his retinue will each have different names in their respective worlds.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"After how much time will this Māra attain unsurpassed bodhi?
Once he has attained bodhi, what shall be the names of that Buddha and his world?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Māra Pāpīyān shall, in a future age, perform the works of Māra before ten thousand Buddhas.
From those Buddhas, he shall hear the Dharma-gate of the Vajra-throne that destroys afflictions and purifies;

furthermore, from those Buddhas, he shall hear the secret, profound rules of conduct, the merits of ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the practices of their respective domains, diligently applying skillful means. Finally, in the presence of the Tathāgata Anantavimaladhvaja, he shall perform the works of Māra; yet there, his roots of goodness will reach full maturity, his mind will attain certainty, he will obtain the radiance of all Buddha-dharmas, and he will resolve upon the Bodhicitta."

Thereafter, having passed through incalculable numbers of Buddhas, he reverently made offerings to their Buddha-dharmas, left the household life to practice the Way, protected and upheld the True Dharma, and transformed and brought to maturity immeasurable sentient beings.

After further passing through forty thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, becoming the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Suviśuddhasthitadharmaprabhāsa. His world shall be named Viśuddhapratiṣṭhita, and his kalpa shall be named Viśuddha.

Furthermore, Ānanda! In the world-system called Pure and Stable Establishment, the land is prosperous and the people are happy; the articles of enjoyment and pleasure possessed by the Tuṣita Heaven palace are exactly like the articles of enjoyment and pleasure experienced by the bodhisattvas in that country.
The lifespan of that Tathāgata Sunirmitadharmaprabha was forty intermediate kalpas; he had an assembly of sixty-four koṭis of śrāvakas and an assembly of twelve thousand great bodhisattvas.

Ānanda! Thus, all these Māras—whether male Māras, female Māras, or the subjects of Māra—all resolve to abide in the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and they are all reborn in that pure world accordingly.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa-suvihita, knowing their profound resolve, bestowed upon them all the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra: The Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha*, Scroll Seven. *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra:
The Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha*, Scroll [Seven].
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of the Great Xingshan Monastery— Grand Master of the Palace (Kaifu Yitongsī), Special Advancement (Tèjìn),

Acting Minister of State Ceremonial (Shì Hónglúqīng), Duke of Sù with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works (Sīkōng), with the posthumous title Dàjiàn, and the formal name Dàguǎngzhì— by Imperial Decree. At that time, the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors within the assembly, seeing Pāpīyas receive the prediction of Bodhi, were all struck with a sense of wonder and marveled, saying:
"How rare and extraordinary, World-Honored One!

Although those various Māras have performed demonic deeds against the Buddha’s well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, they still behold the Tathāgata; their merit has not been in vain, and they have all received the prediction that they shall realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and ultimate nirvāṇa."
"Bhagavān! Is it possible for a son of good family or a daughter of good family who enters the Buddha-dharma with a virtuous mind of faith to measure the merit and karma they thereby obtain?"
"You should know that these are all the spheres of the Buddhas, and cannot be fathomed by other śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and the various devas:
"What you have said is true and not false; it is indeed the sphere of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas."
"Good son! The mind is a phenomenon produced by conditions.

Just as when dyeing or printing cloth, some parts take on the color while other parts do not, so too it is with the mental activities of sentient beings: sometimes afflictions arise and sometimes they do not; likewise, there are those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties."
The Tathāgata establishes the Dharma according to their faculties to teach and transform them, causing them all to understand and awaken, leading them into the Dharma. Good son!
As for afflictions (*kleśa*), they have no location, nor do they have a place of abiding, nor do they accumulate; they arise from the conjunction of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
If one examines this nature of affliction according to reality, it is itself purity;
yet, with intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*), I have called it wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). If one knows it as it truly is, it is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

It is not that one perceives the views of the heterodox and the orthodox as actually existing; rather, if one knows that neither heterodox nor orthodox views give rise to grasping within oneself, this is called entering the path of right view.
Good son! Afflictions are like a skin; their nature is purity. Because they are shrouded by them, the power of the clarity of wisdom is weak, and for this reason, one does not see fundamental purity.
Furthermore, that which possesses conceptual discrimination is called affliction (*kleśa*), while that which is free from conceptual discrimination is called the nature of purity (*viśuddha-dhātu*).
Son of good family!
For example, the great earth rests upon water; water rests upon wind; wind rests upon space; yet within these four elements, space has no support.

Because space is indestructible, immovable, and without accumulation—since it has no accumulation—it abides in accordance with the self-nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; therefore, the triple world is not long-lasting and does not abide, being impermanent and subject to change, whereas the realm of space is not.
In this way, the aggregates, bases, and elements abide dependent upon karma and afflictions;
karma and afflictions abide dependent upon improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*);
and improper mental attention abides dependent upon the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*).

This pure mind is not defiled by adventitious afflictions; all non-rational mental engagements (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), karma, afflictions, aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) exist solely through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
If these causes and conditions are lacking, they do not arise.
That nature of purity has no causes or conditions, nor does it involve any combination; it neither arises nor ceases, being like the nature of space.

Non-reflective mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is like the wind, karma and afflictions are like water, and the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are like earth. Because of this, all phenomena lack solidity; they have no fundamental abiding and are primordially pure.
"Good son! This is called the gateway of the light of the naturally pure dharma.
Because bodhisattvas realize this dharma-gateway, they are not defiled by any of the stains of afflictions, nor do they conceptualize this pure dharma."
Because it is non-conceptual, one extinguishes all discursive thoughts, investigations, and mental preoccupations, thereby realizing the nature of purity;
by realizing this purity, one transcends the realm of Māra;
and by transcending the realm of Māra, one dwells securely in the realm of the Buddhas.
By abiding in the realm of the Buddha, one transcends the realm of sentient beings and enters the immovable dharma-realm;
by entering the immovable, pure dharma-realm, one enters the state of equality and non-differentiation,
which is termed the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable bodhisattvas became entirely free from all obscurations of karma and afflictions and all entanglements of defilement, and they realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the lay follower Śrīgupta rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having now heard from the Buddha this Dharma-gate of the pure liberation, my doubts and regrets have been instantly eliminated. Why is this?

In the past, I once prepared a deep and great fire pit and mixed poison into food, harboring harmful intentions toward the Tathāgata. Yet the World-Honored One’s majestic virtue remained unharmed; although he preached the Dharma for me and I had a slight degree of faith and inclination, my mind still harbored doubts and I continued to feel regret.

Now, in the presence of the Buddha, I have again heard this most profound sutra; the net of doubt has been entirely removed, my mind is free from sorrow or regret, and having attained the light of the Dharma, I have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
“World-Honored One!
At this moment, I am called one of great benefit and have attained extraordinary advantage.
At that time, the Buddha praised the elder Śrīgupta, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

Because you have now heard the Dharma I have preached and have given rise to pure faith and joy, by this cause and condition you shall serve, revere, and make offerings to all the Buddhas throughout the Bhadrakalpa. Under those Buddhas, you shall extensively cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and uphold the True Dharma. After the passing of seven million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Sarvavaraṇaviṣkambhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.”

At that time, the lay follower Śrīgupta, having heard that the Buddha had bestowed upon him the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented occurrence. He immediately removed his magnificent and exquisite necklaces and scattered them over the Buddha, saying these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Now, within my residence there are four great treasuries, filled with immeasurable gold and jewels.
With the first treasury, I bestow gifts upon my wife, children, servants, and attendants;
with the second treasury, I bestow gifts upon all who are poor, lowly, solitary, and beggars."
The third great treasury was given to all the bhikṣus who come and go, as well as to the Saṃgha of the four quarters;
the fourth great treasury was offered to the Tathāgata and his principal bhikṣus.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will cause me to swiftly attain the accomplishment of the merit of giving characterized by non-abiding.
I now wish to leave the household life and receive the precepts within the well-expounded Vinaya of the Tathāgata, in order to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya).
Thereupon, the World-Honored One granted him permission to leave the household life.
At that time, the upāsaka Śrīgupta immediately left the household life and received full ordination.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which the Tathāgata has accumulated over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas—profound and difficult to attain—who shall uphold it after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa?”

At that time, there were sixty koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within that assembly who rose from their seats, joined their palms in homage to the Buddha, and with one voice in unison spoke these verses:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, We shall all be able,
Without sparing our own bodies or lives, To protect and uphold the Buddha’s true Dharma."
Renouncing all fame and profit, And departing from all kinsmen;
Without abandoning this True Dharma, For the sake of realizing Buddha-wisdom.
Even when subjected to revilement and abuse, Or harsh and unwholesome speech,
Because they protect the True Dharma, they are able to endure all such things:
contempt and derision, slander and lack of praise—
they endure all these for the sake of upholding this sutra.
In the future, there will be bhikṣus who dwell upon signs and long for fame and profit;
they will become the companions of Māra and create obstacles to the Dharma.
Those who destroy the precepts and subvert the Dharma will draw near to worldly people.
Because of their greedy attachment to offerings, they do not single-mindedly seek the True Dharma.
They delight in practicing the ways of external paths; ignorant and harboring arrogance, they praise themselves and disturb those who dwell in tranquility.
Abandoning the forest hermitage, they constantly delight in profitless talk;
they take pleasure in practicing evil incantations and remain attached to the view of a self;
or they delight in managing monastic affairs and create obstacles for the Saṃgha.
Abandoning meditative concentration and recitation, they become entangled in worldly affairs;
constantly seeking gain and offerings, they take no pleasure in the precepts or extensive learning;
though they practice giving, their minds are always harboring defilements.
They calculate various notions of a self, yet only think of begging for food;
they delight in visiting the homes of laypeople to discuss worldly matters;
they concern themselves with farming and various secular affairs, as well as trade and commerce.
Delighting in such deeds, they claim for themselves the title of śramaṇa;
yet they remain stubbornly attached to the various realms of existence and cling to manifold views.
When hearing the teaching on the Dharma of true emptiness, they are struck with fear as if facing a deep abyss.
Disbelieving in the fruit of karma, they claim there is no retribution in future lives;
they utter only words of falsehood, declaring what is not Dharma to be Dharma.
In this degenerate age, these bhikṣus possess power equal to that of kings.
In this age of the final dharma, I shall uphold the True Dharma.
Regarding the various sūtras, they neither seek nor read them;
each takes their own views as the teacher, clinging to differences and mutually refuting one another.
Regarding all profound sūtras that accord with liberation,
their minds take no pleasure in speaking of such true Dharma; instead,
they delight in worldly treatises and praise them as rare and marvelous.
Such evil persons as these will, before long, cause the True Dharma to perish.
The subtle and profound sutras, skillful in both letter and meaning,
shall all be destroyed during that age of evil.
When kings act contrary to the Dharma and lack the Way, the common people all flee in exile;
in such an evil age, there is none who does not harbor fear.
We are all fully capable of dwelling within such a degenerate age.
They shall uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma spoken by the Buddha;
even toward sentient beings who destroy the True Dharma,
they shall maintain a mind of loving-kindness and give rise to compassion, by virtue of upholding this sutra.
If I see one who upholds the precepts yet gives rise to craving and attachment, I,
out of compassion, employ skillful means to cause them to abandon it.
If I see one with an evil mind who slanders and destroys the True Dharma;
For their sake, arouse compassion so that they may see my joy;
protect those people according to your strength, refrain from harsh or evil speech,
and do not even converse with them, for they shall then abide in peace by themselves.
Furthermore, by means of the four means of attraction, I shall bring those people to maturity;
I shall cause them to awaken and realize the fault of their delusions.
I shall abandon the clamor and bustle of society and dwell in an araṇya.
Not associating with worldly affairs, like a deer living in freedom;
having few desires and being content, practicing the four noble lineages;
abiding in the precepts and the dhūtas, endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom.
I shall practice without interval for the sake of gentle, tranquil liberation;
when entering a village, I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
If there are those who seek the Dharma, I shall cause them to dwell far away in secluded places.
Maintaining silence and practicing self-cultivation, always dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma;
if there should be anyone present who commits various transgressions,
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I shall examine my own physical conduct.
Abiding in the Dharma, ever tranquil, whether toward those who show respect or those who do not;
as firm as Mount Sumeru, unstained by worldly dharmas—
may I become a guide for those bhikṣus who have violated the precepts.
When others address one with harsh words, observe that this is the ripening of one's own karma;
do not harbor a mind of retaliation, nor conceive thoughts of harming others.
Always abide in the True Dharma, thinking: "This is not something I ought to do."
I am a śramaṇa, yet they lack the conduct of a śramaṇa;
upon hearing my correct instruction, they slander the sūtras,
or even cut off my ears and nose, and they take no pleasure in seeing me.
If one hears the true awakening, one slanders the True Dharma.
In the future, there will be bhikṣus who uphold the True Dharma;
[others] will create obstacles for them, not allowing them to hear the True Dharma.
Regarding divisive speech toward the King and the sowing of discord within the great assembly,
we shall, by the power of the Buddha, cause all to hear the Dharma.
Even in that evil age, we would rather sacrifice our own bodies and lives.
For the sake of upholding the True Dharma, one brings benefit to sentient beings;
first understanding the inclinations of others, one subsequently engages them in conversation.
During the time of future great terrors, one shall abide in this practice of truth.
I ask the Eye of the World, the Dharma King, the Honored One of Radiance:
"By upholding this sutra, how much merit will one obtain?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Ākāśagarbha and all the other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, saying:
“Good son! Suppose one world-system in the eastern direction were divided into thirteen billion great trichiliocosms;

likewise, each of the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir were each divided into thirteen billion great trichiliocosms, and all such worlds were ground down until they became dust.
Furthermore, let one mote of dust represent one world-system.

Suppose there were a person who, starting from the eastern direction, passed through as many world-systems as there are motes of dust and dropped a single mote; then, proceeding further east, passed through another as many world-systems as there are motes of dust and dropped another mote. In this manner, they continued in succession until all those motes of dust were exhausted.
In the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, there is no limit; it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
"Good son! What do you think?
Do you know the number of these minute particles of dust that have been scattered throughout the worlds of the ten directions?"
"No, World-Honored One! Such worlds of atoms can only be thoroughly understood by the Tathāgata through his unimpeded wisdom; no one else is able to know them."
The Buddha said, "Good son!

Suppose all these worlds—both those where atoms were placed and those where they were not—are entirely transformed into a great city with surrounding walls, reaching from the Peak of Existence above down to the limits of the water below; and suppose this city were filled to the brim with pure mustard seeds."
"Take a single mustard seed as one Buddha-world.
Good son, what do you think?"
"Would these worlds of mustard seeds be considered many?
"Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Good son! In this way, regarding these mustard seeds and all those worlds, I know their number; I know them by the hundreds, I know them by the thousands, and even up to the *kiṃkara*, *mimira*, and *akṣobhya* [calculations].”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for the sake of seeking awakening, fill as many worlds as those [mentioned] with the seven treasures and bestow them as gifts upon as many Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwelling in the Dharma of Merit as there are mustard seeds, and honor and make offerings to them;
yet if another person, upon hearing this profound and subtle sūtra, is able to give rise to pure faith and patient acceptance, the merit they obtain will surpass the former merit.
If, on the other hand, there were someone who practiced unobstructed giving for as many times as there are mustard seeds;

or if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, gives rise to a mind free from hindrance toward all sentient beings and abides in the patience of gentleness, contemplating with focused mindfulness for even the duration of seven steps—the merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former.

Furthermore, if there were someone who cultivated various meritorious deeds and thereby attained the status of as many lords of gods, Śakras, Great Brahmā Kings, and Cakravartin kings as there are mustard seeds;

yet another person might receive and uphold this sutra, being able to know impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, nirvana, and tranquility. Having known these things, they give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings and, in order that the lineage of the Three Jewels may not be severed, they resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The merit of such a person surpasses the former merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the Tathāgata will empower this sutra so that, in the future age of the final dharma, it may be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, saying: "Good son!
I entrust this Dharma to the Four Heavenly Kings."
Why is this? It is because these four kings protect and sustain the world, causing this Dharma to remain long in the world and to be widely disseminated.
I shall now further empower the Four Great Heavenly Kings with subtle and wondrous mantras.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
*Tadyathā | duduḷi tṛtṛvajrapati tṛvajra laṅkari āvartani śame śamabhati saṃdhimukhi nigarha pracchada āḥ* |||1||

Nunara unara vigama samāpatti poṭa śuddhi poṭa nugama poṭa śuddhi prajñā mukhya ārya kūli | bhūta-ru-kṣe aniṣya-ccha maṇiṣya-ccha tama-sya-ccha ta-tap-sya-ccha buddha-bhāna dharma-nu-sandi ārya-gaṇa nuga-ma ||
Anaryani-gata-niṛ-stha-prasanna iśvara-panaruka-ṣṭri-kṛtā-anulakṣa-yantu imaṃ dharma-sandi-vijaya-tu nirukti-niḥśeṣa-pratīkṣatu.
*Dharmadhāraṇī*. At that time, [the Four Great Kings said]:
"World-Honored One!
We, the four kings, shall protect and uphold this sutra, ensuring that it remains in the world for a long time into the future."
Wherever this sūtra is circulated, I shall be able to sustain it so that no gods, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, or garuḍas who take no delight in the Dharma can create obstacles;
should there be benevolent deities who delight in the Dharma, I shall cause their minds to attain tranquility;

and should there be any Dharma masters at a Dharma assembly who forget the words and phrases, I shall enable them to remember and uphold them, granting them eloquence and increasing their wisdom and understanding.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
“Excellent, excellent!
You Four Kings are all my sons, born through transformation from the Dharma.”
"By virtue of the causal conditions of my exhorting you to protect the True Dharma, you have become a celestial king; you shall transcend the world and swiftly realize parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja, saying: "Good son!"
"I shall now likewise empower Śakra with mantras, causing him to protect this sutra so that it may long abide in the world.
He spoke the mantra, saying:
"Tadyathā: śuddhe śubhamati śubhavyūhe..."
Nāḍre nāriṇai dūriṇai nāme śame upaśame kuve miṅ kṛle asumukhe dhāraṇi arane śuśruḥ śrāvahiṭi arbini bina saṃde same samavati samarashmi.
Haya-hūhū-khe-khe-kurukulle anatikramaṇīyavajra-mahā-vāsava-praṣṭhe ākhyāta-śakra-nirvāṇa-mantra-nātha-tāya.
*nāvara-makuṭa-dhara iśvara mūrdha-āvahana nivasi svāhā.* At that time, having heard this mantra, Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; the palace where he dwelt shook all over.
Immediately, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of attendants, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We devas shall protect this sutra, widely proclaiming and disseminating it throughout Jambudvīpa so that beings may practice it."

If there be any Dharma masters who receive and uphold this sutra, we, along with our retinues, shall collectively protect them, ensuring they are free from affliction and distress, causing them to experience joy and give rise to pure faith and delight; may all who receive and uphold this sutra achieve fulfillment and be adorned by the Dharma.

Whenever there is a place where the Dharma is being taught—in a royal city, a town, or a village—I shall lead my retinue and go together to that place where the Dharma teacher resides to provide him with protection.
If there are those who treat that Dharma master with contempt or revile him with anger, I shall cause them to give rise to a pure mind;
if there are various māras who create obstacles and difficulties, I shall provide protection for him, causing them all to retreat and disperse so that they find no opportunity.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"

You shall attain sublime mastery over the heavens and abide in mastery over the Dharma; you will be able to roar the lion’s roar in the protection and upholding of the True Dharma at the abodes of all Buddhas. Why is this?
"Kauśika! By being able to receive and uphold the true Dharma of even a single Buddha, one is able to protect the true Dharma spoken by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahā-ākāśagarbha, saying:
“Good son! For the sake of Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, I have explained the meaning of the majestic mantra syllables.
By virtue of this mantra, Mahābrahmā shall protect and uphold this sutra.”
Then he spoke the mantra, saying:
